additional_notes: Used in formal questions with inversion: verb (avoir in the present: « a ») + -t- (a linking sound added when the verb ends in a vowel) + subject pronoun « il » (he/it). Common in written French and formal speech. It can appear in direct questions (« A-t-il… ? ») and in embedded/indirect-style questions after a question word (« Où les a-t-il… ? », « Combien a-t-il… ? »).
target_language_example: A-t-il déjà fini ses devoirs ?
native_language_example: Has he already finished his homework?

additional_notes: Passé composé of acheter (“to buy”) with avoir. Used with il/elle/on or a singular noun as the subject. In English, it often translates simply as “bought.”
target_language_example: Paul a acheté du pain ce matin.
native_language_example: Paul bought some bread this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « acheter » with « avoir »: « il/elle a acheté … » = “he/she bought/has bought …”. « un » changes to « une » before a feminine noun (e.g., « elle a acheté une robe »). With « avoir », « acheté » usually doesn’t change here because the direct object comes after it.
target_language_example: Il a acheté un cadeau pour son frère.
native_language_example: He bought a gift for his brother.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « aider » (to help): « il/elle/on a aidé » = “he/she/one helped / has helped.” Often followed by « à » + infinitive to say what someone helped with: « a aidé à marcher » (helped [someone] to walk), « a aidé à déménager » (helped [someone] move).
target_language_example: Elle a aidé sa sœur à faire ses devoirs.
native_language_example: She helped her sister do her homework.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "appeler" with "avoir": "il/elle/on a appelé" = "he/she/one called" or "has called". Used for making a phone call or calling someone (e.g., calling a friend, calling for someone). Doesn’t mean "appealed" in the English sense.
target_language_example: Il a appelé son ami ce matin.
native_language_example: He called his friend this morning.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « changer » with « avoir » (3rd-person singular: he/she/it changed). Often used with « tout a changé » = “everything changed.” Common pattern: « changer de + noun » = “to change (jobs/direction/etc.)”, e.g., « Il a changé de poste » (He changed jobs/positions).
target_language_example: Après son déménagement, tout a changé.
native_language_example: After his move, everything changed.

additional_notes: Past tense of "commencer" with "avoir" (il/elle/on a commencé à...). It is followed by an infinitive verb to say someone started doing something: "a commencé à + infinitive". For other subjects, change "a" (e.g., "j'ai commencé à", "ils ont commencé à").
target_language_example: Il a commencé à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: It started to rain.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « disparaître » (auxiliary « avoir » + past participle « disparu »). Used for someone/something that is no longer there; for a person it can mean they went missing or vanished (and in some contexts can imply they died, especially in news-style language).
target_language_example: Mon passeport a disparu hier soir.
native_language_example: My passport disappeared last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of dire with il/elle/on or a singular noun as the subject. It often translates as simple past in English: Tom a dit = Tom said. With an indirect object, it can also mean "told": Tom a dit à Marie la vérité = Tom told Marie the truth.
target_language_example: Paul a dit qu'il viendrait demain.
native_language_example: Paul said that he would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Third-person singular passé composé of dire + que. It is used to report what a person or thing said: after a noun, or after il/elle/on. In natural French, que often shortens to qu' before a vowel.
target_language_example: Paul a dit que tout allait bien.
native_language_example: Paul said that everything was fine.

additional_notes: Passé composé of donner. It is used for both concrete and abstract meanings: giving something, giving an order, giving permission, or giving agreement. In English, it is often translated as simple past ('gave') rather than present perfect ('has given').
target_language_example: Elle m'a donné un livre hier.
native_language_example: She gave me a book yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone made a decision to do something: « il/elle/on + a décidé de + infinitive ». This is the passé composé of « décider » and is common for talking about a decision that has been made (often recently). Note: « a décidé de » is 3rd-person singular (he/she/one has decided to).
target_language_example: Tom a décidé de vendre sa maison.
native_language_example: Tom decided to sell his house.

additional_notes: Common in the passé composé: a is the 3rd-person singular form of avoir used with a past participle (for il, elle, on, or a singular noun), and déjà means "already." For other subjects, the auxiliary changes: j'ai déjà, tu as déjà, ils ont déjà, etc.
target_language_example: Elle a déjà vu ce film.
native_language_example: She has already seen this movie.

additional_notes: Passé composé of devoir for il/elle/on or a singular noun. It is usually followed by an infinitive. It can express past necessity ("had to") or a strong guess about the past ("must have"), depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a dû attendre longtemps.
native_language_example: He had to wait a long time.

additional_notes: Passé composé of entendre with il/elle/on. It is used for completed actions in the past, often translated as either "heard" or "has heard" depending on context. It can be followed by a thing heard, or by an infinitive: "a entendu le chien aboyer" = "heard the dog bark." In "en a entendu parler," it means "heard about it."
target_language_example: Marie a entendu un bruit étrange dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: Marie heard a strange noise in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « envoyer » with « avoir »: « il/elle/on a envoyé » = “he/she/one sent/has sent.” Often followed by a direct object (« a envoyé une lettre »). You can also use « envoyer + someone + infinitive » to mean “to send someone to do something”: « Elle a envoyé son fils chercher un médecin » = “She sent her son to look for a doctor.”
target_language_example: Il m'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent me a message last night.

additional_notes: “a essayé de” is the passé composé of “essayer de” and means someone tried (in the past) to do something. It is followed by an infinitive verb: “a essayé de + verb” (e.g., “a essayé de cacher…” = “tried to hide…”). With a pronoun, the pronoun goes before the infinitive: “a essayé de le faire” = “tried to do it.”
target_language_example: Elle a essayé de m’appeler, mais je n’ai pas répondu.
native_language_example: She tried to call me, but I didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Passé composé of avoir with a singular subject (il/elle/on or a singular noun). In natural English it is often translated as simple past 'had', though literally it is 'has had'. Depending on context, it can also mean 'got' or appear in common expressions like a eu raison ('was right').
target_language_example: Tom a eu une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Tom had a good idea.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with a singular subject (il/elle/on or a singular noun). It often means "did" or "made," but the exact English translation depends on the expression: for example, faire une erreur = "make a mistake," and faire partie de = "be part of."
target_language_example: Paul a fait un gâteau pour sa sœur.
native_language_example: Paul made a cake for his sister.

additional_notes: Part of the passé composé of faire with a singular subject: "X a fait un...". It is followed by a masculine singular noun. The exact English verb often depends on the noun that follows: faire un câlin = give a hug, faire un cauchemar = have a nightmare. With a feminine noun, it becomes "a fait une".
target_language_example: Paul a fait un dessin pour sa mère.
native_language_example: Paul made a drawing for his mother.

additional_notes: "a fait" is the passé composé of "faire" (to do / to make): "il/elle a fait" = "he/she did" (literally "has done"). "ça" means "that/it" and refers to a specific action or thing mentioned or understood from context. You can change the subject: "j’ai fait ça" (I did that), "tu as fait ça" (you did that), etc.
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce qu’il a fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did he do that?

additional_notes: Passé composé of « finir » (to finish), 3rd person singular with « avoir »: « il/elle/on a fini ». Use « a fini » + direct object (e.g., « a fini le travail », « a fini ses études ») or « a fini de » + infinitive to mean “finished doing” something (e.g., « a fini de parler »). It can also stand alone to mean “is/was done” when the context is clear (e.g., « Rima a fini. »).
target_language_example: Quand il a fini de parler, il y a eu un silence.
native_language_example: When he finished speaking, there was a silence.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *gagner* with *avoir*: **il/elle/on a gagné** = “he/she/one won”. Often used for winning a game/competition (**gagner un match, un prix**). Note: although *gagner* can sometimes mean “earn” (money), **a gagné** is very often “won” in everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a gagné le match hier soir.
native_language_example: She won the match last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « laisser » (avoir + laissé). Often means “left” (forgot/abandoned: « Elle a laissé son téléphone »), “left behind” as a result/trace (« La blessure a laissé une cicatrice »; « Son discours a laissé une marque »), “let/allowed” (« Qui vous a laissé entrer ? »), or “left (to someone) / bequeathed” in a will (« Il lui a laissé la maison »).
target_language_example: Il a laissé ses clés sur la table.
native_language_example: He left his keys on the table.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "manger" (to eat): "[he/she/it] a mangé". It’s formed with the present of "avoir" (a) + past participle (mangé). Used for a completed action in the past; in English it can be "ate" or "has eaten" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a mangé trop vite.
native_language_example: He ate too fast.

additional_notes: Passé composé of mettre with il/elle/on. It often translates as simple past English: 'he/she/it put.' Used for placing something somewhere, and in some contexts for 'put on' clothes or 'set' something like a table or password.
target_language_example: Elle a mis son téléphone dans son sac.
native_language_example: She put her phone in her bag.

additional_notes: "a passé" is the passé composé of "passer" (he/she/it spent). It’s commonly used with a duration or time period to say how someone spent time: "passer la soirée/la journée" (spend the evening/the day), "passer des années" (spend years). You can add "avec" (with someone) or a place with "à/en" (at/in): "Il a passé la soirée avec ses amis"; "Elle a passé deux ans en France"; "Il a passé trois ans en prison" (= he served three years in prison). Note that "passer" can also mean "to pass" in other contexts, so the meaning depends on what follows.
target_language_example: Sami a passé toute la soirée avec Layla.
native_language_example: Sami spent the whole evening with Layla.

additional_notes: Passé composé of perdre ('to lose'). Used for misplacing something, losing sight of someone, or saying something has diminished, as in a perdu de son éclat ('has lost some of its shine').
target_language_example: Il a perdu son portefeuille dans le train.
native_language_example: He lost his wallet on the train.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre with a singular subject (il/elle/on). It often translates as either simple past or present perfect in English, depending on context. It also appears in common expressions like a pris soin de ('took care of') and a pris le temps de ('took the time to').
target_language_example: Elle a pris le bus ce matin.
native_language_example: She took the bus this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the verb « quitter » = to leave (a place/someone). It’s used with a direct object: « quitter la table / la ville / Boston / les lieux » (no preposition like “from”). Beware: « quitter » is a false friend of English “to quit” (it usually means “to leave,” not “to stop doing”).
target_language_example: Il a quitté la maison très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He left the house very early this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *regarder* with *avoir*: *[subject] + a + regardé* = “(he/she) watched/looked.” Often followed by a direct object (*a regardé la télévision*, *a regardé le sol*) and can also be used with adverbs (*a regardé nerveusement*, *a regardé à nouveau*). Note: *regardé* looks like English “regarded,” but usually means “looked (at)” or “watched” in everyday French.
target_language_example: Il a regardé le film hier soir.
native_language_example: He watched the movie last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "recevoir" (to receive): subject + "a" + "reçu" + object. Used for something someone received in the past (orders, calls, praise, gifts, a letter, etc.). In formal writing you may see "a reçu" translated as "has received" (present perfect) or "received" (simple past), depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle a reçu un message important hier.
native_language_example: She received an important message yesterday.

additional_notes: Passé composé of trouver with il/elle/on or a singular noun subject. In everyday English, it is often translated simply as "found" rather than "has found."
target_language_example: Elle a trouvé ses clés sous le canapé.
native_language_example: She found her keys under the sofa.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **tuer**: **avoir (conjugated) + tué**. Often translates as simple past in English (“killed”), even though it’s literally “has killed.” With **avoir**, **tué** usually doesn’t change form; it only agrees if a direct object comes before the verb (e.g., *La souris qu’il a tuée*).
target_language_example: Il a tué le moteur avant de descendre de la voiture.
native_language_example: He turned off the engine before getting out of the car.

additional_notes: Passé composé of « écrire » (to write): « il/elle/on a écrit ». Used for a completed action in the past (often like simple past “wrote” in English, or “has written” depending on context). Can also refer to what is written somewhere: « Qu'est-ce qu'il y a écrit ? » = “What does it say (what’s written there)?”
target_language_example: Elle a écrit un email à son professeur.
native_language_example: She wrote an email to her teacher.

additional_notes: Form of être used with a singular subject. It often appears in the passive voice with another past participle: a été + past participle = 'was/has been ...'. Depending on context, English often uses simple past ('was') rather than the literal 'has been'.
target_language_example: La porte a été fermée trop tôt.
native_language_example: The door was closed too early.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is singular and the verb is avoir in the form a: il/elle/on a, or a singular noun like Marie or ce magasin. It is followed by a noun to say someone or something has a large quantity of something. With other subjects, a changes: j'ai beaucoup de, tu as beaucoup de, nous avons beaucoup de, etc.
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de travail aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She has a lot of work today.

meaning: as a pair; together (the two of us)
additional_notes: Means “two people together” (not the number 2). Often used after a verb to say you do something as a couple/pair: aller à deux, travailler à deux, voyager à deux. Also used in expressions like “un dîner à deux” (a dinner for two). Note: in correct French spelling, it’s “à deux” with a grave accent.
target_language_example: On peut y aller à deux si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can go there together (just the two of us) if you want.

additional_notes: Used with an (optional) subject to say someone is afraid. Common patterns: "avoir peur de + noun" (a peur de tous les docteurs = is afraid of all doctors) and "avoir peur de + infinitive" (a peur de tomber / de le faire = is afraid to fall / to do it). "a" is the present tense for il/elle/on (he/she/one) in "avoir"; other forms: "j'ai peur de", "tu as peur de", "nous avons peur de", "vous avez peur de", "ils/elles ont peur de".
target_language_example: Il a peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: He is afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: "a" is the present tense (3rd person singular) of "avoir" (to have). "une" is used before a feminine singular noun (une amie, une vitesse, une carrière). In negatives, it becomes "n’a pas une..." or more commonly "n’a pas de..." (e.g., "Il n’a pas d’amie ici.").
target_language_example: Elle a une voiture rouge.
native_language_example: She has a red car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "adorer" + "les" (= "the" for plural nouns). In everyday French, "adorer" often means "to really love" (not necessarily romantic). The noun after "les" is plural (e.g., les gâteaux = cakes).
target_language_example: J'adore les films d'aventure.
native_language_example: I love adventure movies.

additional_notes: Inverted form of "j’ai" used to ask a question (verb before subject): "Ai-je… ?" = "Have I…?" / often "Did I…?" in English depending on context. It’s most common in formal speech and writing; in everyday conversation people often use "est-ce que j’ai… ?" or intonation: "J’ai… ?".
target_language_example: Ai-je bien compris ?
native_language_example: Did I understand correctly?

additional_notes: Used to express liking (a moderate, friendly positive feeling) without the stronger sense of “aimer” alone (which can mean “to love”). Common patterns: “J’aime bien + noun” (I quite like + noun) or “J’aime bien + infinitive” (I like to + verb). Can also soften opinions: “J’aime bien, mais…” (I like it, but…).
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film, mais je ne l'adore pas.
native_language_example: I like this movie, but I don’t love it.

additional_notes: Inversion form of the question "tu aimes…?" (verb + subject). It’s the present tense of "aimer" with "tu": "aimes" + "-tu". Common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear "Tu aimes… ?" or "Est-ce que tu aimes… ?". Use "aimer" for liking things (food, hobbies) and also for loving people; context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Aimes-tu la musique classique ?
native_language_example: Do you like classical music?

additional_notes: Formal or polite question form using inversion: « aimez-vous + noun/infinitive ? ». Often translated as “Do you like…?” (and sometimes “Do you love…?” depending on context). In everyday casual speech, people often use « vous aimez… ? » or « est-ce que vous aimez… ? » instead. Can also be used alone after a choice: « Lequel aimez-vous ? » = “Which one do you like?”
target_language_example: Aimez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

meaning: to go with; to match; to be compatible with
additional_notes: Used to say that two things match well or are compatible (clothes, colors, accessories, styles, etc.). It can also mean that something ‘goes with’ something else in a more general sense (fits, suits). In the negative ("ne pas aller avec"), it means something doesn’t match or doesn’t work well together.
target_language_example: Il choisit une paire de chaussettes pour aller avec son costume.
native_language_example: He chooses a pair of socks to go with his suit.

additional_notes: Used when you leave to fetch someone or something and bring them/it back (or at least retrieve them/it). Common with objects (mon portefeuille, une glace) and people (Maria, grand-mère). Literally it’s “to go + look for,” but in everyday French it often means “go get/pick up.”
target_language_example: Je vais aller chercher les enfants à l’école.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up the kids from school.

meaning: to go to; to go on
additional_notes: Used with en before many places, especially feminine countries, regions, and continents (for example en France, en Europe). It also appears in some set expressions like aller en promenade, where it means going on an activity or outing.
target_language_example: Pourquoi veux-tu aller en Europe ?
native_language_example: Why do you want to go to Europe?

additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase meaning to go and see someone or something. With a person, it often means "go see" or "go visit"; with a film or show, it means "go watch"; and without a direct object, it can mean "go check" or "go see for oneself."
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir le médecin demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: In standard French, the usual form is « y aller », not « aller y ». The sequence « aller y » is generally not used in normal sentence word order, so this entry is best understood as a reference to the components of the expression rather than a standard standalone phrase. In commands, related forms like « vas-y » or « allez-y » can mean « go ahead ».
target_language_example: On dit « y aller », pas « aller y » en français standard.
native_language_example: People say "y aller," not "aller y" in standard French.

additional_notes: Used for going to a place or destination. Often contracts with articles: à + le = au, à + les = aux (for example, aller au cinéma, aller aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Peux-tu aller à la mer demain ?
native_language_example: Can you go to the seaside tomorrow?

additional_notes: Imperative of "aller" + the pronoun "y" ("there"). Often used to encourage or invite someone to do something: "Allez-y !" = "Go ahead!" You can repeat it for emphasis ("Allez-y, allez-y"). Used with both singular and plural "you" (same spelling for "tu" and "vous" forms here); context tells which one.
target_language_example: Allez-y, je vous écoute.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’m listening.

additional_notes: Informal spoken expression (often written “allez, va”). Used to (1) give in or agree after hesitation (“Okay then, fine.”) or (2) encourage someone to continue or do something (“Go on then.”). Built from imperatives of *aller* (“allez” + “va”), but the overall meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Allez va, je t'accompagne jusqu'à la gare.
native_language_example: All right then, I'll walk you to the station.

additional_notes: Used to talk about romantic love toward a person: « être amoureux/amoureuse de + someone ». The adjective agrees with the subject: amoureux (male), amoureuse (female). Often used with intensifiers like « follement » (madly).
target_language_example: Je suis amoureux de toi depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (apprendre à + infinitive) to mean “learn to do something.” It can also mean “teach someone to do something,” often with an indirect object (e.g., Je peux t’apprendre à… / Je peux vous apprendre à…).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre à nager.
native_language_example: I want to learn to swim.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a time/event that happens later than something else. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: après le + noun (après le dîner). For feminine use "après la", for plural "après les", and before a vowel or silent h use "après l’".
target_language_example: On se verra après le travail.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other after work.

additional_notes: With a place or abstract noun, arriver à often means "arrive at" or "reach" (for example, arriver à la station, arriver à une conclusion). With an infinitive, it often means "manage to" or "succeed in" doing something: je n'arrive pas à comprendre = "I can't manage to understand."
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend-il pour arriver à la station ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to arrive at the station?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to tell one person to stop doing something. arrête is the tu-form imperative; with vous, use arrêtez de.
target_language_example: Arrête de te plaindre.
native_language_example: Stop complaining.

additional_notes: Question form of tu as, made with inversion. It is common in more formal or written yes/no questions. When followed by a past participle, English often translates it as 'did you ... ?' rather than 'have you ... ?'.
target_language_example: As-tu fini tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you finish your homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question in the past about something that has happened (or been done) at least once. Literally it’s the inversion question form of "tu as" (= "have you") + "déjà" (= "already"). In questions, "déjà" often translates as "ever" (experience up to now): "As-tu déjà… ?" = "Have you ever… ?" It can also be "already" when asking if something is done yet: "As-tu déjà pris ton médicament ?" = "Have you taken your medicine already?"
target_language_example: As-tu déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

additional_notes: Question form of tu as (“you have”), used when speaking to one person informally. This inverted form with a hyphen is common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday conversation, tu as ... ? is often more common.
target_language_example: As-tu les clés ?
native_language_example: Do you have the keys?

additional_notes: Used as a conversation transition to introduce a new question or bring up something you just remembered (similar to “by the way…”). It can also mean “actually” in the sense of “speaking of the facts / in reality,” but very often it’s just a topic-changer. Often placed at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma: “Au fait, …”.
target_language_example: Au fait, tu as des nouvelles de Marie ?
native_language_example: By the way, have you heard from Marie?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/rester (au lit = in bed) and aller (aller au lit = go to bed). Also used in expressions like faire pipi au lit (“wet the bed”).
target_language_example: Je suis malade, alors je reste au lit aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm sick, so I'm staying in bed today.

additional_notes: Often used after a superlative: « le/la plus … au monde » = “the most … in the world.” Also appears in the expression « mettre au monde » = “to give birth (to),” literally “to bring into the world” (e.g., « Elle a mis au monde un garçon. »).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur restaurant au monde.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the world.

additional_notes: Used to place something in a past era, often before a person, period, or generation: au temps de Napoléon, au temps de mes grands-parents. It often refers to 'back when' something was the case.
target_language_example: Au temps de mes grands-parents, il n'y avait pas d'internet.
native_language_example: In my grandparents' time, there was no internet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about quantity/degree. Common patterns: (1) with a verb: "autant que tu veux/peux" = "as much as you want/can"; (2) in comparisons: "pas autant que" = "not as much as" (e.g., "La Lune ne brille pas autant que le Soleil" = "The Moon doesn’t shine as much as the Sun").
target_language_example: Prends autant que tu veux, il y en a assez pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Take as much as you want; there’s enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or movement around something/someone: «autour de la table» (around the table), «passer autour de moi» (go past/around me). It can also be figurative: «tourner autour de» = to revolve around / be all about (often in «Le monde ne tourne pas autour de vous.»). With time/number/amount, it means approximately: «autour de 20 minutes» (about 20 minutes). Common with body language: «mettre/avoir le bras autour de quelqu’un» = put/have your arm around someone.
target_language_example: On se retrouve autour de 18 h autour du parc.
native_language_example: We’ll meet around 6 p.m. around the park.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different thing. In questions, especially with vouloir or désirer, it often means "anything else?"
target_language_example: Je voudrais autre chose à boire.
native_language_example: I'd like something else to drink.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say that one action happens earlier than another: avant de partir, avant de manger. If the subject changes, French usually uses avant que instead.
target_language_example: Je me lave les mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: I wash my hands before eating.

additional_notes: Means being together/accompanying a female person ("her"). Very common after verbs like "sortir avec elle" (go out with her / date her), "parler avec elle" (talk with her), "être avec elle" (be with her). It’s the feminine form; compare "avec lui" = "with him".
target_language_example: Je veux parler avec elle après le cours.
native_language_example: I want to talk with her after class.

additional_notes: Composed of avec + le. Used before a masculine singular noun: avec le chien, avec le professeur. Unlike à + le or de + le, it does not contract.
target_language_example: Je parle avec le voisin.
native_language_example: I'm speaking with the neighbor.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “with the …” or more generally “with … (plural)”. Unlike à + les → aux and de + les → des, avec does not contract: it stays avec les. Common in many contexts: accompaniment (avec les amis), comparison (avec les leurs), problems involving something (un problème avec les freins), and set phrases like « avec les compliments de la maison » (“with the house’s compliments” = “on the house”).
target_language_example: Je vais au marché avec les voisins.
native_language_example: I'm going to the market with the neighbors.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with a male person. After a preposition like avec, French uses the stressed pronoun lui, not il.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec lui.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with him.

additional_notes: Used for being together with the speaker: physically near them, accompanying them, doing something jointly, or interacting with them. In some contexts, especially with être, it can also mean 'on my side' or 'following what I mean'.
target_language_example: Viens avec moi au marché.
native_language_example: Come with me to the market.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone does something together with the speaker and their group. Common after verbs like venir, aller, rester, and travailler.
target_language_example: Tu peux dîner avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: You can have dinner with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which person someone is with, talking to, competing with, going out with, etc. In everyday speech it often corresponds to “who … with?” (even though “whom” is more formal in English). Word order varies: “Avec qui parles-tu ?” or “Tu parles avec qui ?”.
target_language_example: Tu es avec qui ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who are you with tonight?

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to mean that someone is with something that belongs to him or her. The exact English possessive depends on context, so son can also mean "its." Note that son is used with masculine singular nouns, and also before feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel sound: avec son épée = "with her/his sword."
target_language_example: Il est venu avec son frère.
native_language_example: He came with his brother.

additional_notes: Literally means “with your” (used before a plural noun: tes = “your” for plural things, or one person’s body parts when spoken of in pairs like yeux/pattes). In arguments/insults, “avec tes + noun” can mean “and your …” in a dismissive way (e.g., “Get out of here with your stupid excuses!”).
target_language_example: Arrête avec tes excuses !
native_language_example: Stop with your excuses!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with, accompanying, or sharing something with the person spoken to. "toi" is the stressed form of "tu" used after a preposition like "avec"; for formal or plural "you," use "avec vous."
target_language_example: Je veux venir avec toi.
native_language_example: I want to come with you.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It can mean being together with something/someone, or using something as a tool or means. Compare with "avec une" before a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: Il ouvre la boîte avec un couteau.
native_language_example: He opens the box with a knife.

additional_notes: Used to say something has or includes something: « une chambre avec une douche » (“a room with a shower”), or to describe the tool/means: « avec une bombe » (“with a bomb”). « une » is the feminine form of “a/an”, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (une douche, une bombe).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec une cuillère de sucre.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with a spoonful of sugar.

additional_notes: Question form of vous avez, made by inversion. It is used with vous for formal or plural 'you', especially in writing or careful speech.
target_language_example: Avez-vous le temps de parler ?
native_language_example: Do you have time to talk?

additional_notes: Formal inversion of vous avez used to ask a question. Vous can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you." Often seen in polite speech, writing, and service interactions.
target_language_example: Avez-vous une réservation ?
native_language_example: Do you have a reservation?

additional_notes: Formal question form using inversion: "avez-vous" = "have you" (addressing one person politely, "vous"). "déjà" can mean "already" (something expected by now) or "ever" in questions about life experience, depending on context.
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

additional_notes: Past infinitive of être. It is used to talk about a state or quality that existed before another moment, often after verbs like sembler, devoir, penser, dire, or croire: elle semble avoir été heureuse = she seems to have been happy.
target_language_example: Elle dit avoir été malade la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: She says she was sick last week.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or need. It is followed by a noun or by an infinitive: avoir besoin de quelque chose / avoir besoin de faire quelque chose. Literally, it is closer to 'to have need of.'
target_language_example: Tu pourrais avoir besoin de ceci.
native_language_example: You might need this.

additional_notes: Usually used as: « avoir envie de + noun » or « avoir envie de + infinitive ». It expresses a desire/craving in the moment (often softer than « vouloir »). In the negative: « je n’ai pas envie de… » = “I don’t feel like…”
target_language_example: Je vais avoir envie de prendre un café.
native_language_example: I’m going to feel like having a coffee.

additional_notes: Literally “to have hunger,” but it’s the standard way to say “to be hungry” in French. Use it after another verb like devoir (must) or commencer à (to start to): Il doit avoir faim = He must be hungry.
target_language_example: Il doit avoir faim.
native_language_example: He must be hungry.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something’s appearance or the impression they give. Common patterns: "avoir l'air + adjective" (Il a l'air fatigué. = He looks tired.) and "avoir l'air de + noun/infinitive" (Elle a l'air d'une prof. = She looks like a teacher; Tu as l'air de plaisanter. = You seem to be joking). Often used with "ne pas" for "doesn’t seem/doesn’t look".
target_language_example: Il peut avoir l'air fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He may look tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Means “to be afraid” (literally “to have fear”). Often used with “de” to say what you’re afraid of: “avoir peur de + noun/pronoun” (avoir peur du chien, avoir peur de toi). You can also use “avoir peur de + infinitive” to mean “be afraid to (do something)”: “avoir peur de tomber” (to be afraid of falling).
target_language_example: Suis-je censé avoir peur de toi ?
native_language_example: Am I supposed to be afraid of you?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is correct. Because this entry is listed under the infinitive form, example sentences often place it after another verb, as in "Tu dois avoir raison." Although it looks like "to have reason," that literal translation is usually not how the expression is understood; for "to have a reason," French more often uses "avoir une raison de ...". The opposite is "avoir tort".
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir raison.
native_language_example: You must be right.

additional_notes:
Used with an infinitive: "avoir à + infinitive" (e.g., "j’ai à choisir" is uncommon; you’ll usually see it in forms like "je ne devrais pas avoir à choisir" or "sans avoir à les informer"). Often similar to "devoir" but can sound a bit more formal/impersonal, focusing on necessity/requirement. Common pattern: "ne pas avoir à" = "not have to"; "sans avoir à" = "without having to".
Note: the set phrase "avoir affaire à" means "to be dealing with" (as in "Vous croyez avoir affaire à qui ?"), and it’s different from plain "avoir à".
target_language_example: On peut le faire en ligne sans avoir à appeler le service client.
native_language_example: We can do it online without having to call customer service.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to show a large quantity: beaucoup de travail, beaucoup de bruit. In English, it can correspond to either “many” or “much” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de patience.
native_language_example: She has a lot of patience.

additional_notes: Means “many/a lot of things” in a general sense (often about events, activities, information, or possessions). Very common with verbs like faire (do), révéler (reveal), se passer (happen), acheter (buy), and with en commun (“in common”). Note: don’t confuse with “beaucoup de” + an uncountable noun (e.g., beaucoup d’eau = a lot of water).
target_language_example: J'ai beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Usually appears in the expression avoir besoin de = "to need." It is followed by a noun (J'ai besoin de sommeil) or an infinitive verb (J'ai besoin de parler).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I need your help.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or concession. It is followed by the subjunctive: « bien que + subjunctive » (e.g. « bien que je sois… », « bien qu’il pleuve »). Don’t confuse it with « bien que » meaning “indeed/clearly that” in phrases like « Cela montre bien que… », where « bien » = “clearly/indeed” and « que » = “that” (not the conjunction “although/even though”).
target_language_example: Il continue à travailler, bien que ce soit difficile.
native_language_example: He keeps working, even though it’s difficult.

additional_notes: Used to agree, confirm something, or say something is obvious or expected. It often appears at the start of a sentence, but it can also come after the noun or answer it refers to.
target_language_example: Tu peux compter sur moi, bien sûr.
native_language_example: You can count on me, of course.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something, often as a response. It’s "bien sûr" + "que" followed by a full clause: "Bien sûr que je comprends." You can also use it with "oui" or "non" for emphasis: "Bien sûr que oui !" / "Bien sûr que non !" In more formal or careful French, you may also hear simply "Bien sûr." without "que".
target_language_example: Bien sûr que je vais t’aider.
native_language_example: Of course I’m going to help you.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck. Common patterns: « Bonne chance ! » (on its own), « Bonne chance pour + noun » (e.g., pour ton examen), and « Bonne chance à + person » (e.g., à toi, à tous). Often said when someone is leaving or about to start something challenging.
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton entretien demain !
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used to say that a suggestion is a good one (often as a short reaction: « Bonne idée ! »). It can also mean “the right idea/clever idea” in phrases like « avoir la bonne idée de + infinitive » (“to have the good sense to…”). In « j’en ai une assez bonne idée », it means “a pretty good idea (of it)” = a fairly clear understanding.
target_language_example: Bonne idée : on peut y aller à pied.
native_language_example: Good idea: we can go there on foot.

additional_notes: Used to say goodbye in the evening/night, especially when someone is going to sleep. Often said on its own ("Bonne nuit !") or with a name. Not the same as "bonsoir" (which is a greeting meaning "good evening").
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, à demain !
native_language_example: Good night, see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Contraction of ce + est. Very common for identifying or pointing out a person, thing, or idea. Depending on context, it can mean 'this is', 'that is', or 'it's'.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami.
native_language_example: This is my friend.

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize or confirm something ("indeed / really"). In questions, it can mean "is that really...?" (C'est bien ce que vous vouliez ? = Is that really what you wanted?). In set phrases like "c'est bien noté", it means "noted / duly noted". Depending on context, "c'est bien" can also mean "that's good / that's nice" (talking about a situation), but in your examples it’s mainly emphasis/confirmation.
target_language_example: C'est bien toi sur la photo ?
native_language_example: Is that really you in the photo?

additional_notes: Very common phrase with several close meanings depending on context. It can mean something is enjoyable or pleasant (C'est bon d'être ici = It’s good to be here), that something is good for someone (C'est bon pour toi = It’s good for you), or that something is acceptable/settled/approved (Très bien, c'est bon = OK, it’s fine). In conversation, it can also mean “OK, got it / that’s enough” (C'est bon, j'ai vu = OK, I saw).
target_language_example: C'est bon, on peut y aller.
native_language_example: Okay, we can go.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an idea, fact, or thing and identify it: 'that's what ...'. It is usually followed by a clause such as je pense, j'ai compris, or tout le monde veut.
target_language_example: C'est ce que je veux dire.
native_language_example: That's what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something (“only,” “nothing more than”). Often followed by a noun: « C'est juste un accident » (“It’s just an accident”). Note: « juste » can also mean “fair/accurate/right,” but in this phrase (as in the examples) it usually means “just/only.”
target_language_example: T'inquiète, c'est juste un message.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s just a message.

additional_notes: Used to identify, point out, or define a masculine singular noun or idea. It combines c'est ('it is/this is/that is') with le ('the'). In context, it can also mean 'this is the'. Before a vowel sound, French usually uses c'est l' instead.
target_language_example: C'est le début de l'histoire.
native_language_example: It's the beginning of the story.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself (“It’s me”). It can also be used for emphasis, especially with “c’est moi que…” meaning “I’m the one that…” / “It’s me (that)…”.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, c'est moi.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it's me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that *you* (and not someone else) are the person doing an action. It’s a common French emphasis pattern: “c’est + stressed pronoun (moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles) + qui + verb.” In everyday English you often translate it as “I’m the one who…” or sometimes just with stress: “I did it.”
target_language_example: C'est moi qui paie ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm the one paying tonight.

additional_notes: Used to identify or present something or someone as belonging to me. It is normally followed by a singular noun. mon is usually used with masculine singular nouns, and also before some feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel sound.
target_language_example: C'est mon frère.
native_language_example: This is my brother.

additional_notes: Used to identify something that belongs to a group including the speaker (“our …”). Typically followed by a singular noun (because “notre” agrees with a singular noun regardless of gender): « c'est notre chambre », « c'est notre voiture ». For plural nouns, you usually use « c'est nos … ». Note: in formal writing you normally capitalize and use an apostrophe (« C’est notre »), but in speech and informal text you may see « c'est notre ».
target_language_example: Dis-lui que c'est notre bébé.
native_language_example: Tell him/her that it’s our baby.

additional_notes: Very common spoken/colloquial form of « ce n’est pas » (dropping « ne »). Used to make negative statements: « C'est pas obligé » = “It’s not required.” It can also be used as a question with rising intonation: « C'est pas quelque chose ? » ≈ “Isn’t it something?” In more formal writing, prefer « ce n’est pas ».
target_language_example: C'est pas obligé.
native_language_example: It’s not required.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French and fairly informal. Used to ask for an explanation or definition: “c’est quoi ?” = “what is it?”; with a noun: “c’est quoi le plan ?” = “what’s the plan?” A more neutral/formal alternative is “qu’est-ce que c’est ?” or “quel est … ?” depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est quoi ton adresse ?
native_language_example: What’s your address?

meaning: it’s you who / you’re the one who
additional_notes: Used to emphasize “you” as the person responsible for an action or fact. The verb that follows usually agrees with “toi” (so it’s conjugated as if the subject were “tu”): « c'est toi qui as… », « c'est toi qui fais… ». You can swap in another person: « c'est moi qui… », « c'est lui/elle qui… », etc.
target_language_example: c'est toi qui as fait ce bruit-là ?
native_language_example: Was that you who made that noise?

additional_notes: Used to identify something as belonging to the person you’re talking to: « C'est ton + noun ». « Ton » means “your” and is used before a masculine singular noun (ton cousin, ton avenir) and also before a feminine singular noun starting with a vowel sound (ton excuse).
target_language_example: C'est ton choix.
native_language_example: It's your choice.

additional_notes: Often placed at the end of a sentence to mean 'nothing more' or 'no other reason.' It can sound like a simple conclusion, explanation, or a way to end the discussion.
target_language_example: Je voulais t'aider, c'est tout.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help, that's all.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with emphasis. Most often followed by an adjective ("C'est très + adjective"), e.g., "C'est très bon" (It's very good). It can also be followed by an adverb + verb phrase, e.g., "C'est très bien fait" (It's very well done).
target_language_example: C'est très important pour moi.
native_language_example: It's very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a singular masculine noun: a person, thing, place, or event. Depending on context, it can also mean "he's a" or "she's a". For a feminine noun, use "c'est une".
target_language_example: C'est un bon début.
native_language_example: It's a good start.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good (masculine singular) before a noun: "c'est un bon + nom" (c'est un bon début, c'est un bon exercice). For feminine nouns, use "c'est une bonne …" (e.g. c'est une bonne idée). Note: In careful writing, you’ll often see "C’est" with a capital letter and curly apostrophe, but the phrase itself is "c'est un bon".
target_language_example: c'est un bon début.
native_language_example: It’s a good start.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true. You can say it as a response to agree with someone (“That’s true.”). Often followed by a clause: “C’est vrai que …” = “It’s true that …”.
target_language_example: Oui, c'est vrai, j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: Yes, it's true, I forgot.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize what comes next. Very common pattern: "c'est vraiment + adjective" (C'est vraiment beau.) or "c'est vraiment + noun phrase" (C'est vraiment la fin du monde.). Often expresses surprise, admiration, or annoyance depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment incroyable !
native_language_example: It's really incredible!

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with what someone just said (“that’s right”), to point to the exact thing you mean (“that’s it / that’s what I mean”), or to wrap up a summary (“basically, that’s it”). Often said on its own: « C'est ça ! ». In questions like « Et qu'est-ce que c'est ça ? », a more common/natural phrasing is « Qu'est-ce que c'est que ça ? » (“What is that?”).
target_language_example: Oui, c'est ça : on se retrouve à 18 h devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: Yes, that's it: we'll meet at 6 p.m. in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Common past form of c'est, used to describe, identify, or comment on something in the past. Depending on context, it can mean "it was," "that was," or "this was."
target_language_example: C'était une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It was a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability to do something. Common patterns: "être capable de" + infinitive (Je suis capable de le faire. = I’m able to do it.) or "être capable de" + noun (Il est capable de patience. = He is capable of patience). "Capable" agrees with the subject (capable / capable / capables).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas capable de venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m not able to come tonight.

additional_notes: "ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning "this" (sometimes "that" depending on context). It’s used before a masculine singular noun: ce + noun (ce film). Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, it becomes "cet" (e.g., cet acteur).
target_language_example: J'adore ce film, je l'ai déjà vu deux fois.
native_language_example: I love this movie; I've already seen it twice.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective ce with a masculine singular noun. In French, ce can mean either "this" or "that" depending on context; French does not usually make the same distinction as English here.
target_language_example: J'aime beaucoup ce livre.
native_language_example: I really like this book.

additional_notes: Used to describe or give information about a specific book. Pattern: "ce/cet/cette + noun + est" ("is"). "Ce" is used before most masculine singular nouns (like "livre"); "cet" is used before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h (e.g., "cet arbre est...").
target_language_example: Ce livre est intéressant, mais un peu long.
native_language_example: This book is interesting, but a bit long.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the morning of the current day, or the morning of the day being talked about. Compare with le matin, which usually means "in the morning" or "mornings" in general.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas pris de café ce matin.
native_language_example: I didn't have coffee this morning.

additional_notes: Means “this word/that word,” referring to a specific word identified in context (spoken about, pointed at, written down, etc.). It uses the demonstrative adjective “ce” + a masculine singular noun (“mot”). Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes “cet” (e.g., “cet exemple”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce mot.
native_language_example: I don’t understand this word.

additional_notes: Means a specific problem being discussed or pointed to. "Ce" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective (“this/that”) used before a masculine noun: ce problème. It changes to "cet" before a vowel sound (cet accident) and to "cette" for feminine nouns (cette idée).
target_language_example: Nous devons régler ce problème rapidement.
native_language_example: We need to fix this problem quickly.

additional_notes: Refers to the evening of the current day. In English, "tonight" is often the most natural translation, though the literal meaning is "this evening."
target_language_example: On dîne ensemble ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner together tonight?

additional_notes: An informal way to refer to something when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) the exact name. It can sound dismissive/annoyed (“that dumb thing”), but it can also be neutral depending on tone. Often used for an object, a gadget, an idea, or an activity: « C’est quoi, ce truc ? » = “What is this thing?”
target_language_example: C'est quoi, ce truc ?
native_language_example: What is this thing?

additional_notes: Literally “this type,” but in everyday French it often means “this/that guy” (a man you’re talking about). It’s fairly informal and can sound neutral, familiar, or slightly negative depending on tone and context. Often used with verbs like "se souvenir de" (to remember) or "parler de" (to talk about).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas ce type, mais il a l’air sympa.
native_language_example: I don’t know that guy, but he seems nice.

additional_notes: “Ce fut” is the passé simple (simple past) of “c’est / c’était” and is mostly used in formal writing, literature, or storytelling. In everyday spoken French, people usually say “c’était” instead.
target_language_example: Ce fut un moment inoubliable.
native_language_example: It was an unforgettable moment.

additional_notes: Formal/literary way to say "it was a" in the past. "fut" is the passé simple of "être", so this phrase is mainly found in books, speeches, and historical narration, not everyday conversation. It is used before a masculine singular noun; before a feminine noun, you would say "ce fut une".
target_language_example: Ce fut un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: Contraction of ce que + on. It introduces a clause meaning 'what ...'. on can mean 'we', but it can also be impersonal ('people', 'they', or a general 'you'), so the best English translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu'on mange ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you know what we're eating tonight?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing or idea: often after verbs like voir, savoir, dire, or faire. It can mean both direct 'what' and more formal 'that which.' In patterns like 'X est à Y ce que A est à B,' it means 'what' in a comparison: 'X is to Y what A is to B.'
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what the speaker is saying. Common after verbs like comprendre/voir/savoir (e.g., « Tu comprends ce que je dis ? » = “Do you understand what I’m saying?”). Can also be the subject of a sentence: « Ce que je dis… » = “What I’m saying…”.
target_language_example: Écoute bien ce que je dis.
native_language_example: Listen carefully to what I’m saying.

additional_notes: Built with "ce que" (= "what/that which") + "je fais" (= "I do / I’m doing"). Used to refer to an action you’re doing (or do in general), often after verbs like "savoir" (to know) or "se demander" (to wonder): "Je sais ce que je fais" (I know what I’m doing). The tense can change depending on context (e.g., "ce que je faisais" = what I was doing).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr de ce que je fais.
native_language_example: I’m not sure what I’m doing.

additional_notes: Means “what I want” or “the thing(s) that I want.” It often comes after a verb like dire, savoir, demander, etc.: « Je sais ce que je veux. » = “I know what I want.”
target_language_example: Je sais ce que je veux, mais je ne sais pas comment l'obtenir.
native_language_example: I know what I want, but I don't know how to get it.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action done by “you” (tu). Literally “that which you have done,” but in English it’s usually “what you did/what you’ve done.” Often appears after verbs like voir (to see), réaliser (to realize), regretter (to regret), être reconnaissant pour (to be grateful for), etc.
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à croire ce que tu as fait.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what you did.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an embedded clause meaning “the thing that you are doing.” Very common after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), or in expressions like faire attention à… (to be careful about…). The exact meaning depends on context: it can refer to what you’re doing right now (“what you’re doing”) or more generally (“what you do”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu fais.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing.

additional_notes: Used in an indirect question or statement after another verb (e.g. je sais / je vois / demander) to mean “what you are doing.” It uses the formal/plural “vous.” In a direct question, you often see “qu’est-ce que vous faites ?” instead.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous faites.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you're doing.

additional_notes: Means “what you want” as the thing someone wants. Built with the relative pronoun “ce que” + subject (“vous”) + verb (“voulez”). Often used after another verb: “Je vous donne ce que vous voulez” (I’ll give you what you want). In imperatives, it can feel like “whatever you want”: “Mangez ce que vous voulez” (Eat whatever you want).
target_language_example: Je peux vous préparer ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: I can make you whatever you want.

additional_notes: used to mean “what/that which” when it is the subject of the following verb. Compare with ce que, which is used when “what” is the object of the verb.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I understand what's happening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event or situation (often something that happened earlier). Literally “that which happened.” Common after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), apprendre (to learn), découvrir (to discover): « Je sais ce qui s'est passé. » It can also follow « désolé pour… » to mean “sorry about what happened.”
target_language_example: Personne ne comprend ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: No one understands what happened.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to a situation/event. Literally built from "ce qui" ("what" / "that which") + "se passe" ("is happening"). Often appears after verbs like "comprendre", "savoir", "expliquer", "dire": "Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe" (I don’t know what’s happening). As a direct question you’ll often hear "Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?" (What’s happening?).
target_language_example: Explique-moi ce qui se passe, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Explain to me what’s happening, please.

additional_notes: Future form of c'est / ce + être. It is used to say what something will be like or to identify something in the future. In English, ce can become it, this, or that depending on context.
target_language_example: Demain, ce sera plus facile.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it will be easier.

additional_notes: Conditional form of « c’est » / « c’est + adjective/noun » (from « être »). Used to talk about a hypothetical situation (“it would be nice/crazy…”) or to sound more polite/soften a statement (“would it be possible…?”). Often followed by an adjective or noun: « Ce serait formidable. », or by « de + infinitive »: « Ce serait de la folie de recommencer. »
target_language_example: Ce serait super de te voir demain.
native_language_example: It would be great to see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of "être" (serait) to express a wish, suggestion, or hypothetical situation. Common patterns: "ce serait bien de" + infinitive ("it would be nice to..."); "ce serait bien que" + subjunctive ("it would be good if you..."); "ce serait bien si" + imperfect ("it would be nice if..."). It can also be used ironically in phrases like "Ce serait bien la première fois" ("That would be a first").
target_language_example: Ce serait bien que tu viennes un peu plus tôt demain.
native_language_example: It would be good if you came a bit earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to point to something close, present, or being shown/introduced. "ceci" is more formal and common in writing, presentations, or careful speech; in everyday conversation people often say "c'est" or "ça, c'est…" instead.
target_language_example: Ceci est la première page du document.
native_language_example: This is the first page of the document.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a limitation after what you just said, similar to “that being said” or “however” in English. Often followed by a comma: “Cela étant, …”. It’s a fairly formal/written connector; in speech you might also hear “cela dit” or simply “mais”.
target_language_example: Cela étant, je préfère attendre avant de décider.
native_language_example: That being said, I’d rather wait before deciding.

additional_notes: Feminine singular demonstrative pronoun used to point to a specific thing/person already known from context. Often contrasts with "celle-ci" (= this one). You can use it alone as a short answer: "Celle-là." It replaces a feminine noun (e.g., "cette boîte" → "celle-là").
target_language_example: Prends celle-là, pas celle-ci.
native_language_example: Take that one, not this one.

additional_notes: masculine singular demonstrative pronoun. Used to point to or single out a specific person or thing, often in contrast with another option. It can refer to someone with a slightly dismissive tone depending on context. Related forms: celle-là, ceux-là, celles-là.
target_language_example: Je prends celui-là.
native_language_example: I'll take that one.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person identified by the clause that follows. It can point to a specific person ("Tom est celui qui...") or make a general statement ("Celui qui..."). The form changes with gender and number: "celle qui," "ceux qui," "celles qui."
target_language_example: Celui qui arrive en dernier ferme la porte.
native_language_example: Whoever arrives last closes the door.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to tell someone to stop an action: « Cesse de + infinitive ». In the negative, « ne cesse de + infinitive » often means “keeps (doing)” / “won’t stop (doing)” (repeated or continuous action). « Cesse » is the tu-form command (imperative) of « cesser »; you may also see « cessez de » (vous) or « cesse de » with another subject (e.g., « il/elle cesse de… »).
target_language_example: Cesse de te plaindre et aide-moi.
native_language_example: Stop complaining and help me.

additional_notes: Means “this place” when referring to a specific location. "Cet" is the masculine singular demonstrative (“this”) used before a vowel sound (endroit). Use "cet endroit" for places spoken about in the moment or already known from context.
target_language_example: J'aime bien cet endroit, il est très calme.
native_language_example: I really like this place; it’s very quiet.

additional_notes: "Cet" is the masculine singular form of "ce" used before a word starting with a vowel sound (like "homme", which has a silent h): "ce garçon" but "cet homme". Used to point out a specific man (often one already known from context).
target_language_example: Je ne fais pas confiance à cet homme.
native_language_example: I don't trust this man.

additional_notes: Means “during the current year” (the year we are in now). Often placed at the end of the sentence to specify when something happens: Je pars en juin cette année. Can also go at the beginning for emphasis: Cette année, je voyage moins.
target_language_example: Cette année, je vais apprendre le français.
native_language_example: This year, I'm going to learn French.

additional_notes: "cette" is the feminine singular demonstrative adjective meaning "this/that". Use "cette femme" to point out or refer back to a specific woman (in the situation or already mentioned). Compare: "cet homme" (this/that man), "cette fille" (this/that girl), "ces femmes" (these/those women). Note: French "femme" usually means "woman" (or "wife" depending on context), not the same as English "femme" in expressions like "femme fatale".
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas cette femme, mais elle me semble sympathique.
native_language_example: I don't know this woman, but she seems nice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific girl (not just “a girl”). "cette" is the feminine singular form of the demonstrative adjective (like “this/that”); in English you choose “this” or “that” based on context.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu parles toujours de cette fille ?
native_language_example: Why do you always talk about that girl?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current/particular occasion (often contrasting with other times: “not like the other times”). Common in warnings or emphasis: “Cette fois, tu es allé trop loin.” It can also go at the end of the sentence for emphasis: “Tu es allé trop loin, cette fois.”
target_language_example: Cette fois, je vais le faire correctement.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to do it properly.

additional_notes: Often means literally “this story” (something someone told you), as in J’ai déjà entendu cette histoire (“I’ve already heard this story”). In everyday speech it can also mean “this whole situation/affair,” sometimes with an annoyed tone, as in Cette histoire commence à durer (“This whole thing is starting to drag on”). Note: histoire can mean “story” or “history,” so don’t automatically translate it as “history” in these contexts.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de cette histoire.
native_language_example: I’m fed up with this whole thing.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "cette" (= "this/that") with a feminine singular noun like "maison". It points to a specific house (one you’re indicating in context). For extra emphasis you can say "cette maison-ci" (this house here) or "cette maison-là" (that house there).
target_language_example: J’aime bien cette maison, mais elle est trop chère.
native_language_example: I like this house, but it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Means “this/that night,” depending on context. Often used to set the time for an event: “Cette nuit, …” = “Tonight, …”. It can also refer to a specific night in the past when the context is clearly about a story/event (“that night”).
target_language_example: Cette nuit, je ne peux pas sortir.
native_language_example: Tonight, I can't go out.

additional_notes: "cette" means "this" for a feminine singular noun; "photo" is feminine (short for "photographie"). Used to point to a specific photo that’s physically present, being shown, or already mentioned (e.g., in a chat, on your phone, in an album).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’envoyer cette photo ?
native_language_example: Can you send me this photo?

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific sentence/phrase in context (often one you just read, wrote, or are discussing). "Cette" is the feminine singular form of "this" and agrees with "phrase" (feminine). Note: French "une phrase" often means a full sentence, not just a short phrase.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous expliquer cette phrase ?
native_language_example: Can you explain this sentence?

additional_notes: "cette" is the feminine singular demonstrative adjective used with a feminine noun like "voiture". It can mean either "this" or "that" depending on context; you can add "-ci" (cette voiture-ci = this car here) or "-là" (cette voiture-là = that car there) to be more specific.
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas cette voiture.
native_language_example: I don’t like this/that car.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens daily. Often goes at the end of the sentence (Je viens ici chaque jour), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport chaque jour.
native_language_example: I work out every day.

additional_notes: Uses "chez" + a stressed pronoun (lui = him) to mean "at/to someone’s home or place". Often refers to the person’s home, but can also mean their place in general (their apartment, house, office, etc.). You can change the pronoun: chez moi (my place), chez toi (your place), chez elle (her place), chez nous (our place), etc.
target_language_example: On va chez lui après le travail.
native_language_example: We’re going to his place after work.

additional_notes: Used with chez + a stressed pronoun to talk about someone's home or place. With verbs like être or rester, it means being at your place; with aller or venir, it can mean going to your place.
target_language_example: On peut dîner chez moi ce soir.
native_language_example: We can have dinner at my place tonight.

additional_notes: Means “at/to our home/our place.” With a verb of motion (aller, rentrer, venir), it often means “to our place”; with a verb describing where something happens (habiter, parler, manger), it means “at our place.” It can also mean “in our country/our region” in broader contexts (e.g., politics: « une armée chez nous » = “an army in our country”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve chez nous après le travail.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at our place after work.

additional_notes: "Chez" means "at someone’s place / home." With "toi" it refers to the listener: "chez toi" = your home/your place. Often used with movement verbs: "Va chez toi" (go to your place), "Rentre chez toi" (go back home). It can also be used more generally to mean "in your home" or "with you" (in your personal life): "Je veux que tu te sentes chez toi" = I want you to feel at home.
target_language_example: Tu peux rester chez toi ce soir.
native_language_example: You can stay at your place tonight.

additional_notes: Means “at your home/house” or “to your home,” depending on the verb: with location verbs (être, rester, manger, etc.) it’s usually “at your place,” and with movement verbs (rentrer, aller, accompagner, etc.) it’s usually “to your home.” Can also be used more generally as “where you are/where you belong” (e.g., in a seat or role).
target_language_example: Je peux passer chez vous vers 18 h.
native_language_example: I can stop by your place around 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration or the amount of time needed, left, or spent. Very common with verbs like durer (to last), rester (to remain), and prendre (to take).
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour y aller ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get there?

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to a feminine singular noun ("une …"). Very common in similes: "rouge comme une betterave" (red like a beetroot), "nager comme une pierre" (swim like a stone). For masculine nouns, use "comme un"; for plural, "comme des".
target_language_example: Il est têtu comme une mule.
native_language_example: He’s as stubborn as a mule.

additional_notes: Used to compare with an unreal, hypothetical, or “pretend” situation. Very common in the pattern « faire comme si… » = “to act/pretend as if…”. Often followed by the imperfect or pluperfect in French (even when English uses “as if + past” too): « comme si tu savais tout » (as if you knew everything), « comme si rien ne s’était passé » (as if nothing had happened).
target_language_example: Il parle comme si tout était de sa faute.
native_language_example: He talks as if it were all his fault.

additional_notes: Used to ask or explain how something happens or works, with cela referring to a thing or situation already mentioned or understood from context. Cela is more formal than ça, so in everyday speech you will often hear comment ça... instead.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment cela s'est passé.
native_language_example: I don't know how that happened.

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's state or how things are going. It is often followed by a name or noun: Comment va Ben ? / Comment va votre fille ? On its own, Comment va ? is a short, casual way of asking how things are going, similar to Comment ça va ?
target_language_example: Comment va ton frère aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How is your brother doing today?

additional_notes: Used in speech to ask for an explanation or react with surprise. In a normal question it can introduce “how does that…?”: « Comment ça se termine ? » = “How does it end?” With a surprised tone (often followed by a noun/adjective), it means “What do you mean?” / “How come?”: « Comment ça, fichu ? » = “What do you mean, ruined?”
target_language_example: Comment ça, tu pars déjà ?
native_language_example: What do you mean, you're leaving already?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it’s the negative form of "tu comprends" (you understand) with "ne" dropped (full form: "tu ne comprends pas"). Used to say you don’t understand something, or to ask "You don’t understand?"
target_language_example: Je comprends pas pourquoi il est en colère.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why he’s angry.

additional_notes: Used to say you trust someone/something will help or be dependable: compter sur + person/thing (Je peux compter sur toi/elle). It can also mean "to be counting on" in the sense of expecting something to happen: compter sur + noun/pronoun, and sometimes compter sur + infinitive (Je compte sur toi pour m'aider / Je compte sur venir demain).
target_language_example: Tu peux compter sur moi si tu as besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: You can count on me if you need help.

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: verb + hyphen + subject pronoun (tu). It comes from the verb « connaître » (to know/be familiar with), used for people, places, and things you’re acquainted with (not for facts—use « savoir » for that). Often used like « Connais-tu Marie ? » = “Do you know Marie?”
target_language_example: Connais-tu ce quartier ?
native_language_example: Do you know this neighborhood?

additional_notes: Informal spoken French: this is the negative form of "(je/tu/il…) ne connais pas" with "ne" dropped. Used with "connaître" for knowing a person/place or being familiar with something (facts, rules, a topic). More formal/written: "je ne connais pas…" / "je ne vous connais pas".
target_language_example: Désolé, je connais pas ce quartier.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Formal question form (inversion) of « vous connaissez…? ». Used to ask if someone is familiar with a person/thing/place (connaître). For knowing a fact or how to do something, French often uses « savoir » instead.
target_language_example: Connaissez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to say that an action keeps going or is resumed: continuer à + infinitive (continuer à dormir, continuer à avancer). Often translates as “keep doing” in everyday English.
target_language_example: Même si c’est difficile, je vais continuer à essayer.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, I’m going to keep trying.

additional_notes: Common spoken/informal shortening of the full negation "ne … pas": "je crois pas" = "je ne crois pas". Used to express doubt or disagreement ("I don’t think so"), or lack of belief/trust: "je te crois pas" (I don’t believe you), "j’y crois pas" (I don’t believe it / I don’t buy it). Can be followed by "que" + a clause: "je crois pas que…" (I don’t think that…).
target_language_example: Je crois pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used most often after "je" as "je croyais que tu..." to introduce what you thought/believed about someone else ("I thought you..."). "croyais" is the imperfect of "croire" (to think/believe), often used for a past belief/assumption that may have been wrong or later changed.
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu venais ce soir.
native_language_example: I thought you were coming tonight.

additional_notes: Contraction of ce + est. Very common for identifying someone or something, pointing something out, or making a general comment. Depending on context, it can mean "it's," "this is," or "that is."
target_language_example: C’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It's a good idea.

additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Depending on context and tone it can mean: (1) reassurance/approval: “It’s fine/OK.” (2) stopping someone: “That’s enough / OK, stop.” It can also literally mean “it’s good” (e.g., food: « C’est bon ! » = “It’s tasty!”).
target_language_example: C’est bon, je vais m’en occuper.
native_language_example: It’s okay, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to show agreement or acceptance. Often comes with "être" (être d'accord = to agree): "Je suis d'accord" (I agree), "Tu es d'accord ?" (Do you agree?/Is that okay with you?), "On est d'accord" (We agree/We’re agreed). "D'accord ?" can also be used like “OK?” to check that someone understands or accepts.
target_language_example: D'accord, on se retrouve à 18 h.
native_language_example: Okay, we’ll meet up at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "elle" ("de elle" → "d'elle"). Used after verbs and expressions that take "de", e.g. "s'occuper de" (to take care of), "penser de" (to think of/about), "parler de" (to talk about). The exact meaning depends on the verb: often "about her" with opinions, and "of her" with possession/origin.
target_language_example: Je m'inquiète d'elle.
native_language_example: I'm worried about her.

additional_notes: Means “from here” in terms of place/distance (often with expressions like loin/pas loin d'ici = far/not far from here). It can also be used after verbs of leaving or removing someone: partir/s'en aller/se tirer/sortir d'ici = to leave/get out of here. In casual speech you may hear stronger/slangy verbs with it (e.g., je me casse d'ici), but “d'ici” itself is neutral.
target_language_example: On n'est pas très loin d'ici.
native_language_example: We're not very far from here.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "où". Most often used in questions to ask the origin of someone/something: "D’où viens-tu ?" = "Where are you from?" / "D’où ça vient ?" = "Where does that come from?" It can also be used more figuratively to ask for the source of information: "D’où tu sais ça ?" = "How do you know that?" In statements, it can also mean "hence/therefore" ("… d’où …" = "… which is why …").
target_language_example: D'où vient cette idée ?
