additional_notes: Often means “luck” in general (good or bad): « La chance est aveugle. » It can also mean an opportunity you should take: « saisir la chance » = “to seize the opportunity.” Common phrases: « avoir de la chance » (to be lucky), « bonne chance ! » (good luck!).
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance : tu as encore une chance de réussir.
native_language_example: You're lucky: you still have a chance to succeed.

additional_notes: Literally the object used to open a lock: « la clé de la porte » (“the key to the door”). It’s also used figuratively to mean the main point/solution: « la clé de cette affaire » (“the key to this case/matter”). Often followed by « de » + noun to say “the key to/for …” (e.g., « la clé du succès »).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas la clé de la voiture.
native_language_example: I don’t have the car key.

additional_notes: Often refers to the room (the kitchen): « Nettoie la cuisine. » It can also mean the activity of cooking, especially in « faire la cuisine » (to do the cooking) or « être à la cuisine » (to be in the kitchen / busy cooking). In restaurants, « fermer la cuisine » means the kitchen stops serving food.
target_language_example: Ce soir, c'est moi qui fais la cuisine.
native_language_example: Tonight, I'm the one doing the cooking.

additional_notes: Time expression meaning the most recent time something happened. Often used alone (Je l’ai fait la dernière fois. = I did it last time) or in questions (Quand… la dernière fois ? = When… last time?). In “C’est la dernière fois”, it often means “This is the last time” as a warning/firm decision. You can also use it with a clause: “la dernière fois que + subject + verb” (the last time that…).
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai vu qu’une seule fois, et la dernière fois, c’était en juin.
native_language_example: I only saw him once, and the last time was in June.

additional_notes: Refers to your family/relatives or family unit (parents, children, close relatives). Often used in set phrases like «dans la famille» (“in the family”). «Famille» is also used in expressions about family support/benefits (e.g., «aide à la famille»).
target_language_example: Je vais passer le week-end avec la famille.
native_language_example: I’m going to spend the weekend with the family.

additional_notes: Usually means "the woman." In context, especially in phrases like "la femme de...", it can also mean "the wife of...".
target_language_example: La femme de Marc travaille ici.
native_language_example: Marc's wife works here.

additional_notes: Includes the definite article la, so it refers to a specific window. In context, it can also appear in expressions like à la fenêtre, meaning 'at the window'.
target_language_example: La fenêtre est fermée.
native_language_example: The window is closed.

additional_notes: Can mean either 'girl' or 'daughter' depending on context. In family expressions like la fille de mon frère or la fille de votre père, it means 'daughter'; otherwise it often means 'girl'.
target_language_example: La fille de Paul habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: Paul's daughter lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Means “the end” of something (a story, a movie, a line, an event, a period of time). Common patterns: “à la fin” = “at the end / in the end”; “jusqu’à la fin” = “until the end”; “la fin de …” = “the end of …”. In phrases like “Le meilleur pour la fin”, it means “save the best for last.”
target_language_example: Je garde le dessert pour la fin.
native_language_example: I’m saving dessert for last.

additional_notes: Means a forest/woods (a large area covered with trees). It’s a feminine noun, usually used with an article: "la forêt" (the forest), "une forêt" (a forest). Often appears with prepositions like "dans la forêt" (in the forest), "derrière la forêt" (behind the forest).
target_language_example: On se promène dans la forêt après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We go for a walk in the forest after lunch.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a train station (often "la gare" or "la gare SNCF"). Common in directions with prepositions like "près de" (near), "en face de" (opposite/across from), and "pour" (to/for) + a destination.
target_language_example: On se retrouve devant la gare à 18 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of the station at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Can refer to war in general or to a specific war, depending on context. French often uses the definite article where English may simply say "war" in a general sense.
target_language_example: La guerre n'est jamais une solution.
native_language_example: War is never a solution.

additional_notes: Often refers to the day as a span of time or how the day went/feels (duration, experience): «passer la journée», «la journée a été longue», «la journée est presque finie». Contrast: «le jour» is more like “the day” as a calendar day or in expressions like “one day”; «la journée» focuses on the whole day’s course. In «pendant la journée / dans la journée», it means “during the day / in the daytime” (as opposed to at night).
target_language_example: On a passé la journée à visiter le musée.
native_language_example: We spent the day visiting the museum.

additional_notes: Usually means “language” (French, Berber, etc.), but it can also mean the physical “tongue” in your mouth. In the expression « tirer la langue », it means “to stick out your tongue.”
target_language_example: J'apprends la langue française depuis un an.
native_language_example: I've been learning the French language for a year.

additional_notes: Usually means a written message sent by mail/post. Common verbs: écrire une lettre (to write a letter), lire une lettre (to read a letter), envoyer une lettre (to send a letter), poster/mettre une lettre à la poste (to mail a letter), recevoir une lettre (to receive a letter). Can also mean a letter of the alphabet in other contexts.
target_language_example: J’ai reçu la lettre ce matin.
native_language_example: I received the letter this morning.

additional_notes: Refers to the legal law/rules of a country or society. Common with verbs like respecter la loi (obey the law), changer la loi (change the law), modifier la loi (amend the law), and faire respecter la loi (enforce the law / make people obey the law).
target_language_example: Il faut respecter la loi.
native_language_example: You have to obey the law.

additional_notes: Means “light” in the sense of brightness/illumination (from a lamp, the sun, etc.). Often used with negation for emphasis: “pas même la lumière” = “not even the light.” Note: it’s a feminine noun, so it usually takes "la" (or "une" for “a light”).
target_language_example: J'ai allumé la lumière parce qu'il fait sombre.
native_language_example: I turned on the light because it's dark.

additional_notes: Refers to the body part. In French, body parts often use the definite article where English uses a possessive: il me tient la main = "he's holding my hand," not usually "the hand." Also appears in expressions like mettre la main sur, meaning "to get hold of" or "to find."
target_language_example: Elle me prend la main pour traverser la rue.
native_language_example: She takes my hand to cross the street.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to a house or home in general. maison can mean either a physical house or a home, depending on context. la is the feminine singular definite article ('the').
target_language_example: La maison est très calme le matin.
native_language_example: The house is very quiet in the morning.

additional_notes: Refers to the sea/ocean (salt water). Common in phrases like "à la mer" (to the seaside / to the sea) and "ça sent la mer" (it smells like the sea—salty, sea air). Often contrasted with "la montagne" (the mountains) and different from "un lac" (a lake).
target_language_example: En été, on va souvent à la mer.
native_language_example: In summer, we often go to the seaside.

additional_notes: Often used with "à" to mean going to/in the mountains as a region for outdoor activities: "aller à la montagne" (go to the mountains), "être à la montagne" (be in the mountains). It can also mean a single mountain depending on context (e.g., pointing to one mountain).
target_language_example: Cet été, on va à la montagne pour faire des randonnées.
native_language_example: This summer, we're going to the mountains to go hiking.

additional_notes: Usually means “death” in a general sense or referring to someone’s death. Common patterns: “à la mort de [quelqu’un]” = “upon/at the time of [someone]’s death”; “la cause de la mort” = “cause of death.” French often uses “la mort” where English might drop “the.” Can also be used in figurative/literary ways (e.g., personifying Death as “la Mort”).
target_language_example: À la mort de son grand-père, il a quitté la ville.
native_language_example: After his grandfather’s death, he left the city.

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical or unchanged from something else, or that you had the same experience. Often used with "c'est" ("c'est la même chose" = "it's the same thing") or with verbs like "faire" and "vivre" ("faire/vivre la même chose" = "do/go through the same thing").
target_language_example: On a choisi la même chose au restaurant.
native_language_example: We chose the same thing at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Means “snow” (the weather / the white frozen precipitation). Often used with verbs like “tomber” (to fall): « Il neige » = “It’s snowing”; and “fondre” (to melt): « La neige a fondu » = “The snow melted.” You’ll also see « à cause de la neige » = “because of the snow.”
target_language_example: On ne peut pas sortir à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: We can’t go out because of the snow.

additional_notes: Common general word for food in a meal or in general. Often used when talking about meals, restaurants, travel, or what you eat (e.g., "Et la nourriture ?" = "And the food?").
target_language_example: J'aime la nourriture française, surtout le fromage.
native_language_example: I like French food, especially cheese.

meaning: the news (a specific piece of news)
additional_notes: Refers to a particular item of news or information someone learns/hears (“the news” in the sense of a specific development). Common with verbs like entendre (to hear), apprendre (to learn), annoncer (to announce), and with emotional reactions (surprise, joie, tristesse, etc.). Not the same as le journal (newspaper) or les informations (the news program/news in general).
target_language_example: Avez-vous entendu la nouvelle à la radio ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you hear the news on the radio this morning?

additional_notes: Literally means "the night," but French often uses the article where English does not: je travaille la nuit = "I work at night." It can refer to the nighttime in general or to what happens during the night.
target_language_example: J'aime marcher la nuit quand il fait frais.
native_language_example: I like walking at night when it's cool.

additional_notes: Means the previous night (the night before today). Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas bien dormi la nuit dernière.
native_language_example: I didn’t sleep well last night.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “peace” (no war, calm). In expressions like “Fiche-moi la paix !” or “Laisse-moi la paix !”, it means “leave me alone” (informal/strong). Also used in “faire la paix” = “make peace” (stop fighting, reconcile).
target_language_example: Après la dispute, ils ont fait la paix.
native_language_example: After the argument, they made peace.

additional_notes:
Often used in set phrases:
- « en valoir la peine » = “to be worth it” (e.g., « Ça en vaut la peine. »)
- « (Ce n’est) pas la peine » = “no need / don’t bother / not worth it”
- « avoir de la peine » = “to feel sad / to feel sorry (for someone)”
Meaning depends on context: it can be emotional (“sorrow”) or practical (“effort/trouble”).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la peine de te dépêcher, on a le temps.
native_language_example: No need to hurry; we have time.

additional_notes: Short for "la photographie". Very common in everyday French for a photograph or an image (printed or digital). Used with verbs like "prendre" (take a photo) and "faire" (take/shoot a photo): "Qui a fait la photo ?" = Who took the photo?
target_language_example: Qui a fait la photo ?
native_language_example: Who took the photo?

additional_notes: Most commonly means “room” in a home/building context: La pièce est grande (The room is big). It can also mean “coin” (money) or “piece/part” depending on context. The article changes with gender/number: la pièce (a/the room), une pièce (a room), des pièces (rooms / coins).
target_language_example: On va manger dans la pièce à côté.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat in the room next door.

additional_notes: Often means the available space/room for someone or something: « Il y a de la place ? » = “Is there room/space?” With « la place », it’s usually a specific spot/seat/place (often one person’s spot): « Je te garde la place » = “I’m saving you a seat/spot.” In informal speech, « je suis dans la place » can mean “I’m here / I’m around (on the scene).”
target_language_example: Je te garde la place à côté de moi.
native_language_example: I’m saving you the seat next to me.

additional_notes: Refers to the sandy (or pebbly) area by the sea or a lake where people swim or relax. Often used with common verbs like aller à la plage (to go to the beach), être à la plage (to be at the beach), and en face de la plage (across from/opposite the beach).
target_language_example: On va à la plage cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this afternoon.

additional_notes: Common weather noun. Used with weather verbs like « il pleut » (it’s raining) or with « accompagner » (to come with) and « cesser » (to stop): « la pluie a cessé » = “the rain stopped.”
target_language_example: On a annulé le pique-nique à cause de la pluie.
native_language_example: We canceled the picnic because of the rain.

additional_notes: Very common way to say “most (of)” people or things. Often used as **la plupart de + noun/pronoun**: *la plupart des gens*, *la plupart d’entre vous*, *la plupart de mon temps*. It can also stand alone as a pronoun: *La plupart pensent que…* Even though **la plupart** is grammatically singular, it usually refers to a plural group, so the verb is often **plural**: *La plupart sont d’accord.*
target_language_example: La plupart de mes amis habitent loin d’ici.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live far from here.

additional_notes: Means “most of” something. It’s usually followed by a plural noun: most often you’ll see it as “la plupart des + plural noun” (des = de + les), e.g. “la plupart des gens” = most people. With a verb, French often uses a plural verb after “la plupart” (La plupart sont…), though singular can sometimes occur when focusing on the group as one whole.
target_language_example: La plupart des étudiants arrivent en avance.
native_language_example: Most of the students arrive early.

additional_notes: Feminine singular superlative form used with an adjective (or adverb) to mean “the most … / the …-est”: e.g., « la plus simple » = “the simplest”. It agrees with the noun: « le plus » (masc. sing.), « la plus » (fem. sing.), « les plus » (plural). Often followed by an adjective: « la plus grande », « la plus fière ».
target_language_example: C'est la plus belle robe du magasin.
native_language_example: It’s the most beautiful dress in the store.

additional_notes: Refers to the police force or police officers as a group. In French, it is commonly used with the definite article: la police.
target_language_example: La police est arrivée rapidement.
native_language_example: The police arrived quickly.

additional_notes: Means “apple” (the fruit). In French, it’s usually used with an article: une pomme (an apple), la pomme (the apple). Also appears in food phrases like “gâteau à la pomme” (apple cake).
target_language_example: Tom a lavé la pomme avant de la manger.
native_language_example: Tom washed the apple before eating it.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific door. "Porte" means "door," and "la" is the singular definite article used with it. It can be a room door, front door, fridge door, etc., depending on context.
target_language_example: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form of « le/la premier/première ». Used for a woman/girl or a feminine noun: « Elle est la première de sa classe » (she’s the top/first in her class), « la première neige » (the first snow). Common pattern: « la première à + infinitive » = “the first to …” (e.g., « la première à venir » = the first to come). In English, “premier” usually means a head of government, so don’t translate it that way here.
target_language_example: C'est Marie qui est arrivée la première.
native_language_example: Marie was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific question (often one that was just asked or is being discussed). Common verbs: “poser la question” = to ask the question; “répéter la question” = to repeat the question; “la question se pose” = the question comes up / arises.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas compris la question.
native_language_example: I didn't understand the question.

additional_notes: Refers to radio as a device or radio broadcasting in general. Often used with verbs like écouter (to listen to) and allumer/éteindre (to turn on/off). Can also be followed by a type of station or programming (e.g., la radio kabyle).
target_language_example: J'écoute la radio le matin en voiture.
native_language_example: I listen to the radio in the morning in the car.

additional_notes: “La rivière” is a feminine noun meaning a river (a natural flowing waterway). In everyday French, “une rivière” typically refers to a river that flows into another river; for a river that flows into the sea, French often uses “un fleuve.”
target_language_example: Nous nous promenons le long de la rivière.
native_language_example: We’re taking a walk along the river.

additional_notes: Usually means a physical road/street for cars, bikes, etc. Common with verbs like traverser la route (cross the road), quitter la route (leave the road), and au milieu de la route (in the middle of the road). In expressions: barrer la route à quelqu’un = block someone’s way; dégager la route = clear the road. Figurative: ne pas tenir la route = not hold up / not make sense (e.g., a theory or excuse).
target_language_example: Attention, un enfant traverse la route !
native_language_example: Careful, a child is crossing the road!

additional_notes: Means a street in a town/city. Common with prepositions like "dans la rue" (in the street), "au bout de la rue" (at the end of the street), and with verbs like "traverser la rue" (to cross the street) or "descendre/remonter la rue" (to go down/up the street).
target_language_example: Il y a une boulangerie dans la rue d’à côté.
native_language_example: There’s a bakery on the next street.

additional_notes: Means “the answer” to a question, problem, or test. It can also mean a “response” to a request or situation. Often followed by "à" to specify what it answers: "la réponse à une question" (the answer to a question).
target_language_example: J'attends la réponse du médecin.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for the doctor's answer.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning a planned gathering, often in a professional or organizational context. Common with verbs like "avoir lieu" (to take place) and "se tenir" (to be held): "La réunion a lieu / se tient à 10h." It can also mean a "reunion" (family/class reunion), but in everyday work/school contexts it usually means "meeting".
target_language_example: La réunion se tiendra demain matin à neuf heures.
native_language_example: The meeting will be held tomorrow morning at nine o'clock.

additional_notes: “La salle” is a general word for an indoor space where people gather or something happens (a room, hall, venue). Common uses include: *la salle de classe* (classroom), *la salle de cinéma* (movie theater screening room), *la salle de sport* (gym). In contexts like renting or events, it often means a function room/venue (*louer la salle entière* = rent the whole room/hall).
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans la salle après le cours.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the room after class.

additional_notes: Means the week after the current one. Often used with future plans or to postpone something: "(à) la semaine prochaine". You can also say "la semaine prochaine" on its own without "à".
target_language_example: Je commence mon nouveau travail la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: I start my new job next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are at a certain moment (a problem, context, or set of circumstances): la situation politique/économique, la situation actuelle. Often followed by an adjective (bonne, mauvaise, grave) or specified with de + noun: la situation de l'entreprise.
target_language_example: On doit discuter de la situation avant de décider.
native_language_example: We need to discuss the situation before deciding.

additional_notes: Common informal shortening of « la télévision ». Used with verbs like « regarder la télé » (to watch TV) and « éteindre la télé » (to turn off the TV).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on regarde la télé.
native_language_example: After dinner, we watch TV.

additional_notes: Refers to television in general (the medium) or the physical TV set, depending on context. Common with verbs like regarder (to watch), allumer (to turn on), éteindre (to turn off), and fonctionner (to work). Often shortened to "la télé" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: On regarde la télévision ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we watching TV tonight?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the physical head, but in some expressions it can also suggest the mind or thoughts. With body parts, French often uses the definite article where English uses a possessive: secouer la tête = shake your/her head. It also appears in many idioms, such as avoir une idée derrière la tête (to have something in mind / an ulterior motive).
target_language_example: J'ai mal à la tête.
native_language_example: I have a headache.

additional_notes: Refers to meat as food (animal flesh). Often used with a specific animal: "la viande de bœuf" (beef), "la viande de porc" (pork), "la viande de lapin" (rabbit). In shops/restaurants you may also hear "la viande" contrasted with "le poisson" (fish).
target_language_example: Je ne mange pas la viande, mais je mange du poisson.
native_language_example: I don’t eat meat, but I eat fish.

additional_notes: Usually refers to life in general or a person's life. French often uses the article here where English simply says "life." Common expressions include donner la vie (give life / give birth), perdre la vie or laisser la vie (lose one's life), coûter la vie (cost someone their life), and devoir la vie à quelqu’un (owe someone your life).
target_language_example: La vie est plus simple à la campagne.
native_language_example: Life is simpler in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about life. It’s often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: “La vie est courte” (Life is short), “La vie est souffrance” (Life is suffering). In English you usually drop the article (“life is…”) even though French keeps it (“la vie est…”).
target_language_example: La vie est pleine de surprises.
native_language_example: Life is full of surprises.

additional_notes: Refers to an urban place. In French, ville can mean either “city” or “town” depending on context; with la, it usually means a specific city or town already known from the situation.
target_language_example: J'adore me promener dans la ville le soir.
native_language_example: I love walking around the city in the evening.

additional_notes: A definite noun phrase for a specific car; in some contexts it can also refer to cars in general. "Voiture" is feminine, so it takes "la".
target_language_example: La voiture est devant la maison.
native_language_example: The car is in front of the house.

additional_notes: Refers to what is true or factual. French usually uses the article here: dire la vérité = "tell the truth".
target_language_example: Dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: Tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Imperative form of laisser used when speaking to one person (tu). It is very often followed by an infinitive: laisse-moi entrer = let me in, laisse-moi prendre ton sac = let me take your bag. On its own, it can also mean "leave me" or "leave me alone," depending on context.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi finir, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Let me finish, please.

meaning: to drop; (figurative) to give up, quit, forget it/let it go
additional_notes: Literally means “to let fall.” With a direct object, it can mean to physically drop something (« Laisse tomber ça » = “Drop that.”). Very commonly used figuratively to mean “give up,” “quit,” or as an interjection “Forget it!” / “Let it go!” (« Laisse tomber ! »). Can be used with an object (« laisser tomber la boisson » = “give up alcohol”) or on its own (« Je ne vais pas laisser tomber » = “I’m not going to give up.”).
target_language_example: Je ne vais pas laisser tomber !
native_language_example: I’m not going to give up!

additional_notes: Most often means an office (the workplace or office room): « quitter le bureau » = to leave the office. It can also mean a desk (the piece of furniture), especially with location words like « sous le bureau » (under the desk). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Elle a déjà quitté le bureau, mais une pièce a roulé sous le bureau.
native_language_example: She has already left the office, but a coin rolled under the desk.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific bus, or to buses in general depending on context. Common with verbs like attendre (to wait for), prendre (to take/catch), rater (to miss). Note: for the mode of transport, French more often uses « en bus » (by bus) rather than « par le bus », but « le bus » is required when referring to the bus as a concrete, identifiable vehicle.
target_language_example: J’ai attendu le bus pendant dix minutes.
native_language_example: I waited for the bus for ten minutes.

additional_notes: Refers to a very young child (a baby). Often used for babies and toddlers; you can also hear it used affectionately for someone (e.g., a partner: « mon bébé »). In « faire le bébé », it means “to act like a baby” (to whine/behave immaturely).
target_language_example: Le bébé dort dans sa poussette.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping in his/her stroller.

additional_notes: Usually refers to coffee as a drink in general (e.g., liking coffee) or a specific coffee being discussed (e.g., the coffee on the table). When ordering, French often uses "un café" for one serving, but "le café" is common for general statements or when the context identifies the coffee.
target_language_example: Elle aime le café.
native_language_example: She likes coffee.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase made of the definite article le ("the") and chat ("cat"). Used for a specific cat, or for "the cat" in a general sense.
target_language_example: Le chat dort sur le canapé.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a path/track or the route to get somewhere (often in directions: « montrer le chemin » = “show the way”). It can also be used more figuratively to mean someone’s journey or approach in life (e.g., « le chemin est le but » = “the journey is the goal”). Masculine noun: « le chemin », « un chemin ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quel est le chemin le plus court pour aller au centre-ville ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s the shortest way to get to downtown?

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase: le means "the" with a masculine singular noun, and chien means "dog." It can refer to a specific dog, and in some contexts French also uses the definite article for animals in a general sense.
target_language_example: Le chien dort sous la table.
native_language_example: The dog is sleeping under the table.

additional_notes: Most often means “the sky” (what you see above you). It can also mean “heaven,” especially in expressions or a religious sense. Common pattern: "le ciel est..." (the sky is...).
target_language_example: Ce soir, le ciel est plein d'étoiles.
native_language_example: Tonight, the sky is full of stars.

additional_notes: Very common word with several idiomatic uses depending on the verb/context. 1) Physical or emotional “hit”: « encaisser le coup » = “take the blow / handle the shock.” 2) An attempt: « tenter le coup » = “give it a try.” 3) A move/trick/typical thing to do: « le coup classique » = “the classic move/trick.” 4) With « valoir »: « ça valait/vaut le coup » = “it was/is worth it,” and « ça vaut pas le coup » = “it’s not worth it.”
target_language_example: On peut tenter le coup, mais je ne sais pas si ça vaut le coup.
native_language_example: We can give it a try, but I don’t know if it’s worth it.

additional_notes: Used for the final or most recent person, thing, or event, depending on context. It can come before a noun (le dernier vol = the last flight) or stand alone (je suis le dernier = I'm the last one). It changes for gender and number: la dernière, les derniers, les dernières.
target_language_example: Je prends le dernier train pour Paris.
native_language_example: I'm taking the last train to Paris.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens on Sundays in general (a habit). With days of the week, French often uses “le” to mean “on (that day) / on (that day) in general”. For one specific upcoming/previous Sunday, you can also say “dimanche” without “le” (e.g., “Dimanche, je travaille.”).
target_language_example: Le dimanche, on prend un café en terrasse.
native_language_example: On Sundays, we have a coffee on a patio.

additional_notes: Means “the doctor” (a medical doctor). In everyday French, you can also say "le médecin". Used when talking about a specific doctor already known in the situation (e.g., your doctor, the doctor on call).
target_language_example: Le docteur va te recevoir à 15 h.
native_language_example: The doctor will see you at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Refers to the main meal in the evening (common meaning in France). In some regions/families, it can be used for the midday meal instead—context tells you which meal. Common verbs with it: préparer / faire le dîner (make dinner), cuire le dîner (cook dinner), le dîner est prêt (dinner is ready).
target_language_example: Je fais le dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm making dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Usually means literal fire/flames (a building fire, a campfire). Common related phrases: « le feu prend » = “the fire catches/starts (spreads)”; « allumer le feu » = “to light the fire”; « par le feu » can mean “by fire” (burning) and, in military contexts, can also refer to “by gunfire.”
target_language_example: Attention, il y a le feu dans la cuisine !
native_language_example: Watch out, there’s a fire in the kitchen!

additional_notes: "Le" means "the" for a masculine singular noun, so "le film" usually refers to a specific movie/film. In everyday French, "un film" / "le film" often means "a movie" / "the movie." With verbs like "accélérer", it can mean speeding up/fast-forwarding the video (e.g., "accélérer le film" = fast-forward the movie).
target_language_example: On regarde le film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we watching the movie tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to the French language. In French, language names often take the definite article after verbs like parler, apprendre, enseigner, and comprendre, even though English usually just says "French" without "the." Also note the spelling difference: français = the language/adjective, while Français (capitalized) can mean a French person.
target_language_example: Je comprends un peu le français, mais je ne le parle pas bien.
native_language_example: I understand a little French, but I don't speak it well.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific boy. Le is the masculine singular form of 'the', so this phrase is for one identifiable male child or young man in context.
target_language_example: Le garçon joue dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The boy is playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Refers to a garden or yard area (often behind/around a house). Used with the definite article: "le" (the). You’ll also see it without an article after some prepositions, e.g. "dans le jardin" (in the garden).
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Usually means a specific day or occasion, as in le jour de... ('the day of...') or le jour où... ('the day when...'). When contrasted with la nuit or used with durant, it can mean 'daytime'.
target_language_example: Je travaille le jour et je me repose la nuit.
native_language_example: I work during the day and rest at night.

additional_notes: Most often means a newspaper (the physical paper or the newspaper as an organization). For a personal diary, French usually says "un journal intime" or "un carnet". It can also be used in expressions like "le journal de l’école" (the school newspaper) or "le journal télévisé" (the TV news).
target_language_example: J’achète le journal tous les matins.
native_language_example: I buy the newspaper every morning.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase: livre means "book," and it is masculine, so the singular definite form is le livre. In connected speech, le often becomes l' before a vowel sound, but not here.
target_language_example: Où est le livre que tu lis ?
native_language_example: Where is the book that you're reading?

additional_notes: Refers to a (physical) store/shop where you buy things. Common in phrases like "le magasin de fleurs" (the flower shop) and "dans le magasin" (in the store).
target_language_example: Ceci est le magasin le moins cher de la ville.
native_language_example: This is the cheapest store in the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning in general or as a regular time of day. Often follows a verb to mean “in the morning” (Je travaille le matin = I work in the morning / in the mornings). With a specific day, it can mean “the next morning / that morning” (Le matin suivant = the following morning).
target_language_example: Le matin, je bois un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: In the morning, I drink a coffee before leaving.

additional_notes: Means a specific point in time (“the moment”), often used to talk about when something should happen: “le moment de + infinitive” (the time to do something), “le moment présent” (the present moment), “ce n’est pas le moment” (it’s not the right time), “le moment est venu” (the time has come), “le moment opportun” (the right/appropriate time).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas le moment de parler de ça.
native_language_example: This isn’t the right time to talk about that.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the world in general: the planet, life on earth, or human society. In some contexts, it can also suggest people in general.
target_language_example: Je veux voyager et voir le monde.
native_language_example: I want to travel and see the world.

additional_notes: Used to describe what the world is like (often with an adjective or noun phrase): « le monde est compliqué », « le monde est un endroit dangereux ». Note: « le monde » usually means “the world,” but it can also refer to “people/society” in general depending on context. Don’t confuse it with « tout le monde est » = “everyone is.”
target_language_example: Parfois, le monde est injuste.
native_language_example: Sometimes, the world is unfair.

additional_notes: Means “the doctor” (male doctor or doctor in general). Common with verbs like appeler (call) and consulter (see/consult a doctor): « Appelle le médecin » = “Call the doctor”; « consulter le médecin » = “to see the doctor.”
target_language_example: J'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at the doctor's tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people or things are identical in some way. It often comes before a noun, as in le même livre ('the same book'), and changes for gender and number: la même, les mêmes. It is often followed by que to compare: le même ... que ('the same ... as').
target_language_example: Nous avons le même professeur de français.
native_language_example: We have the same French teacher.

additional_notes: Usually means “the new + [masculine singular noun]” (e.g., le nouveau président = the new president). It can also be used on its own as a noun to refer to a new person/thing in a group (“the newcomer”). For feminine, use la nouvelle; for plural, les nouveaux / les nouvelles.
target_language_example: Le nouveau n'a pas encore appris tous les noms.
native_language_example: The newcomer hasn't learned all the names yet.

additional_notes: used to form the superlative: le/la/les plus + adjective or adverb means "the most" or "-est" depending on the English word (for example, le plus beau = "the most beautiful"). After a verb, it means "most" (for example, plaire le plus = "please the most"). In le plus ... possible, it gives the idea of "as ... as possible." French also often uses this form where English would say "more" when comparing two things.
target_language_example: C'est le sport que j'aime le plus.
native_language_example: It's the sport I like the most.

additional_notes: Usually refers to having control or influence (political, social, or personal). It can also mean the ability/capacity to do something depending on context (e.g., avoir le pouvoir de + infinitive = “to be able to / to have the power to”).
target_language_example: Il veut garder le pouvoir.
native_language_example: He wants to stay in power.

additional_notes: Used for the first person or thing in a sequence, in time, or in rank. Before a noun: le premier jour = the first day. Used on its own, it can mean 'the first one' or simply 'first'. It agrees with gender and number: la première, les premiers, les premières.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé le premier.
native_language_example: I arrived first.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much something costs. Common in shopping/negotiation: « Quel est le prix ? » (What’s the price?), « réduire le prix » (lower the price), « le prix reflète la demande » (price depends on demand).
target_language_example: Je trouve que le prix est trop élevé.
native_language_example: I think the price is too high.

additional_notes: Means a difficulty, question, or situation that needs to be examined or solved. Often used with verbs like "repérer" (identify), "résoudre" (solve), and "examiner" (look into). Note: "problème" is masculine, so it takes "le" (or "un problème").
target_language_example: On a trouvé le problème, maintenant il faut le résoudre.
native_language_example: We found the problem; now we have to solve it.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean “the next (one)”: le prochain train (the next train), le prochain bus (the next bus), le prochain village (the next village). It agrees with the noun: la prochaine (fem. singular), les prochains / les prochaines (plural). Also, in a different context, "le prochain" can mean "your neighbor / fellow human" (e.g., aimer son prochain), but in everyday travel-style contexts it usually means “the next.”
target_language_example: Le prochain métro arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The next subway arrives in five minutes.

additional_notes: Often means “teacher” (at school, language class, etc.), not only a university professor. For a female teacher, you’ll often hear/see: « la professeure » (formal) or « la prof » (informal).
target_language_example: Le professeur explique la leçon.
native_language_example: The teacher explains the lesson.

additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains after something has been taken/used/eaten. Common patterns: "le reste de + noun" ("le reste de votre équipe" = "the rest of your team") and as a pronoun-like noun by itself ("Je prends le reste" = "I’ll take the rest").
target_language_example: Je vais finir le reste plus tard.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the rest later.

additional_notes: Refers to a male monarch (a king). It’s usually used with an article (le roi) or with a modifier: le roi de + place/country ("the king of...") or le roi + name/title ("King Louis"). Feminine: la reine ("the queen").
target_language_example: Le roi de France a vécu au château de Versailles.
native_language_example: The king of France lived at the Palace of Versailles.

additional_notes: Refers to the sun in the sky. Common with verbs like se lever (to rise) and se coucher (to set): « Le soleil se lève » (the sun rises), « Le soleil se couche » (the sun sets).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le soleil brille.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining.

additional_notes: French uses the same word for both 'time' and 'weather'. In expressions like avoir le temps and prendre le temps de, it means 'time' or 'enough time'; with words like beau, mauvais, changer, or permettre, it means 'weather'.
target_language_example: Tu as le temps de prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Do you have time to grab a coffee?

additional_notes: Refers to a railway train. With le, it usually means a specific train understood from context. Common beginner phrases include prendre le train (take the train), rater le train (miss the train), and attraper le train (catch the train).
target_language_example: Nous attendons le train sur le quai.
native_language_example: We're waiting for the train on the platform.

additional_notes: Usually means “work” in general or “the job/task that needs to be done,” as in finishing or doing something specific. With the definite article (le), it can refer to work as a concept (e.g., work is a duty) or to a particular piece of work already known in context (“finish the work”).
target_language_example: On doit finir le travail avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to finish the work before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means a telephone (landline or phone in general). Used with common verbs like décrocher le téléphone (to pick up the receiver/answer), le téléphone sonne (the phone is ringing), and le téléphone ne fonctionne pas (the phone isn’t working). In French you often say au téléphone for “on the phone” (e.g., Je suis au téléphone).
target_language_example: Je n'entends rien : le téléphone ne fonctionne pas.
native_language_example: I can’t hear anything: the phone isn’t working.

additional_notes: Refers to the wind (moving air). Often used with verbs like "souffler" (the wind blows) and expressions like "emporté par le vent" (blown away by the wind). Can also be used with adjectives such as "violent" to describe strong wind.
target_language_example: Le vent souffle très fort aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: The wind is blowing very strongly today.

additional_notes: "Chercher" means "to look for" and often, in contexts like these (especially with "aller/venir"), it naturally means "to go and get / fetch" someone or something. "Le" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" and it comes before the verb: "Allez le chercher" = "Go get him/it." (For "her/it" feminine: "la chercher"; for "them": "les chercher".)
target_language_example: Je vais le chercher à la gare.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick him/it up at the train station.

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him/her" depending on context). "Le croire" is the infinitive "to believe it/him/her," often used after another verb: "refuser de le croire" (refuse to believe it) or "être assez [adj] pour le croire" (be [adj] enough to believe it).
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à le croire.
native_language_example: I can't believe it.

additional_notes: `le` is the direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “that,” or sometimes “so,” placed before `dire`. It refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. Depending on the sentence, English may use “say it,” “say that,” or “say so”; with another pronoun, `me le dire` can mean “tell me.”
target_language_example: Je n'ose pas le dire.
native_language_example: I don't dare say it.

additional_notes: Used when le stands for a thing, action, or idea already understood from context. In French, the object pronoun comes before the infinitive, so you get le faire where English says do it.
target_language_example: On va le faire ensemble.
native_language_example: We're going to do it together.

additional_notes: Here, le is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "that," not the article "the." It refers to a fact or piece of information already mentioned or understood from context. In French, object pronouns come before the infinitive, so le savoir corresponds to English "to know it/that."
target_language_example: Je préfère le savoir maintenant.
native_language_example: I'd prefer to know it now.

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (for a masculine noun/person). With an infinitive like "trouver", the pronoun comes before the verb: "Je vais le trouver" = "I'm going to find it/him."
target_language_example: On va le trouver ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to find it together.

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "it," placed before the infinitive "voir." It often appears after verbs like vouloir, aller, devoir, or refuser: "je veux le voir," "aller le voir." The exact English translation depends on what "le" refers to in context.
target_language_example: Je dois le voir ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to see him tonight.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun meaning “yours” that replaces a noun (“yours” = “your one/thing”). It agrees with the thing possessed, not the person: le vôtre (masc. singular), la vôtre (fem. singular), les vôtres (plural). Often used in comparisons: « plus … que le vôtre » = “more … than yours.” Not used before a noun (use « votre/vos » before a noun).
target_language_example: Je cherche mon manteau, pas le vôtre.
native_language_example: I’m looking for my coat, not yours.

additional_notes: Plural of « l’autre » (“the other”). Used to refer to the rest of a group already known from context (“the others”). Can refer to people or things depending on context. In comparisons you often see « plus … que les autres » (“more … than the others”). Related phrase: « les uns les autres » = “each other / one another.”
target_language_example: Je vais attendre les autres devant le café.
native_language_example: I’m going to wait for the others in front of the café.

additional_notes: "Les" is the plural form of "the". In French, "les + plural noun" is often used to talk about a whole group/species in general (e.g., "Les chats aiment dormir" = "Cats like to sleep"). Note that French "chat" means "cat" (not English "chat" = online talk).
target_language_example: Les chats dorment beaucoup.
native_language_example: Cats sleep a lot.

additional_notes: In French, hair on your head is usually said in the plural: *les cheveux* (literally “the hairs”). With grooming verbs, French often uses *se* + the definite article: *Elle se lave les cheveux* = “She washes her hair” (not *ses cheveux* in most cases).
target_language_example: Je dois me sécher les cheveux.
native_language_example: I have to dry my hair.

additional_notes: Plural of « le chien » (“dog”). « Les » is the plural definite article (“the”), but in French it’s also used to talk about a whole category in general: « Les chiens aiment jouer. » = “Dogs like to play.”
target_language_example: Les chiens sont souvent très fidèles.
native_language_example: Dogs are often very loyal.

additional_notes: Often refers to things in general or to how a situation is going, not just physical objects. French usually keeps les here even where English simply says "things," as in les choses vont bien or arranger les choses.
target_language_example: Les choses vont mieux maintenant.
native_language_example: Things are going better now.

additional_notes: Used for exactly two people or things. Before a plural noun, it often means 'both' ('les deux parties' = 'both parties'). On its own, it can mean 'both of them' or 'the two' ('pas les deux' = 'not both / not the two').
target_language_example: Je prends les deux.
native_language_example: I'll take both.

additional_notes: A definite plural phrase: les means "the" and enfants means "children/kids." It can refer to a specific group of children, children in general, or be used when speaking directly to children, as in "Bonsoir, les enfants." Note that enfant looks like English "infant," but it usually means "child," not specifically a baby.
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Means “women” in general, or “the women” when referring to a specific group already known from context. Often used in general statements (e.g., about women as a group).
target_language_example: Les femmes aiment souvent discuter entre elles.
native_language_example: Women often like to chat with each other.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article: "les" = "the" (plural), "filles" = "girls". Often used to address a group directly ("Allez, les filles" = "Come on, girls"). Depending on context, "les filles" can also mean "girls/young women" in general, or "the daughters" (e.g., talking about someone’s children).
target_language_example: Les filles arrivent dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The girls are arriving in five minutes.

additional_notes: Plural of « la fleur ». Often used for real flowers (bouquet, garden, etc.). The article « les » means “the” for plural nouns.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté les fleurs pour ma mère.
native_language_example: I bought the flowers for my mom.

additional_notes: Informal/slang way to refer to police officers. Often used in casual speech; in more neutral/formal contexts, prefer "la police" (the police) or "les policiers" (police officers).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, les flics arrivent !
native_language_example: Hurry up, the cops are coming!

additional_notes: A casual way to refer to or address a group of boys or men. In everyday speech, it can also be used like English "guys" when talking to friends. Best avoided in formal situations.
target_language_example: Bonne chance, les gars !
native_language_example: Good luck, guys!

additional_notes: Usually refers to people in general. In everyday French, les gens often translates simply as "people," even though it literally includes the article "the."
target_language_example: Les gens sont très gentils ici.
native_language_example: People are very nice here.

additional_notes: Plural of "l'homme". Most often means "the men" (male people). In a general, universal sense it can also mean "humans / mankind" (e.g., talking about humans as a species). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Les hommes et les femmes n'ont pas toujours les mêmes habitudes.
native_language_example: Men and women don’t always have the same habits.

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition (e.g., dans les mains = in (someone’s) hands; entre les mains de = in the hands of / under the control of). With body parts, French often uses a reflexive verb + definite article: se laver les mains = to wash your hands (not *wash your the hands*). Also used in fixed expressions like avoir du sang sur les mains = to have blood on your hands (be responsible).
target_language_example: Lave-toi les mains après être allée aux toilettes.
native_language_example: Wash your hands after going to the toilet.

additional_notes: Commonly used literally for words in a language. Also appears in fixed expressions: "lire derrière les mots" = read between the lines (look beyond the literal words); "les actes en disent plus long que les mots" = actions speak louder than words; "les mots me font défaut" = I can’t find the words; "vous m'enlevez les mots de la bouche" = you took the words right out of my mouth (you said exactly what I was about to say).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas les mots pour te remercier.
native_language_example: I don’t have the words to thank you.

additional_notes: Means “the rules” in general (rules of a game, school/work rules, guidelines, etc.). In everyday French, "les règles" can also mean “a period/menstruation” in the right context, so listen for clues (health, dates, symptoms).
target_language_example: Quelles sont les règles ici ?
native_language_example: What are the rules here?

additional_notes: Emphatic pronoun used to stress that the person (il/lui) does something personally, not someone else: « Il l’a fait lui-même » = “He did it himself.” It can also mean “in person” (« Il doit venir lui-même »). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Related pattern: « être soi-même » = “to be yourself”; « Je lui ai dit d’être lui-même » = “I told him to be himself.”
target_language_example: Il a réparé la voiture lui-même.
native_language_example: He fixed the car himself.

additional_notes: Used with the indirect object pronoun "lui" (= to him/her). Very common pattern: "demander à quelqu’un (de + infinitive)" → "lui demander de faire quelque chose" (to ask him/her to do something). With two pronouns, the order is "le/la/les" + "lui" + verb: "le lui demander" (to ask him/her for it / to ask him/her that). Beware: "demander" usually means "to ask (for)" or "to request", not "to demand" in English.
target_language_example: Je vais lui demander de m’aider demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask him/her to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to or about one person: lui means "to him" or "to her." With dire, English often uses "tell" rather than "say," as in lui dire quelque chose = "tell him/her something."
target_language_example: Je vais lui dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell her the truth.

additional_notes: "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her” (and sometimes “to them” in more formal French). It usually goes before the verb: "Je vais lui donner…" = “I’m going to give him/her…”. With another pronoun, the order is typically: le/la/les + lui (e.g., "le lui donner" = “give it to him/her”).
target_language_example: Je vais lui donner les clés ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to give him/her the keys tonight.

additional_notes: Used with parler à quelqu’un. Here, lui means “to him” or “to her” and comes before the verb. It can refer to either a male or female person; for “to them,” use leur parler.
target_language_example: Je dois lui parler avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I need to talk to him/her before the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to point to a place that is away from the speaker, often farther away than just là. It can refer to a physical place or a more general distant location.
target_language_example: Je vois la gare là-bas.
native_language_example: I can see the station over there.

additional_notes: Points to something (a place, container, room, situation, etc.) and means “inside that/there.” Often used when talking about what’s contained in something (“Il y a quelque chose là-dedans.”), or who is inside (“Ils sont là-dedans.”). Can also be used more abstractly to mean “in that (situation/thing).”
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il y a quelqu'un là-dedans.
native_language_example: I think there's someone in there.

additional_notes: Used to point to a higher place (a roof, a hill, upstairs, a platform, etc.). In some contexts it can also mean “up in heaven” (talking about someone who has died). Often used with verbs like être/aller/sauter/regarder: « Il est là-haut », « Va là-haut », « Sauter de là-haut ».
target_language_example: Je crois que mes clés sont là-haut, sur l’étagère.
native_language_example: I think my keys are up there, on the shelf.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **dire** with the indirect object pronoun **me** (→ **m'** before a vowel). Used to report what someone said to you: **Il/Elle m'a dit ...** = “He/She told me ...”. Often followed by a clause (**que...**) or a yes/no answer (**oui/non**).
target_language_example: Il m'a dit qu'il arrivait demain.
native_language_example: He told me he was arriving tomorrow.

additional_notes: A combination of m' ('me/myself') and en. The pronoun en usually refers back to something already mentioned and often means 'of it', 'about it', or sometimes 'from it', depending on the verb. So m'en parler = 'tell me about it', m'en servir = 'use it', and m'en souvenir = 'remember it'. In s'en aller, it is part of the fixed verb meaning 'to go away'. It is not usually used on its own; it comes before a verb.
target_language_example: Tu peux m'en parler après le dîner.
native_language_example: You can tell me about it after dinner.

additional_notes: "Chambre" usually means a bedroom (at home) or a hotel room. You’ll hear it in practical phrases like "Quel est le numéro de ma chambre ?" (What is my room number?) and "Portez-le sur le compte de ma chambre" (Charge it to my room account).
target_language_example: Je rentre dans ma chambre pour me reposer.
native_language_example: I’m going back to my room to rest.

additional_notes: Means “my family” (family members, relatives). It’s the possessive adjective + noun: ma (my, feminine singular) + famille. You can also say "ma famille et moi" = "my family and I".
target_language_example: Je vais dîner avec ma famille ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my family tonight.

additional_notes: A common, standard way to refer to your wife. While femme by itself often means "woman," with a possessive like ma, ta, or sa it often means "wife" from the context.
target_language_example: Ma femme arrive ce soir.
native_language_example: My wife is arriving tonight.

additional_notes: Literally "my daughter" (ma + fille). Most often used to talk about your daughter: "Avez-vous vu ma fille ?". It can also be used when speaking directly to a girl/young woman as an affectionate or encouraging address (a bit like "my girl"), especially in casual speech: "Vas-y, ma fille." / "À fond ma fille.".
target_language_example: Je vais chercher ma fille à l’école.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my daughter from school.

additional_notes: "Ma" means "my" (feminine singular). "Maison" means "house/home" and is feminine, so it uses "ma" (not "mon"). Used to talk about the place where you live or a house you own. In commands, you’ll often see it with prepositions: "devant ma maison" (in front of my house), "de ma maison" (out of my house), "chez moi" is another common way to say "at my place/home".
target_language_example: Je rentre à ma maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I go back to my house after work.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: ma means "my" and mère means "mother." In everyday speech, French speakers often say maman for "mom."
target_language_example: Ma mère travaille à la maison aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: My mother is working from home today.

additional_notes: A straightforward possessive phrase. ma means "my" with a feminine singular noun, and sœur means "sister."
target_language_example: Ma sœur habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: A basic possessive phrase: ma + vie. It can refer literally to someone's life/existence, or more emotionally to their personal world, experiences, and important relationships.
target_language_example: Tu es très important dans ma vie.
native_language_example: You are very important in my life.

additional_notes: "ma" means "my" and agrees with a feminine singular noun like "voiture" (car). With a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h, French uses "mon" instead of "ma" (e.g., "mon amie").
target_language_example: Je ne trouve plus ma voiture.
native_language_example: I can't find my car anymore.

additional_notes: Combination of "mais" (but) + "c'est" (it's/that's). Used to contrast with what was just said or to insist on a fact. Often followed by a noun or phrase ("mais c'est lui" = "but that's him") or by a clause/expression ("mais c'est comme ça" = "but that's how it is"). Can also start a sentence to express mild disagreement or emphasis.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas d'accord, mais c'est ton choix.
native_language_example: I don't agree, but it's your choice.

additional_notes: A very common combination of mais + il used to introduce a contrast. Depending on context, il can refer to a male person, to "it," or be impersonal in expressions like il faut and il y a.
target_language_example: Il parle souvent de partir, mais il reste toujours ici.
native_language_example: He often talks about leaving, but he always stays here.

additional_notes: "Mais" means "but" and "on" is a very common subject pronoun meaning either "we" (often in spoken French instead of "nous") or "people/you/they" in a general sense. So "mais on..." is used to contrast what was just said with what "we" do/think, or what people in general do/think. The verb that follows is conjugated in the 3rd person singular (e.g., "on est", "on ira").
target_language_example: Mais on n'a pas le choix.
native_language_example: But we don’t have a choice.

additional_notes: Used to add a contrast while partially negating what came before: something is true, but with an exception/limit. It can be followed by a noun/pronoun (mais pas toi), an adjective/adverb comparison (mais pas autant que…, mais pas aussi… que…), or a quantity/choice (mais pas les deux). Often you’ll see it without repeating the verb because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Je veux bien venir, mais pas ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m happy to come, but not tonight.

additional_notes: Common way to start a contrast or correction: "mais" = "but" and "ça" refers to something general (“that/it/this situation”). Often followed by a verb: "Mais ça vaut le coup" (But it’s worth it), "Mais ça viendra" (But it will come / it’ll happen). Sometimes used alone for emphasis: "Mais ça, oui" = “But that, yes / But that part, yes.”
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas prêt, mais ça va aller.
native_language_example: I’m not ready, but it’ll be fine.

additional_notes: Formed with the object pronoun me and dire. In French, object pronouns usually come before the infinitive, so me dire often corresponds to English tell me, especially after verbs like pouvoir, devoir, or vouloir.
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ton nom ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me your name?

additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me" / "me" and it comes before the verb: "Tu vas me donner..." = "You’re going to give me...". In the imperative, it usually moves after the verb with a hyphen: "Donne-moi..." = "Give me...". The meaning depends on what follows (a thing, permission, a day off, your word, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand?

additional_notes: This can be either object pronoun + faire ("make me" / "do something to me") or the "me" form of se faire. In the pattern me faire + infinitive or past participle, it often means "get/have something done to oneself" or "be on the receiving end" of an action: me faire comprendre = make myself understood, me faire crier dessus = get yelled at, me faire enregistrer = get checked in.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to get my hair cut tomorrow.

additional_notes: Expression built on laisser (“to leave/let”) + indirect object pronoun me (“me”). Often means either (1) to leave someone alone/stop bothering them, or (2) to allow someone to do something. Common patterns: “me laisser + adjectif” (e.g., me laisser seul/seule = leave me alone; agree in gender/number), “me laisser + infinitif” (e.g., me laisser le faire = let me do it), “me laisser + nom” (e.g., me laisser un message = leave me a message). Register depends on context; with “Veuillez…”, it is formal/polite.
target_language_example: Veuillez me laisser un message.
native_language_example: Please leave me a message.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dire" (to say/tell) plus two object pronouns: "me" = to me, and "le" = it (often a whole idea, fact, or piece of information). The pronouns come before the verb: "Tu dois me le dire" (You have to tell me). With an infinitive, they also go before the infinitive: "Il va me le dire" (He’s going to tell me).
target_language_example: Tu peux me le dire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me now?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "manquer" (to miss/to lack). The person who is missed is the subject: "Il/Elle me manque" = "I miss him/her" (literally, "he/she is missing to me"). You can change the object pronoun: "tu me manques" (I miss you), "je te manque" (you miss me).
target_language_example: Tu me manques.
native_language_example: I miss you.

additional_notes: "Me" is the indirect object pronoun (to me) and comes before the verb: "Tu peux me parler." Often used with "de" to mean "talk to me about": "Me parler de ton travail" (talk to me about your job). In questions it can appear as "veux-tu me parler ?" or with "tu"-style word order: "Tu veux me parler ?".
target_language_example: Tu peux me parler si quelque chose ne va pas.
native_language_example: You can talk to me if something isn’t going well.

additional_notes: From the verb *plaire* (“to please”). The thing you like is the grammatical subject: *Cette cravate me plaît* = “I like this tie” (literally, “This tie pleases me”). In the negative: *ne me plaît pas* = “I don’t like it.” Also common in expressions like *je fais ce qui me plaît* (“I do what I like / whatever I want”).
target_language_example: Ce film me plaît beaucoup, mais mon frère ne m'en plaît pas du tout.
native_language_example: I really like this movie, but my brother doesn’t like it at all.

additional_notes: From the verb « rappeler » (most often: “to remind”). Pattern: « quelque chose me rappelle X » = “something reminds me of X” (Cela me rappelle nos vacances). With a person: « Elle me rappelle sa mère » = “She reminds me of her mother.” « rappeler » can also mean “to call back” (Je te rappelle).
target_language_example: Ce parfum me rappelle mon enfance.
native_language_example: That smell reminds me of my childhood.

additional_notes: In most of these examples, se rendre à + place means 'to go to' or 'make one's way to', often a bit more formal than aller. With a person + adjective, rendre means 'make' or 'cause': me rendre heureux = 'make me happy'. The pronoun changes depending on who is involved (me, te, se, nous, vous).
target_language_example: Je dois me rendre à l'aéroport tôt demain.
native_language_example: I have to go to the airport early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “kill me” (tuer = “to kill,” me = “me”). Often used literally in threats or questions (“Vous voulez me tuer ?” = “Do you want to kill me?”). It can also be used exaggeratively to mean “make me suffer / be extremely upset,” especially in phrases like “Mon père va me tuer” (“My dad is going to kill me” = “He’s going to be furious”) or “Même si ça doit me tuer” (“even if it kills me,” i.e., even if it’s extremely hard/exhausting).
target_language_example: Si ma mère apprend ça, elle va me tuer.
native_language_example: If my mom finds out, she’s going to kill me (i.e., she’ll be furious).

additional_notes: Literally refers to someone seeing you. The pronoun me comes before voir in French. Depending on context, it can mean to see you, come see you, visit you, or meet with you.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir me voir demain ?
native_language_example: Can you come see me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Means your closest friend. It often comes with a possessive: "mon/ton/son meilleur ami". Change it for gender/number: "meilleure amie" (female best friend), "meilleurs amis / meilleures amies" (plural).
target_language_example: Elle a invité son meilleur ami à la fête.
native_language_example: She invited her best friend to the party.

additional_notes: Plural of "mon ami". "Mes" is used before a plural noun (both masculine and feminine). "Amis" can refer to a group of male friends or a mixed-gender group; for an all-female group you typically say "mes amies".
target_language_example: Merci d'être venus, mes amis.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming, my friends.

additional_notes: Means “my parents” (usually your mother and father). It’s the plural of "mon parent" and uses "mes" (my, plural). Often used when talking about family, responsibility, rules at home, etc. In speech, "Mes parents ?" can be a surprised or questioning repeat: “My parents?”
target_language_example: Je vais dîner avec mes parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm having dinner with my parents tonight.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/actions, like English “better than.” It often follows a verb: "faire mieux que" (do better than), "être mieux que" (be better than), "nager mieux que" (swim better than). "Mieux" is the comparative form of "bien" (well).
target_language_example: Je peux faire mieux que ça.
native_language_example: I can do better than that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize or contrast the speaker’s opinion/choice with someone else’s (often in spoken French). It’s like starting with “Me, I…” or “As for me…” in English. You can use it to disagree politely, to insist, or to highlight your personal point of view.
target_language_example: Moi, je préfère rester ici.
native_language_example: Me, I’d rather stay here.

additional_notes: Used to agree or add that the same thing applies to you too. It often comes after a statement ("Je viens." — "Moi aussi.") or inside a sentence for emphasis ("Je ressens, moi aussi, la même chose."). You’ll also commonly see it after "pour" as "pour moi aussi" (= “for me too / for me as well”).
target_language_example: Je veux y aller, moi aussi.
native_language_example: I want to go too.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend, or to address someone directly as "my friend." For a female friend, French uses mon amie.
target_language_example: Paul est mon ami depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: Paul has been my friend for a long time.

additional_notes: “Bureau” can mean either the room where you work (“office”) or the piece of furniture you work at (“desk”). Context tells you which: a location like “au deuxième étage” suggests an office (room), while describing it as old/new often suggests a desk. In English, “bureau” can also mean an “agency” (e.g., “travel bureau”), but in French “un bureau” in everyday speech most often means “office/desk.”
target_language_example: Je suis dans mon bureau, tu peux entrer ?
native_language_example: I’m in my office; can you come in?

additional_notes: "Mon" is the possessive adjective for "my" used with a singular masculine noun ("chien" is masculine). It can also be used before some feminine nouns that start with a vowel sound (e.g., "mon amie").
target_language_example: Mon chien adore jouer au parc.
native_language_example: My dog loves playing at the park.

additional_notes: An affectionate way to address someone you love (partner, spouse, sometimes a child). It agrees with the person you’re talking to: to a man/boy you say « mon chéri »; to a woman/girl you usually say « ma chérie » (or « mon chérie » before a vowel sound, e.g., « mon chérie, Anna »). Often used like “dear” in English: « Voilà, mon chéri. »
target_language_example: Viens ici, mon chéri, j’ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: Come here, my darling, I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Literally means “my heart” (mon + cœur). Used both literally for the physical heart (e.g., talking about health: « Mon cœur bat… ») and figuratively as an affectionate way to address someone, similar to “my dear / sweetheart” (« Au revoir, mon cœur. »).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, mon cœur, je suis là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, sweetheart, I’m here.

additional_notes: Literally “my child.” Often used as a term of address (vocative) when speaking to a child (or sometimes to someone younger) to sound caring, comforting, or firm: « Concentre-toi, mon enfant. » It can also refer to one’s child in general (« Mon enfant est curieux… »). In « Elle porte mon enfant », it means “she is carrying my child” (pregnant with my baby).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, mon enfant, je suis là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, my child, I’m here.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to refer to your male child. It is made from mon ("my") + fils ("son").
target_language_example: Mon fils habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My son lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: A possessive noun phrase for the speaker's male sibling. mon means 'my' before a singular masculine noun, and frère means 'brother'.
target_language_example: Mon frère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My brother lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: "Mon" means "my" (used before a masculine singular noun). "Mari" means "husband." In French you also say "mon mari" even if the speaker is a woman.
target_language_example: Mon mari rentre tard ce soir.
native_language_example: My husband is coming home late tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say your name (your family name or full name, depending on context). Often appears in questions like « Quel est votre/ton nom ? » (“What is your name?”). « mon » is the masculine singular possessive adjective (used with masculine nouns like « nom »).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas donner mon nom.
native_language_example: I don't want to give my name.

additional_notes: Very informal/friendly way to address someone (like “buddy” or “mate”), or to talk about your friend. Literally “my buddy.” Usually refers to a male friend; you may also hear "ma pote" for a female friend (more common in casual speech: "une pote" / "une copine").
target_language_example: T'inquiète, mon pote, je suis là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, buddy, I’m here.

additional_notes: A basic family expression for talking about your father. Mon is the possessive form used with the masculine singular noun père.
target_language_example: Mon père travaille à la maison le vendredi.
native_language_example: My father works from home on Fridays.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father with a job, nationality/origin, a characteristic, etc. After "est" you can use: a profession (often without an article): "Mon père est médecin."; an adjective: "Mon père est occupé."; or a noun phrase with an article: "Mon père est un gros fumeur." For origin, you often add "de/du/de la/des": "Mon père est du Donegal."
target_language_example: Mon père est très gentil.
native_language_example: My father is very kind.

additional_notes: This is just the noun "monde" (world) + the verb "est" (is). Very common in statements like "Ce monde est..." (This world is...). In sentences like "dans le monde" (in the world), you can get "dans le monde est..." meaning "in the world, ... is" (often used when talking about the most common/biggest/etc.).
target_language_example: Le monde est grand, mais on peut se sentir seul.
native_language_example: The world is big, but you can feel lonely.

additional_notes: Used with negation to emphasize that something is absent/unknown/impossible, often implying “not in the slightest.” Commonly appears as “ne … même pas” (formal) or without “ne” in speech (“j’sais même pas…”). It can also be used on its own as a short answer: « Même pas ! » = “Not even!”
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai même pas vu.
native_language_example: I didn’t even see him/her.

additional_notes: Contraction of ne + ai. It appears with je to form je n'ai..., the negative of j'ai (“I have”). It is usually completed by another negative word such as pas, plus, or rien: je n'ai pas..., je n'ai plus..., je n'ai rien....
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: I don't have time.

additional_notes: Contraction of "ne" + "en" used in negatives. "En" replaces something introduced by "de" (or a quantity) and often means “of it/of them” or “any (of it/them)” in English. Common patterns: "n'en ... pas" (don’t have any / don’t want any), "n'en ... plus" (can’t take it anymore / no more), "n'en ... jamais" (never any / never about it), "n'en ... rien" (nothing of it), "n'en" can also refer back to a whole idea/topic: "Vous n'en avez jamais parlé" = “You never talked about it.”
target_language_example: Je n'en ai plus.
native_language_example: I don't have any left.

additional_notes: A tag question added to the end of a statement (or sometimes used alone) to seek confirmation or agreement. Often used like English “isn’t it?” / “right?” / “okay?”. Can follow both formal “vous” and informal “tu” sentences.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, n'est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: We’re meeting again at 6 p.m., right?

meaning: not any / no / none (negation pattern: ne ... aucun)
additional_notes: Used to express the absence of any person/thing. In standard French, **ne** comes before the verb and **aucun/aucune** comes after the verb (often before a noun): *Je n’ai aucun + nom.* **Aucun** agrees in gender/number with the noun: **aucun** (masc.), **aucune** (fem.). In informal speech, **ne** is often dropped (*J’ai aucun…*), but this entry reflects the standard form.
target_language_example: Je ne vois aucun problème.
native_language_example: I don’t see any problem.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean 'to never do' something, often after verbs like regretter, craindre, or essayer. With a conjugated verb, French usually uses ne ... jamais around the verb: Je ne vais jamais là-bas.
target_language_example: J'essaie de ne jamais oublier mes clés.
native_language_example: I try to never forget my keys.

additional_notes: Usually used as the discontinuous restriction pattern « ne ... que », meaning 'only' rather than a true negation. In normal sentences, other words usually come between ne and que, so the exact contiguous string « ne que » is most often seen when the expression is being cited or discussed. Ne typically goes before the conjugated verb, and que goes before the word or phrase being limited: « Je n'ai que cinq euros » = 'I only have five euros.' In informal spoken French, the ne is often dropped.
target_language_example: La tournure « ne que » signifie « seulement » en français.
native_language_example: The expression "ne que" means "only" in French.
