meaning: to be located; to be found
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone or something is: se trouver quelque part = to be / be found somewhere. With a noun object, it can also mean to find or get something for oneself, as in se trouver un travail or se trouver un appartement. In the location sense, it is usually not translated literally as 'to find oneself'.
target_language_example: Mon livre doit se trouver quelque part dans la chambre.
native_language_example: My book must be somewhere in the room.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression, not certainty. Pattern: [subject] + semble être + noun/adjective/past participle. Common with impersonal subjects: « ça semble être… », « il semble être… ». With « me/te/lui… »: « Il me semble être… » = “He seems to me to be… / He strikes me as…”.
target_language_example: Ce plan semble être le meilleur pour l’instant.
native_language_example: This plan seems to be the best for now.

additional_notes: "Ses" is the plural possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (also "its"). It’s used before a plural noun (here, "parents"). The owner is understood from context (e.g., "elle" → her; "il" → his).
target_language_example: Elle va dîner chez ses parents ce soir.
native_language_example: She’s going to have dinner at her parents’ place tonight.

additional_notes: Used with "si" + a subject pronoun to introduce an indirect yes/no question ("ask if/whether..."). Here "elle" = "she".
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas si elle vient ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't know if she’s coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or hypothesis with je (“I”). Very common at the start of conditional clauses: si je peux... (“if I can...”), si je savais... (“if I knew...”); in polite expressions, si je peux me permettre means “if I may.”
target_language_example: Si je finis tôt, je t'appelle.
native_language_example: If I finish early, I'll call you.

additional_notes: Introduces a condition. In everyday French, on very often means 'we' instead of nous. In general statements, it can also mean 'you', 'one', or 'people'. With the imperfect, as in si on changeait..., it often makes a suggestion: 'what if we...?' or 'how about...?'
target_language_example: Si on part tôt, on évitera les embouteillages.
native_language_example: If we leave early, we'll avoid the traffic jams.

additional_notes: Used to give someone a choice or soften a suggestion/offer: «Tu peux venir, si tu veux.» It can also sound like a challenge or condition when followed by an action: «Suis-moi si tu veux…» In «Si tu veux, oui.», it means “if you want (to), yes” = “sure, if you’d like.”
target_language_example: On peut en parler maintenant, si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can talk about it now, if you want.

additional_notes: Used to offer an option politely ("Je peux... si vous voulez" = "I can... if you’d like"), or to introduce a condition ("Si vous voulez y aller, allez-y" = "If you want to go, go"). In speech it can also soften what you say, like “so to speak / as you will,” but for beginners it’s usually just “if you want/if you’d like.”
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver à 18h, si vous voulez.
native_language_example: We can meet at 6 p.m., if you'd like.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with an impersonal subject (“that/it”). Very common in polite phrases like “si ça ne t’embête pas” (if you don’t mind) and “si ça t’intéresse” (if you’re interested). Usually followed by a verb: “si ça arrive…”, “si ça vaut le coup…”.
target_language_example: On peut partir plus tôt, si ça te va.
native_language_example: We can leave earlier, if that works for you.

additional_notes: "son" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the friend; French doesn’t mark the owner’s gender here. "ami" is masculine; for a female friend you usually say "son amie" (pronounced the same as "son ami"). Also note: "son" is used (instead of "sa") before a feminine noun that starts with a vowel or silent h (e.g., "son amie") to make pronunciation easier. In context, "son ami" can mean a male friend or her boyfriend.
target_language_example: Je suis allé au cinéma avec son ami.
native_language_example: I went to the movie theater with his/her friend.

additional_notes: Means “his/her/their son,” depending on who “son” refers to (it’s an adjective of possession, not the owner’s gender). Used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a consonant (son fils, son frère). Compare: sa fille (“his/her/their daughter”).
target_language_example: Il a appelé son fils après l'école.
native_language_example: He called his son after school.

additional_notes: Means “someone’s name.” In French, the possessive adjective agrees with the noun that follows: because "nom" is masculine, you use "son" even if the owner is a woman ("son nom" can mean “her name”). For emphasis you can also say "à lui" (his) / "à elle" (hers): "son nom à elle".
target_language_example: Je connais son nom, mais j’ai oublié son prénom.
native_language_example: I know his/her last name, but I forgot his/her first name.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (son) to emphasize that something belongs specifically to that person/thing: “his/her/its own …”. The exact meaning of son depends on who owns it (his/her/its) and on the noun that follows (it’s about the noun’s gender/number, not the owner’s). Related forms: sa propre (feminine singular), ses propres (plural). Often used to stress individuality or something separate from others (e.g., son propre monde = his own world).
target_language_example: Elle veut avoir son propre appartement.
native_language_example: She wants to have her own apartment.

additional_notes: Means “his father” or “her father” depending on who “son” refers to. In French, the possessive adjective agrees with the noun possessed (père is masculine), so you say son père even when talking about a woman’s father (e.g., Son père à elle…).
target_language_example: Son père travaille à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: Her/His father works at the hospital.

additional_notes: Means “his/her work” (the owner depends on context). In French, “son” is used before a masculine singular noun like “travail” (even if the owner is a woman). It can refer to someone’s job or to their work/effort on a task or project. Note the common confusion: “travail” looks like English “travel” but means “work.”
target_language_example: Elle est fière de son travail.
native_language_example: She is proud of her work.

additional_notes: Used in formal/standard question formation with inversion: verb + subject pronoun ("sont" + "elles"). Refers to "they" for an all-female group or feminine plural nouns (e.g., "les lumières... sont-elles..."). Often used with a following adjective/noun ("Sont-elles grandes ?") or with a past participle in compound tenses ("Sont-elles venues ?"). In speech, many people also ask questions without inversion (e.g., "Elles sont grandes ?").
target_language_example: Sont-elles prêtes pour le départ ?
native_language_example: Are they ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used to form a question with inversion: verb + subject pronoun. Common in more formal written/spoken French (instead of simply using intonation: "Ils sont ici ?" or "Est-ce qu’ils sont ici ?"). Often follows a noun subject: "Tom et Marie sont-ils apparentés ?" (= Are Tom and Marie related?).
target_language_example: Sont-ils déjà arrivés ?
native_language_example: Have they arrived already?

additional_notes: "sont" is the 3rd-person plural of "être" (to be), used with plural subjects (they/you-plural, or multiple things/people). "très" means "very" and goes before the adjective or adverb it intensifies: "sont très + adjective" (e.g., "sont très nerveux").
target_language_example: Ces chaussures sont très confortables.
native_language_example: These shoes are very comfortable.

meaning: to come out of; to get out of
additional_notes: Used for leaving a place, container, situation, or state: sortir de la maison = come/go out of the house. With a direct object, it can mean taking someone or something out of something: sortir quelqu’un de l’eau = take someone out of the water. It is also used figuratively, as in sortir de sa retraite = come out of retirement.
target_language_example: Je dois sortir de ma retraite et retourner à la vie publique.
native_language_example: I have to come out of retirement and return to public life.

additional_notes: Question form of "je suis" ("I am") using inversion: verb + subject pronoun. Common in more formal/written French; in everyday speech, you often hear "Est-ce que je suis… ?" or "Je suis… ?". The adjective or noun usually follows: "Suis-je prêt(e) ?", "Suis-je un idiot ?". In the feminine, you may see agreement on the adjective (e.g., "Suis-je invitée ?").
target_language_example: Suis-je en retard ?
native_language_example: Am I late?

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) In the pattern **sur ce que / sur ce qui**, it means **“about/with regard to what…”**: *Je reviens sur ce que j’ai dit* (“I’m coming back to what I said”).
2) At the start of a sentence, **Sur ce, …** is a linking expression meaning **“thereupon / with that”**, to move the story along (“and then…”): *Sur ce, il se leva et sortit.*
target_language_example: Sur ce, on a décidé de partir.
native_language_example: With that, we decided to leave.

additional_notes: Means something is located/placed on top of the table (touching it). Often used with "il y a" (there is/are), or with verbs like "poser" (to put down/place) and "mettre" (to put).
target_language_example: Tu peux laisser tes clés sur la table ?
native_language_example: Can you leave your keys on the table?

additional_notes: A very common combination of sur + le, used before a masculine singular noun. Most often it means physical position ('on the'): sur le bureau. It can also mean 'about the' with topics: un livre sur le cinéma.
target_language_example: Le livre est sur le bureau.
native_language_example: The book is on the desk.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: sur + les. Most often means physical position/contact (“on the tables”), but can also be more abstract (“on the topic of…”). Note: unlike à + les → aux and de + les → des, sur + les does not contract.
target_language_example: Il y a des livres sur les tables.
native_language_example: There are books on the tables.

additional_notes: Used after the preposition « sur ». Very common with verbs like « savoir / dire / apprendre quelque chose sur lui » (“to know/say/learn something about him”). It can also be literal/physical: « pointer/viser quelque chose sur lui » (“to point/aim something at him”) or « rester sur lui » (“stay on him / keep your focus/aim on him”). « lui » is the stressed pronoun used after prepositions (not *sur il*).
target_language_example: Je ne sais rien sur lui.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about him.

additional_notes: Often used in the expression « prendre sur soi » (“to force yourself to stay calm / to put up with it”). With « moi », « je prends sur moi » means “I hold it in / I make an effort to cope,” not the literal “I take on me.”
target_language_example: J'ai pris sur moi pour ne rien dire.
native_language_example: I held it in so I wouldn’t say anything.

additional_notes: "sur" usually means "on" or "onto". "son" is a possessive meaning "his/its" (and sometimes "her" when the possessed noun is masculine or starts with a vowel sound: e.g., "sur son épaule" = "on her shoulder"). Used for physical position ("sur son dos"), movement ("monter sur son vélo"), or more abstract topics ("sceptique sur son succès" = "skeptical about his success", "quelque chose sur son identité" = "something about his identity").
target_language_example: Il a posé son sac sur son bureau.
native_language_example: He put his bag on his desk.

additional_notes: Common combination of the preposition "sur" + the masculine singular indefinite article "un". Often used for: (1) physical position: "sur un canapé" = "on a sofa"; (2) topic/subject: "sur un cas" = "about a case"; (3) working on something: "sur un projet" = "on a project"; (4) ratios/probability: "une chance sur un million" = "one chance in a million".
target_language_example: Je travaille sur un projet important en ce moment.
native_language_example: I’m working on an important project right now.

additional_notes: Used after être (or other verbs like être/rester) to express certainty. Common patterns: être sûr de + noun/pronoun (Je suis sûr de ça. / Il est sûr de lui = he’s confident), and être sûr de + infinitive (Je suis sûr de pouvoir venir = I’m sure I can come). With an infinitive, it can also mean someone is “certain to” do something (Il est sûr de gagner = He’s certain to win).
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de vouloir partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used in formal/written questions with subject–verb inversion: verb + “-t-” + “elle”. The “-t-” is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (e.g., "mène-t-elle", "dérange-t-elle", "loge-t-elle"). It can mean “does she...?”, “is she...?”, “will it...?”, etc., depending on the verb tense and context. More common in writing than in everyday speech (where people often use "Est-ce qu'elle... ?" or a statement with rising intonation).
target_language_example: Arrivera-t-elle à temps ?
native_language_example: Will she arrive on time?

additional_notes: Used in formal subject-verb inversion with il to ask a question or after certain expressions: parle-t-il, y a-t-il, pleuvra-t-il. The added -t- has no meaning; it is only there to make pronunciation smoother when the verb would otherwise run directly into il.
target_language_example: Parle-t-il français ?
native_language_example: Does he speak French?

meaning: told you / said to you (has told you)
additional_notes: Contraction of "te a dit" → "t’a dit": "t’" is the shortened form of "te" (to you) before a vowel, and "a dit" is the passé composé of "dire" (he/she/it has said/told). Common in questions about what someone told you (e.g., "Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a dit ?").
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a dit ?
native_language_example: What did he tell you?

additional_notes: Contraction of "te aime" → "t'aime" ("te" becomes "t'" before a vowel or silent h). Used with a subject: "je t'aime" = "I love you"; "il/elle t'aime" = "he/she loves you." Depending on context, "aimer" can mean "to love" (people) or "to like" (things/activities), but with a person it’s often "love."
target_language_example: Je t'aime beaucoup, mais je dois partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I love you a lot, but I have to leave now.

additional_notes: Very common informal/spoken contraction of "tu as". Used both literally for possession ("t'as un stylo ?" = "do you have a pen?") and as the auxiliary "avoir" in the past tense (passé composé): "t'as senti ?" = "did you smell/feel it?" In careful writing, use "tu as" instead.
target_language_example: T'as déjà mangé ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already?

additional_notes: Usually a contraction of te + en. Here en can mean things like 'about it', 'some/any', or 'from there', depending on the verb. In casual speech, t'en can also be a shortened tu en, as in t'en penses quoi ? Because of this, t'en does not have one fixed English translation by itself.
target_language_example: Je t'en parlerai demain.
native_language_example: I'll tell you about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: informal contraction of tu es, very common in speech and casual writing. It is used with tu, and in questions it often means "are you ...?"; in statements, "you're ...". Avoid it in formal writing.
target_language_example: T'es prêt pour le départ ?
native_language_example: Are you ready to leave?

additional_notes: "Ta" means "your" when talking to one person informally (tu) and the noun is feminine singular. "Femme" can mean "woman" in general, but in everyday conversation "ta femme" usually means "your wife" (your spouse).
target_language_example: Tu viens avec ta femme ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with your wife tonight?

additional_notes: A direct way to say "your mother" when speaking to one person you address as tu. For formal speech or when speaking to several people, French uses votre mère instead.
target_language_example: Ta mère arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: Your mother is arriving in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Literally "your life" (ta = your, informal singular). Common in set phrases like "gagner ta vie" = "to earn a living" and "toute ta vie" = "your whole life". In a threat, "prendre ta vie" means "to take your life" (to kill you).
target_language_example: Fais attention : ta vie pourrait en dépendre.
native_language_example: Be careful: your life could depend on it.

additional_notes: Used to express a large quantity. Use **tant de + noun** (often plural): *tant de fruits* = “so many fruits”. With an uncountable noun it’s “so much”: *tant de travail* = “so much work”. Often used in exclamations/questions: *Pourquoi tant de… ?* (“Why so much/so many…?”).
target_language_example: Il y a tant de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: There are so many things to do today.

additional_notes: Most often means “as long as” or “while,” setting a condition or time limit: « Pas tant que je serai là » = “Not while I’m here.” Common patterns: « tant que + verb » (as long as/while…), « tant que tu veux » (as much/for as long as you want). Also used in « tant que vous y êtes » = “while you’re at it.”
target_language_example: Tu peux rester ici tant que tu veux.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you want.

additional_notes: “Te” is the object pronoun meaning “you” (to you). “Demander” usually means “to ask” or “to request,” often followed by a noun (te demander un service = ask you a favor) or by “de” + infinitive (te demander de faire quelque chose = ask you to do something). It’s a common false friend: “demander” usually does NOT mean “to demand.”
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander de m’aider demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the object pronoun te before dire and means speaking to one person you address with tu. Very common after another verb: je peux te dire, je veux te dire, je vais te dire. For formal or plural 'you', use vous dire instead.
target_language_example: Je veux te dire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I want to tell you something.

additional_notes: "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (or sometimes "you" as the direct object) and it usually comes before the verb: « Je peux te donner de l'argent. » = “I can give you money.” With an infinitive, it also goes before the infinitive: « Je vais te donner… » / « Puis-je te donner… ». Note: « donner » looks like English “donate,” but it usually just means “to give” in general.
target_language_example: Je vais te donner mon numéro demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you my number tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is te + faire. te can mean either "yourself" (reflexive) or "you" (object), so the exact meaning depends on what follows: te faire des amis = "make friends," te faire de mal = "hurt yourself," te faire comprendre = "make yourself understood," te faire rire = "make you laugh," te faire examiner = "get yourself examined / have yourself examined."
target_language_example: Tu peux te faire aider si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can get help if you want.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive phrase made of object pronouns + verb: **te** = “to you” and **le** = “it” (masculine “it/that”). In French, these pronouns usually come **before** the verb: *Je dois te le dire* (“I have to tell you”). Common in phrases like **Combien de fois faut-il te le dire ?** = “How many times do I have to tell you?” If the “it” is feminine, it becomes **te la dire**.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas te le dire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I can’t tell you today.

additional_notes: Most often, this is the verb "montrer" (to show) with the indirect object pronoun "te" = "to you": "Je vais te montrer" = "I’m going to show you." In some contexts, especially with places like "ici" or "là", "te montrer" can mean "to show yourself / to appear" (often implying you shouldn’t be there): "Comment oses-tu te montrer ici ?" = "How dare you show your face here?"
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer où c'est.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you where it is.

additional_notes: Means “to talk/speak to you” when addressing one person with tu (informal singular). The object pronoun te comes before the verb: Je veux te parler (I want to talk to you). With a conjugated verb it’s also placed before the verb: Je te parle (I’m talking to you).
target_language_example: Je peux te parler un instant ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

additional_notes: From the verb plaire. French often uses this structure where the thing liked is the subject: ça te plaît ? literally means “does that please you?” = “do you like that?” Te means “to you” for one person informally.
target_language_example: Ce restaurant te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as tu. te is the direct object pronoun 'you', so te voir means 'to see you'. For formal speech or when talking to more than one person, French uses vous voir instead.
target_language_example: Je suis content de te voir.
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you.

meaning: to care about; to be attached to; to really want to; to insist on
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- tenir à + noun/pronoun = to care about / be attached to something: « Je tiens à mon livre. »
- tenir à + infinitive = to really want to do something: « Je tiens à vous aider. »
- tenir à ce que + subjunctive = to insist that: « Je tiens à ce que tu viennes. »
Often implies something is important to the speaker.
target_language_example: Je tiens à ce que tout le monde soit à l’heure.
native_language_example: I insist that everyone be on time.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "tes" with the plural noun "parents". "Tes" is used with "tu" (talking to one person informally). With "vous" (formal or plural), you say "vos parents".
target_language_example: Tu peux demander à tes parents s'ils viennent ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you ask your parents if they’re coming tonight?

additional_notes: Emphatic form of "toi" used to stress that *you personally* do something (often like “do it yourself”). Common in commands: "Dis-lui toi-même" (Tell him yourself), "Répare-le toi-même" (Fix it yourself), "Va voir toi-même" (Go see for yourself). Also used after prepositions: "sur toi-même" (on yourself).
target_language_example: Fais-le toi-même, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it yourself, please.

additional_notes: Used to include the person you’re talking to in something that applies to someone else. Often comes after the verb ("Il a peur, et toi aussi.") or at the end of the sentence ("Tu vas mourir toi aussi."), and can also be said alone as a reply ("Moi aussi." / "Toi aussi."). Uses the stressed pronoun "toi" for emphasis (not "tu"). In negatives, French usually uses "toi non plus" (“you neither”) instead of *toi aussi*.
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, et toi aussi.
native_language_example: I'm tired, and you are too.

additional_notes: Uses stressed (tonic) pronouns: toi (you) + moi (me). It often adds emphasis, like “just you and me” or “you and I, together.” It can be placed at the start of a sentence for focus (“Toi et moi, …”). When it’s the subject, the verb is plural: “Toi et moi, nous sommes…” or simply “Toi et moi sommes…” (both are common).
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on peut y arriver.
native_language_example: You and me, we can do it.

additional_notes: Means “your friend” when you’re talking to one person (singular “your”). "Ton" is the masculine singular possessive adjective used with "ami" (male friend, or mixed/unspecified gender in some contexts). For a female friend you usually say "ton amie" (still "ton" because "amie" starts with a vowel sound) or "ta copine" in some contexts (can also mean girlfriend).
target_language_example: Ton ami vient avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: Your friend is coming with us tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "ton" (your) with a singular masculine noun: "frère". "Ton" is also used before feminine singular nouns that start with a vowel or silent h (e.g., "ton amie").
target_language_example: Tu peux parler à ton frère après l'école.
native_language_example: You can talk to your brother after school.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address with "tu" (informal singular). For formal "you" (one person), use "votre nom"; for more than one person, use "vos noms". Often appears in questions like "C'est quoi ton nom ?" or "Et ton nom ?".
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas compris : c'est quoi ton nom ?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand: what’s your name?

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used when speaking to one person informally (tu). It refers directly to that person's father. For formal speech or when speaking to more than one person, use votre père.
target_language_example: J'ai parlé avec ton père hier.
native_language_example: I spoke with your father yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the past participle "été" (from "être") to say something has been true up to now: "j'ai toujours été…" (I have always been…), "il/elle a toujours été…" (he/she has always been…). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase.
target_language_example: On a toujours été proches, même après le déménagement.
native_language_example: We’ve always been close, even after the move.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun. It usually means 'all the' (tous les passagers = all the passengers), and in recurring time expressions it often means 'every' (tous les jours = every day). The feminine form is 'toutes les'.
target_language_example: Tous les enfants dorment déjà.
native_language_example: All the children are already asleep.

additional_notes: Usually means something happens daily. It is sometimes also used more loosely in expressions like ce n'est pas facile tous les jours, meaning something is not easy day after day or all the time.
target_language_example: Je vais à l'école à pied tous les jours.
native_language_example: I walk to school every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything you have or all the people/things in your group: Tous mes + plural noun. It combines "tous" (all) with "mes" (my, plural). Changes with gender/number: "tous mes" (masc. plural or mixed group), "toutes mes" (fem. plural only), and before a vowel sound you also see "tous mes" (e.g., "tous mes amis").
target_language_example: Tous mes amis sont déjà partis.
native_language_example: All my friends have already left.

additional_notes: Means “all of his/its” before a plural noun: tous ses + noun (e.g., tous ses doigts = all his fingers). Used with masculine plural nouns; with feminine plural nouns it’s toutes ses. With a singular noun you’d use tout son / toute sa.
target_language_example: Elle a perdu tous ses papiers.
native_language_example: She lost all her papers.

additional_notes: Used for being alone or doing something without help. It often translates as "alone," "by yourself," or "on your own." The form changes to match the person: toute seule, tout seuls, toutes seules.
target_language_example: Je peux le faire tout seul.
native_language_example: I can do it on my own.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all people in general. It often takes a singular verb in French: for example, tout le monde est là = everyone is here. Literally it is 'all the world,' but the usual meaning is 'everyone.'
target_language_example: Tout le monde connaît cette chanson.
native_language_example: Everyone knows this song.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. It can be neutral, or it can suggest annoyance depending on context.
target_language_example: Il est tout le temps en retard.
native_language_example: He's late all the time.

additional_notes: A very common, fully compositional phrase: tout = "everything" and est = "is." It is used to describe the overall state or quality of things, often followed by an adjective or fixed expression, as in tout est différent, tout est possible, or tout est en ordre.
target_language_example: Tout est prêt pour demain.
native_language_example: Everything is ready for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common reassuring phrase meaning there’s no problem. Often used as a statement (Tout va bien.) or as a check-in question (Tout va bien ? = “Are you okay?/Is everything okay?”). You can add “ici” (here) or “pour toi/vous” (for you) to be more specific.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Means something lasts or happens for the entire day (duration). It often answers “how long?”: Elle a dormi toute la journée. / Ça a pris toute la journée. Note the agreement: “journée” is feminine, so it’s “toute” (not “tout”). You can use it with past, present, future, or conditional to talk about the length of time.
target_language_example: On a marché toute la journée.
native_language_example: We walked all day.

additional_notes: Used to express duration over the entire night (from evening until morning). It often comes right after the verb: "danser toute la nuit", "attendre toute la nuit", "parler toute la nuit".
target_language_example: On a travaillé toute la nuit pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We worked all night to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun. It often means "all the," and in some general statements it can correspond to English "every." The masculine plural form is "tous les."
target_language_example: Toutes les fenêtres sont ouvertes.
native_language_example: All the windows are open.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something lasts) or an age. Common patterns: "depuis trois ans" = "for three years" (continuing up to now); "il y a trois ans" = "three years ago"; "ça fait trois ans que ..." = "it’s been three years since ..."; "quand j'avais trois ans" = "when I was three (years old)".
target_language_example: Ça fait trois ans que j’habite ici.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for three years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (durant trois jours = for three days) or a time delay (trois jours après = three days after). Can also be said alone (“Trois jours.”) as a short answer or for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je reste à Paris trois jours.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Paris for three days.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say there is more than needed or desirable: "trop de + nom". With uncountable nouns it’s usually "too much" (trop de travail = too much work); with plural countable nouns it’s usually "too many" (trop de pages = too many pages). Often follows a verb like "avoir" or "donner": "On a trop de...", "Il/Elle me donne trop de...".
target_language_example: Il y a trop de bruit ici, je n’arrive pas à travailler.
native_language_example: There’s too much noise here; I can’t manage to work.

additional_notes: A common pattern meaning to find or come up with something, followed by a masculine singular noun: trouver un travail, trouver un moyen. With a reflexive pronoun, as in se trouver un..., it can mean 'find yourself' or 'get yourself' something. The article changes with the noun: un, une, des.
target_language_example: Elle espère trouver un appartement bientôt.
native_language_example: She hopes to find an apartment soon.

additional_notes: Used to strongly compliment someone or something, or to describe pleasant conditions (especially the weather: « Il fait très beau » = “The weather is really nice”). Agreement: « beau » changes with gender/number (très belle, très beaux, très belles).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il fait très beau, alors on va se promener.
native_language_example: Today the weather is really nice, so we're going for a walk.

additional_notes: Most often used to say that someone does, knows, or understands something very well. It can also be said by itself to show agreement, acceptance, or approval, like "all right" or "very good."
target_language_example: Elle parle très bien français.
native_language_example: She speaks French very well.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise something or someone. It agrees with what it describes: très bon (masc.), très bonne (fem.), très bons / très bonnes (plural). Common with senses: Ça a très bon goût. (tastes really good), Ça sent très bon. (smells really good).
target_language_example: Ce gâteau est très bon, tu veux en goûter ?
native_language_example: This cake is really good—do you want to taste some?

additional_notes: "Tu aimes" uses the informal singular "tu" (to one person you know well). It can be a statement ("you like") or a question ("do you like?") depending on intonation or a question mark. Often followed by a noun ("tu aimes la glace") or an infinitive ("tu aimes faire de la randonnée").
target_language_example: Tu aimes ce film ?
native_language_example: Do you like this movie?

additional_notes: Formed from tu + as (from avoir). Used when speaking to one person informally. It can mean possession ('you have') and is also very often used as the auxiliary in the passé composé, as in tu as couru = 'you ran' / 'you have run'.
target_language_example: Tu as un stylo ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "dire" with "tu" (informal singular "you"). Often followed by a quoted word/sentence ("Tu as dit non.") or by "que" + a clause ("Tu as dit que tu pouvais.").
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu viendrais demain.
native_language_example: You said you would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with tu (2nd person singular): used to say what someone did/has done. In questions, it can be a statement word order with rising intonation: « Tu as fait bon voyage ? » = “Did you have a good trip?” Often followed by a noun (« tu as fait ton travail ») or an infinitive (« tu as fait quoi ? » is more informal).
target_language_example: Tu as fait tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you do your homework?

additional_notes: Literally "you have seen" (passé composé of voir), but in everyday English it’s usually "did you see…?" when asking a question about something someone noticed. Uses "tu" (informal "you"), so it’s used with friends, family, kids, etc. You can add an object or clause: "Tu as vu nos dessins ?" (Did you see our drawings?), "Tu as vu à quelle vitesse… ?" (Did you see how fast…?).
target_language_example: Tu as vu le film hier soir ?
native_language_example: Did you see the movie last night?

additional_notes: Past form of "tu es" (you are): "tu" + "as" (have) + past participle "été" (been). Used with adjectives and nouns ("tu as été courageuse", "tu as été mon ami") and in passive constructions ("tu as été embauchée" = you were hired). Agreement can appear in the feminine/passive (e.g., "courageuse", "embauchée").
target_language_example: Tu as été très patient avec moi.
native_language_example: You were very patient with me.

additional_notes: Singular informal/familiar form of avoir with tu. It can be a statement ("you have") or, with intonation, a yes/no question ("do you have?"). It also appears in common expressions like tu as mal ? = "are you in pain?".
target_language_example: Tu as une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or confirm that what they said is correct. Literally “you have reason.” You can also use it at the start of a sentence (“Tu as raison, …”) or on its own as a short reply.
target_language_example: Tu as raison, on devrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re right, we should leave now.

additional_notes: Used with tu, the informal singular 'you'. It introduces a masculine singular noun: tu as un + noun. With a feminine noun, use tu as une. In very informal speech and writing, it is often shortened to t'as un.
target_language_example: Tu as un message pour moi ?
native_language_example: Do you have a message for me?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone was supposed to do something in the past (often expressing regret, criticism, or that it was the better choice). It’s the past conditional of devoir (“to have to / must”). It’s followed by an infinitive: tu aurais dû + infinitive (e.g., tu aurais dû partir).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have warned me earlier.

additional_notes: Literally “you understand.” Used with *tu* (informal “you”), often as a question to check understanding: *Tu comprends ?* It can also work like a tag question to seek confirmation, similar to “you understand, right?” or “you know?” (*Tu comprends, n’est-ce pas ?*). Intonation (rising) often signals it’s a question.
target_language_example: Tu comprends ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I mean?

additional_notes: Uses connaître (not savoir): it’s about knowing a person/place/thing, being familiar with something, or recognizing a name. Often used in questions: «Tu connais Tom ?» = “Do you know Tom?” / «Tu connais ce nom ?» = “Do you recognize this name?” Because it uses «tu», it’s informal (to one person you address casually).
target_language_example: Tu connais ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

additional_notes: Literally “you believe that.” Used to ask someone what they think, often before another clause: « Tu crois que ça va marcher ? » = “Do you think it’ll work?” Very often it’s rhetorical and challenging/skeptical, like “You really think…?” or “You think I didn’t notice?” In more formal situations you’d use « vous croyez que… » or « tu penses que… ».
target_language_example: Tu crois que je vais te croire, moi ?
native_language_example: You think I’m going to believe you?

additional_notes: Used to give advice, recommendations, or a gentle warning. It is the conditional form of devoir with tu, so it often sounds softer and less direct than a command.
target_language_example: Tu devrais te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: You should rest a little.

additional_notes: "Tu dis" is the informal (tu) way to say "you say/you’re saying" (2nd person singular) with the verb "dire" (to say/tell). It’s often used in questions to react to what someone just said: "Qu’est-ce que tu dis ?" = "What are you saying?" You can add an object after it: "tu dis ça" (you say that), "tu dis la vérité" (you tell the truth).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu dis ? Je n’ai jamais dit ça !
native_language_example: What are you saying? I never said that!

additional_notes: Present-tense form of devoir with tu. It usually expresses obligation and is followed by an infinitive: tu dois partir = 'you have to leave.' In some contexts, it can also express a strong assumption, as in Tu dois avoir raison = 'you must be right.'
target_language_example: Tu dois finir tes devoirs avant le dîner.
native_language_example: You have to finish your homework before dinner.

additional_notes: "Tu dois" is the present tense of "devoir" (must/have to) + the infinitive "être" (to be). It can express a real obligation ("you have to be...") or a guess/deduction (often in a sympathetic way: "you must be tired"). The adjective that follows usually agrees with "tu" (e.g., with a woman: "tu dois être fatiguée").
target_language_example: Après une si longue journée, tu dois être épuisé.
native_language_example: After such a long day, you must be exhausted.

additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" or an amount/quantity, so "tu en as" often means "you have some (of it/them)" (e.g., "Tu en as un autre" = you have another one). It’s also the base of common expressions: "tu en as de la chance" (you’re lucky), "tu en as l’air" (you look like it), "tu en as marre" (are you fed up?), "tu en as peur" (are you afraid of it?). In questions, you’ll often see it with words like "encore" (still/more), "déjà" (already), "assez" (enough), or "pour longtemps" (for long).
target_language_example: Tu en as encore ?
native_language_example: Do you still have some (left)?

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être used with tu, the singular informal/familiar 'you'. It usually means 'you are', but before a past participle with certain verbs it also helps form the passé composé, where English often uses 'you have' or a simple past: tu es rentré = 'you came back / you have returned'.
target_language_example: Tu es très gentil.
native_language_example: You are very kind.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is present/has arrived: «Dieu merci, tu es là.» It can also be a check-in question meaning “Are you there?” (in person or on the phone): «Chérie, tu es là ?» With time words it means “you’ve been here/there (since…)”: «Ça fait combien de temps que tu es là ?» Note: «là» can mean “here” or “there” depending on context; English usually uses “here” when speaking to the person.
target_language_example: Enfin, tu es là ! Je t’attendais.
native_language_example: Finally, you’re here! I was waiting for you.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of faire with tu, the informal singular "you." Depending on context, it can also mean "you're doing" or "you're making." Faire is very common in many expressions, so the natural English translation often depends on the words that follow, as in faire confiance (trust), faire partie de (be part of), or faire une erreur (make a mistake).
target_language_example: Tu fais du bon travail.
native_language_example: You're doing good work.

additional_notes: Contraction of "tu" + "l'" + "as" (present of "avoir"). "l'" is the direct object pronoun "le" or "la" shortened before a vowel (it can mean “him/it” or “her/it,” depending on context). It’s typically followed by a past participle to form the passé composé: "tu l'as mis" (you put it / you put him), "tu l'as vu" (you saw him/it), etc. Word order in questions can be: "Où tu l'as mis ?" or "Tu l'as mis où ?"
target_language_example: Tu l'as trouvé où ?
native_language_example: Where did you find it?

additional_notes: Means “you know it/that” (the pronoun "le" refers to something already understood from context). Often used as a quick reminder or emphasis in the middle or at the end of a sentence: "Je ne peux pas, tu le sais" (“I can’t, you know that”). Can also introduce a shared fact, like “as you know”: "Comme tu le sais..." You’ll also hear it with a tag question: "Tu le sais, pas vrai ?" (“You know, right?”).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, tu le sais.
native_language_example: I’m tired, you know that.

meaning: you have (to me) / you did (to me)
additional_notes: Made of **tu** (informal “you”), **m’** (short for **me**, “me/to me”), and **as** (“have,” 2nd-person singular of **avoir**). It’s commonly used to form the **passé composé** before a past participle: **tu m’as appelé** = “you called me.” It can also appear in questions: **Tu m’as compris ?** = “Did you understand me?” Use **vous m’avez** instead when speaking formally or to more than one person.
target_language_example: Tu m'as appelé ?
native_language_example: Did you call me?

additional_notes: A very common combination of pronouns: tu is informal singular "you," and me means "me" or "to me." It is used when talking to one person you know well, and in French me usually comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Tu me fais rire.
native_language_example: You make me laugh.

additional_notes: Used with "faire" to mean someone causes you to do/feel/appear something. Very common pattern: "tu me fais + infinitive" (e.g., "tu me fais rire" = you make me laugh). In the example, it’s part of the expression "faire passer quelqu’un pour + noun" = "to make someone look like / to make someone out to be".
target_language_example: Tu me fais attendre depuis une heure.
native_language_example: You’ve been making me wait for an hour.

meaning: you don’t have / you haven’t / you didn’t (with avoir in the negative, 2nd-person singular)
additional_notes: Negative form of « tu as » (you have). It uses « ne … pas » around « avoir », with elision before a vowel: « tu n'as pas ». Common patterns: « tu n'as pas + noun » (you don’t have …) and « tu n'as pas + past participle » (you haven’t/didn’t …). In casual spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « t'as pas ».
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas dit ça.
native_language_example: You didn’t say that.

additional_notes: From parler with tu, used for one person you know well or speak to casually. It can mean either "you speak" or "you talk," depending on context. In questions, French often keeps the same word order: Tu parles aussi allemand ? = "Do you also speak German?" With de, it often means "you’re talking about" something: Tu parles du divorce ?
target_language_example: Tu parles trop vite.
native_language_example: You speak too fast.

additional_notes: "Tu penses" is the informal singular (tu) form of "penser" (to think). It can be a statement ("you think") or, with question intonation/"?", a question ("do you think?"). Common patterns: "penser à" + noun/thing = to think about (Dis-moi à quoi tu penses.); "penser que" + sentence = to think that (Tu penses que c'est vrai ?).
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'on a le temps ?
native_language_example: Do you think we have time?

additional_notes: Uses informal singular tu, so it is used when speaking to one person you know well, a child, or someone your age in a casual context. It can express ability, permission, or possibility. Peux is the tu form of pouvoir.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: You can come with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you or to you (often as a request). It’s built from "tu peux" (you can) + "me" (me), so it usually needs a verb after it: "Tu peux me + [verb] ?" You can make it a bit more polite by adding "s’il te plaît" or using "tu pourrais me...".
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire l’heure, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the time, please?

additional_notes: "Tu pourrais" is the conditional of "tu peux" (you can). It’s used to suggest a possibility ("you could become…"), to give advice/criticism ("you could do better"), or to make a polite request (often like "could you…?", sometimes with "s'il te plaît"). It uses "tu" (informal singular "you"), so it’s for friends, family, kids, etc.
target_language_example: Tu pourrais m'aider ce soir, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you help me tonight, please?

additional_notes: Present tense of « rester » used with « tu » (you, informal singular). Often followed by « avec + person » (“with”). It can sound like a firm statement (“you’re staying”) and may be used like an instruction depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu restes ici avec moi.
native_language_example: You stay here with me.

additional_notes: Literally means "you know". In speech, intonation decides whether it is a statement or a question ("do you know...?"), and it is also often used as a conversational filler like English "you know". Use it with tu; with vous, say "vous savez".
target_language_example: Tu sais, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: You know, I prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker assumes the listener already knows, often to remind them or emphasize a point. Uses "tu" (informal singular "you"), so it’s for friends, family, kids, etc. In speech it can also sound a bit like English "you know," before continuing.
target_language_example: Tu sais que je n’aime pas le café.
native_language_example: You know I don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Future tense of "être" (to be), used to talk about what someone will be like or what situation they’ll be in later. Often appears after time expressions like "quand" (when): "quand tu seras..." = "when you are / when you’ll be ...".
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tu seras prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject tu before a reflexive or pronominal verb. It often corresponds to English 'you' or 'yourself,' but English does not always translate it literally: tu te dépêches ? = 'are you hurrying?'. Before a vowel or silent h, te becomes t' (for example, tu t'appelles).
target_language_example: Tu te sens bien aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel well today?

additional_notes: Uses tu, the singular informal 'you'. On its own, tu vas can mean 'you are going'; followed by an infinitive, it commonly forms the near future: 'you're going to ...'.
target_language_example: Tu vas venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Are you going to come with us?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular subject tu, so it is for one person you know well. In everyday French, it is often used as a question without inversion: Tu veux...? = Do you want...? It also appears in expressions like tu veux dire...? meaning do you mean...?
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

additional_notes: From venir. Often used to ask if someone is coming along, joining an activity, or following someone. In a statement, it can mean 'you’re coming' or 'you come.' If it is followed by de + infinitive, it means 'you have just ...' (for example, tu viens de dire = 'you just said').
target_language_example: Tu viens avec nous au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Can be literal (seeing something with your eyes) or used to explain something or check that the other person understands, like "you see" or "see?". Because it uses tu, it is for one person you speak to informally.
target_language_example: Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you see what I mean?

additional_notes: Imperfect form of être with tu, used for describing a past state, condition, location, or ongoing situation. Tu is singular and informal, so this is used with one person you address as tu, not vous.
target_language_example: Tu étais très calme hier.
native_language_example: You were very calm yesterday.

additional_notes: Means an unplanned event where something goes wrong, often involving injury or damage. Common collocations: "un accident de voiture" (a car accident), "avoir un accident" (to have an accident), "c'est un accident" (it's an accident).
target_language_example: Il a eu un accident de voiture hier soir.
native_language_example: He had a car accident last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of one year (how long something lasts). Often used after a verb like partir/vivre/rester: « partir un an » = “to leave for a year.” In time expressions with « il y a » (ago): « il y a un an » = “a year ago.”
target_language_example: Je vais travailler à l'étranger un an.
native_language_example: I'm going to work abroad for a year.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to mean one more or a different one. It changes with gender and number: une autre, d'autres, les autres. It can also stand alone as a pronoun: Tu en veux un autre ? = Do you want another one?
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un autre livre.
native_language_example: I'm going to take another book.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form of bon used before a noun. Most often it simply means "a good," but with some nouns it can also suggest a respectable or fairly large amount, like "a solid" or "a good-sized." The feminine form is une bonne.
target_language_example: C'est un bon livre pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: It's a good book for learning French.

additional_notes: Means a gift/present you give to someone (for a birthday, to thank them, etc.). Common patterns: « offrir un cadeau à quelqu’un » (to give someone a gift), « faire un cadeau à quelqu’un » (to give someone a gift), « un cadeau pour + occasion/person » (a gift for…), « un cadeau de la part de + personne/groupe » (a gift from…).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un cadeau pour ma sœur.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my sister.

additional_notes: Most often means the drink (“I’d like a coffee”). Depending on context, it can also mean the place: in French, a typical neighborhood bar can be called “un café” (like “in a café / coffee shop”). With verbs like prendre/boire, it usually means the drink: « prendre un café » = “have a coffee.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve au café pour prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the café to have a coffee?

additional_notes: Means “a cat.” Note: “un” is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a”). The plural is “des chats” (“some cats”).
target_language_example: J'ai un chat noir à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a black cat at home.

additional_notes: Means “a dog.” “Un” is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Use “un chien” when talking about any dog in general or introducing a dog for the first time. Plural: “des chiens” (some dogs).
target_language_example: J'aimerais un chien, mais mon appartement est trop petit.
native_language_example: I'd like a dog, but my apartment is too small.

additional_notes: Basic meaning is 'a hit' or 'a blow'. Depending on context, it can also mean one attempt or one go (en un coup = 'in one go'). In the casual expression boire un coup, it means 'have a drink'.
target_language_example: On va boire un coup après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a drink after work?

additional_notes: Means a place/location in a general sense (a physical place). Often followed by an adjective to describe it: un endroit charmant (a charming place), un endroit sûr (a safe place).
target_language_example: On cherche un endroit calme pour parler.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a quiet place to talk.

additional_notes: Means a movie/film. Common with verbs like "voir un film" (to see a movie), "regarder un film" (to watch a movie), "aller voir un film" (to go see a movie), and "tourner un film" (to shoot/make a movie). Note: "Ce n'est qu'un film" means "It's just a movie" (not serious / not real).
target_language_example: On va regarder un film ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch a movie tonight.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a boy” (a male child/teen). In a restaurant context, « garçon ! » can mean “waiter!”, but it can sound rude; people often prefer « s’il vous plaît » or « excusez-moi » to get someone’s attention.
target_language_example: Il y a un garçon dans le parc.
native_language_example: There is a boy in the park.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form used before a noun. It often means big or large in physical size, but with abstract nouns it can mean great or strong (for example, un grand sens des responsabilités = a strong/great sense of responsibility). With people, it can mean tall or grown-up depending on context. The feminine form is une grande.
target_language_example: Nous avons un grand jardin.
native_language_example: We have a big garden.

additional_notes: Means “a big/large” (masculine singular) and is used before a masculine noun: un gros problème (a big problem), un gros risque (a big risk), un gros tube (a big tube). With people it can mean “a big guy” (size/build): un gros type. In some contexts it can mean “heavy” in the sense of doing/using a lot: un gros fumeur = a heavy smoker. Feminine: une grosse; plural: des gros / des grosses.
target_language_example: On a un gros problème : la voiture ne démarre pas.
native_language_example: We have a big problem: the car won’t start.

additional_notes: Basic way to say an adult male person. un is the masculine singular indefinite article ('a'/'an'). In some contexts, it can also emphasize number: 'one man.' homme begins with a silent h, so it behaves like a vowel-starting word.
target_language_example: J'ai vu un homme dans la rue.
native_language_example: I saw a man in the street.

additional_notes: Used to mean a very short time. Common with polite requests like « Excuse-moi un instant » (“Excuse me for a moment”). With « dans un instant », it means “in a moment / very soon.”
target_language_example: Attends un instant, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, please.

additional_notes: In these examples, it means at an unspecified time in the future: 'one day' or 'someday.' It can also literally mean 'one day' as a time unit depending on context.
target_language_example: Un jour, j'irai à Paris.
native_language_example: One day, I'll go to Paris.

additional_notes: A general word for a message (text, email, note, voicemail, etc.), depending on context. Common with verbs like envoyer un message (to send a message) and laisser un message (to leave a message). « Vous avez un message » means “You have a message.”
target_language_example: Je t'envoie un message ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sending you a message tonight.

additional_notes: Refers to a short period of time. Depending on the verb, English may translate it as "a moment," "for a moment," or "for a while": donne-nous un moment = "give us a moment," parler un moment = "talk for a moment."
target_language_example: Attends un moment, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, please.

additional_notes: Literally means “a word.” Very common in phrases like « J’ai un mot à te dire » (“I have something to tell you / I need a quick word with you”) or « Juste un mot » (“just a word,” often meaning “just one quick thing”). It can be used both for an actual word and for a short comment or message.
target_language_example: Tu as une minute ? J’ai un mot à te dire.
native_language_example: Do you have a minute? I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Means a medical doctor. Often used with verbs like "voir" (to see a doctor), "consulter" (to consult a doctor), or "demander à" (to ask a doctor): "Tu devrais voir un médecin." / "Tu devrais demander à un médecin."
target_language_example: Tu devrais voir tout de suite un médecin.
native_language_example: You should see a doctor right away.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something as new: un nouveau plan, un nouveau modèle. Before a vowel sound or silent h, French usually uses un nouvel instead (for example, un nouvel ami).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté un nouveau téléphone.
native_language_example: I bought a new phone.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un petit poisson = a small fish. It can describe physical size, a small amount, or make something sound more modest, friendly, or casual, as in un petit coup de main ?
target_language_example: Je voudrais un petit café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a small coffee, please.

additional_notes: Most often means “a plan” (an idea/strategy or set of steps): *J’ai un plan.* It can also mean “a map,” especially a city map or floor plan: *un plan de Paris*, *le plan de l’immeuble*. In *un plan de secours*, it means a backup plan (contingency plan).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'ai un plan de secours.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a backup plan.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a difficulty, malfunction, or situation that needs fixing. Common patterns: « Il y a un problème » (There’s a problem), « un problème avec + noun » (a problem with…), and « ce n’est pas un problème » (it’s not a problem / no problem).
target_language_example: Désolé, il y a un problème avec ma carte bancaire.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s a problem with my bank card.

additional_notes: Literally “a dream” (something you see while sleeping), and very commonly used figuratively for something ideal, unbelievable, or too good to be true (e.g., « C’est un rêve ! » = “It’s a dream!” / “I must be dreaming.”). In « un rêve qui se réalise », it means a dream/goal that comes true.
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à y croire : c’est un rêve !
native_language_example: I can’t believe it: it’s a dream!

additional_notes: Means there is exactly one (and not more). Often implies contrast with many others: “Il y a… mais un seul…”. It agrees with the noun: un seul (masc.), une seule (fem.). Common set phrases include “pas un seul…” (“not a single…”) and “un seul à la fois” (“only one at a time”). Can also stand alone when the noun is understood: “Un seul suffit.” (“One is enough.”).
target_language_example: Je n’en veux qu’un seul, merci.
native_language_example: I only want one, thanks.

additional_notes: Very common with **faire un tour** = “to go for a walk / go around / take a little trip (often not very long)”. **Un tour de manège** is “a ride (one round) on a carousel/ride”. **Un tour de la ville** means “a drive/walk around the city” (often sightseeing). With **prendre quelqu’un pour un tour**, it means “to pick someone up for a ride/trip (around)”.
target_language_example: On va faire un tour au parc ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk around the park?

additional_notes: Informal, very common way to refer to an object, idea, or matter when you don't name it precisely. Like English "thing" or "something." Depending on context, truc can also mean a tip or trick, but in these examples it means "thing/something."
target_language_example: J'ai un truc à te demander.
native_language_example: I have something to ask you.

additional_notes: Literally means 'a glass', but it often refers to a serving of a drink, especially in social situations. Common with verbs like offrir/payer un verre ('buy someone a drink') and servir un verre ('pour a drink').
target_language_example: On va prendre un verre après le travail.
native_language_example: We're going for a drink after work.

additional_notes: Used when "vrai" is placed before a noun to emphasize that someone/something really fits that category: "un vrai écrivain" = "a real writer". Often followed by a noun; on its own it can mean "a real/true one" when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Avec ce talent, tu es un vrai artiste.
native_language_example: With that talent, you’re a real artist.

additional_notes: Often used in common expressions: «jeter un œil (à/sur) …» = “to take a look (at) …” (quickly/briefly); «garder un œil sur …» = “to keep an eye on …” (watch/monitor); «lancer un œil noir» = “to give a dirty look / glare.”
target_language_example: Je vais jeter un œil à ton message.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a look at your message.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun, or on its own when the noun is understood from context. It can mean either an additional one or a different one, depending on the situation. Compare with masculine singular un autre.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une autre tasse de café.
native_language_example: I'd like another cup of coffee.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: une belle nuit (a beautiful night), une belle voix (a beautiful voice), une belle chanson (a beautiful song). It’s the feminine form of the adjective "beau"; for a masculine noun you usually use "un beau" (e.g., un beau jour).
target_language_example: C'est une belle journée pour se promener.
native_language_example: It's a beautiful day for a walk.

additional_notes: Means one beer (a single beer). Common when ordering or offering a drink. In invitations like « inviter quelqu’un à une bière », it means “to invite someone out for a beer.” Use « s'il te plaît » with someone you address as « tu », and « s'il vous plaît » with « vous » (polite or plural).
target_language_example: On prend une bière après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we have a beer after work?

additional_notes: Feminine form of the adjective "bon" (good). Used with feminine nouns: "une bonne personne" (a good person), "une bonne place" (a good seat), "une bonne mère" (a good mother). It usually comes before the noun in these common phrases. Note: "une bonne" can also mean "a maid/housekeeper" in some contexts, but in the examples here it’s just "a good" + a feminine noun.
target_language_example: Elle a trouvé une bonne idée.
native_language_example: She found a good idea.

additional_notes: Often used for an opportunity to do something or to succeed. Common patterns: "donner/laisser une chance (de + infinitive)" = "give/leave a chance (to do something)" (e.g., "Donne-moi une chance de le prouver"), and "avoir une chance ?" = "do I have a chance?" (possibility of success). Note: "la chance" can also mean "luck," but "une chance" is usually a specific chance/opportunity in context.
target_language_example: J’aimerais une chance de recommencer.
native_language_example: I’d like a chance to start over.

additional_notes: A very general way to refer to an object, idea, fact, or matter without naming it specifically. In natural English, it is often translated as 'something' depending on the context.
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: There's one thing I don't understand.

additional_notes: Used for something incorrect you did or said (a mistake) or a more general error (e.g., in a calculation). Common with: « faire une erreur » (to make a mistake).
target_language_example: J'ai fait une erreur dans ce calcul.
native_language_example: I made a mistake in this calculation.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase: une is the feminine singular form of "a/an." In some contexts, femme can also mean "wife," but une femme usually means "a woman."
target_language_example: J'ai vu une femme dans le jardin.
native_language_example: I saw a woman in the garden.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a single occasion. It can also appear in storytelling to mean something like 'once' or 'one day' (for example, Il était une fois... = 'Once upon a time...'). In the longer expression une fois que, it means 'once/when' followed by a clause.
target_language_example: Je suis allé à Paris une fois.
native_language_example: I went to Paris once.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: une grande + noun (e.g., une grande maison = a big house). Depending on context, "grande" can mean physical size (big) or importance/quality (great). Not usually used alone; it needs a noun after it.
target_language_example: C'est une grande décision.
native_language_example: It's a big decision.

additional_notes: Most often means “a story” (real or fictional): une histoire vraie = “a true story.” It can also mean “history” (especially in academic or broad contexts, e.g. l’histoire de France = “the history of France”). In everyday speech, une histoire can also mean “a situation/issue” (e.g. C’est une autre histoire. = “That’s another matter.”).
target_language_example: Il m’a raconté une histoire drôle.
native_language_example: He told me a funny story.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like « avoir » (to have) and « penser à » (to think of): « J’ai une idée. » = “I have an idea.” You’ll also see « une idée en tête » (“an idea in mind / in your head”). In « avoir une idée derrière la tête », it often suggests you have a plan or ulterior motive (something you’re not saying openly).
target_language_example: J’ai une idée : on peut partir plus tôt demain.
native_language_example: I have an idea: we can leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually means a written message you send/receive (often by mail). Also note: "une lettre" can mean "a letter" of the alphabet in other contexts (e.g., "la lettre A"), but in these examples it’s a message.
target_language_example: J'ai écrit une lettre à ma sœur.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my sister.

additional_notes: "Une maison" usually means a physical house/building (as opposed to an apartment). It can also mean "home" in a general sense depending on context. Common expansions: "une maison en ville" (a house in the city), "une maison de location" (a rental house), "une maison de deux chambres" (a two-bedroom house), "une maison avec un jardin" (a house with a garden).
target_language_example: On cherche une maison près de l'école.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a house near the school.

additional_notes: Literally means 'a minute.' It can refer to a short amount of time, or be used on its own to ask someone to wait briefly.
target_language_example: Attends une minute, j'arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I'm coming.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean “a new …” (e.g., une nouvelle vie, une nouvelle entreprise). Agreement: masculine is un nouveau (un nouveau travail), plural is de nouveaux / de nouvelles. Note: nouvelle can also be a noun meaning “a piece of news” or “a short story,” but in your examples it’s the feminine form of the adjective “new.”
target_language_example: Elle cherche une nouvelle maison.
native_language_example: She’s looking for a new house.

additional_notes: Literally “a small (feminine)” (une + petite). It’s usually followed by a feminine noun: « une petite île » = “a small island”, « une petite question » = “a quick/little question” (a polite way to introduce a short question). It can also be used without the noun when the context is clear (e.g., ordering a small size).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j’ai une petite question.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a quick question.

additional_notes: Means a photograph. Very common with verbs like prendre une photo (to take a photo) and avoir une photo (to have a photo). Note the article changes: une photo (a photo) vs la photo (the photo).
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre une photo de nous ?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of us?

additional_notes: Often used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say something will be quick: Donnez-moi une seconde. / Excusez-moi une seconde. You also hear it with expressions like Dans une seconde (“in a second”), Je n’en ai que pour une seconde (“it’ll only take a second”), and Pas une seconde (“not a second / not for a moment”).
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, j’arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Means a period of seven days. Common time phrases: "dans une semaine" = in a week (from now); "pendant/durant une semaine" or "pour une semaine" = for a week (duration); "en une semaine" = in a week (time needed to complete something).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans une semaine.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a week.

additional_notes: Means “a life” in general. Very common with adjectives (une vie stressante = a stressful life; une vie meilleure = a better life) and with verbs like mener/avoir/vivre (mener une vie tranquille = to lead a quiet life). In expressions like « Une vie est en jeu », it means someone’s life is at stake.
target_language_example: Il veut mener une vie plus simple.
native_language_example: He wants to lead a simpler life.

additional_notes: "Vieille" is the feminine form of "vieux" (= old). Most often it’s used before a feminine noun: "une vieille photo" (an old photo), "une vieille voiture" (an old car). Used on its own ("une vieille"), it usually means an old woman/old lady and can sound dismissive depending on context; "une vieille femme" is more neutral.
target_language_example: C'est une vieille maison, mais elle est solide.
native_language_example: It’s an old house, but it’s sturdy.

additional_notes: Means “a car.” It’s feminine, so you use une/la/ma voiture. In French, voiture usually refers to a regular passenger car; for “a vehicle” in general, you can also say un véhicule.
target_language_example: Il y avait une voiture dans l'allée.
native_language_example: There was a car in the driveway.

additional_notes: Usually either (1) the near future with il/elle/on: va + infinitive = 'is going to ...', or (2) a command: va + infinitive = 'go ...'. With faire, English may use either 'do' or 'make' depending on the context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on va faire demain ?
native_language_example: What are we going to do tomorrow?

additional_notes: Part of the near-future pattern aller + infinitive. Here va is the il/elle/on form of aller, and te means singular informal 'you'. In sentences like Il va te chercher or Ça va te plaire, te comes before the infinitive and means 'you' as the object of the next verb.
target_language_example: Ça va te faire rire.
native_language_example: It's going to make you laugh.

additional_notes: Near-future form: "aller" (here: "va" = he/she/it goes) + infinitive "être". Used to say something is expected to happen soon or is planned/likely. Changes with the subject: je vais être, tu vas être, il/elle/on va être, nous allons être, vous allez être, ils/elles vont être.
target_language_example: Demain, ça va être difficile.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be difficult.

additional_notes: With clothes, colors, or styles plus an indirect object pronoun (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur), it means something suits someone or looks good on them. With a person as the subject, it means someone is fine or doing well.
target_language_example: Cette chemise te va bien.
native_language_example: That shirt looks good on you.

meaning: to be better; to be preferable
additional_notes: Commonly used in the impersonal structure: « il vaut mieux + infinitive » = “it’s better to … / you’d better …”. You can also compare two things: « X vaut mieux que Y » = “X is better than Y / preferable to Y”. Note that the verb conjugates (il vaut, ça vaut, etc.), so you won’t always see the infinitive form « valoir ».
target_language_example: Il vaudrait mieux valoir mieux que d'abandonner.
native_language_example: It would be better to be better than to give up.

additional_notes: Used to urge or encourage someone to do something, often before another verb: Vas-y, réponds. Depending on tone, it can sound supportive, impatient, or challenging. This is the informal singular form; with vous, use allez-y.
target_language_example: Vas-y, essaie encore.
native_language_example: Go ahead, try again.

additional_notes: Means to accompany the speaker. Often used in questions or invitations: « Tu veux (bien) venir avec moi ? » = “Do you want to come with me?” You can switch pronouns depending on who you’re talking to: « venir avec moi » (me), « venir avec nous » (us). In a direct command you’ll often hear « Viens avec moi ! » (informal) or « Venez avec moi ! » (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu peux venir avec moi au magasin ?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to the store?

additional_notes: With a person, place, or thing after de, this expression shows origin, source, or cause. It can mean where someone is from, where something comes from, or what is causing something: Ça vient de moi = "it's because of me / it's coming from me." Note: venir de + infinitive is a different common pattern meaning "have just".
target_language_example: Ça doit venir de moi.
native_language_example: It must be coming from me.

additional_notes: Used for movement toward the speaker or the place being talked about as 'here'. It's a straightforward combination of venir + ici.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir ici une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward something masculine singular (le). Common in phrases like "vers le haut" (upwards) or "vers le Nord" (toward the North). For other genders/numbers: "vers la" (feminine), "vers les" (plural), "vers l’" (before a vowel). It can also be used for approximate time (e.g., "vers le soir" = around evening).
target_language_example: Tourne vers le pont, puis continue tout droit.
native_language_example: Turn toward the bridge, then keep going straight.

additional_notes: Common combination of vouloir + être. This exact form, veut être, is the present-tense third-person singular: it is used with il, elle, on, or a singular noun subject. It is often followed by an adjective, noun, profession, or role.
target_language_example: Mon fils veut être pilote.
native_language_example: My son wants to be a pilot.

additional_notes: Question form of tu veux, using inversion. It is used to ask whether someone wants something or wants to do something. It can sound a bit more formal, direct, or literary than everyday tu veux ... ?
target_language_example: Veux-tu venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us?

additional_notes: “Veux” is the “I want” form of vouloir. It’s followed by an infinitive: “je veux aller …” = “I want to go …”. Often used with a place (“je veux aller à Paris”) or with expressions like “aller mieux” (“to get better”): “je veux aller mieux” = “I want to feel better / get better.”
target_language_example: Je veux aller au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Literally “come here.” Can be used in two main ways: (1) as a statement about where you come/go regularly: « Je viens ici chaque jour. » (“I come here every day.”); (2) as an order/invitation: « Viens ici ! » (“Come here!”). It uses the verb venir (“to come”); « viens » is used with tu (informal singular).
target_language_example: Viens ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: Often used as a friendly invitation to get someone’s attention and show them something. In examples like « Allez, viens voir » or « Peter, viens voir ! », it’s the informal singular imperative (talking to one person you address as tu). It can also be the present tense « je viens voir… » meaning “I’m coming to see…” / “I’m here to see… (someone)”, especially when visiting a person (e.g., a doctor).
target_language_example: Viens voir, j’ai trouvé tes clés !
native_language_example: Come and see, I found your keys!

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) "venir de" + infinitive (here: "vient de" for "il/elle/on") expresses the recent past: something happened very recently. Example pattern: "Il vient de partir" = "He has just left".
2) "venir de" + noun/place indicates origin or source: "Elle vient de Russie" = "She comes from Russia"; "Ça vient de l'ambassade" = "It comes from the embassy".
You can usually tell which meaning is intended by what follows "de" (infinitive vs. noun/place).
target_language_example: Quelque chose vient de se passer.
native_language_example: Something just happened.

additional_notes: "vit" is the 3rd-person singular present of "vivre" (to live). "vit dans" is used with a place (real or figurative): "Il vit dans une maison" (a house), or "Elle vit dans ses souvenirs" (her memories).
target_language_example: Il vit dans un petit appartement à Paris.
native_language_example: He lives in a small apartment in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to talk about looking at something (often something you’re about to be shown).
