Common in phrases like "viens/venez voir ça" (come and see this/that), "attends/attendez de voir ça" (wait till you see this/that), and "aller voir ça" (go and have a look). "Ça" usually means "this/that" depending on context.
target_language_example: Viens voir ça, c’est incroyable !
native_language_example: Come check this out, it’s incredible!

additional_notes: Common spoken/informal negative form where "ne" is dropped: "je vois pas" = "je ne vois pas" (I don’t see). Used both for literal sight (not seeing something) and figurative meaning (not understanding / not noticing): "Tu vois pas ce qui se passe ?" = "Don’t you see what’s happening?"
target_language_example: Je vois pas pourquoi tu es en colère.
native_language_example: I don’t see (understand) why you’re angry.

additional_notes: "Vos" is the possessive adjective for "your" when speaking to one person formally (vous) or to multiple people (you all). It agrees with the noun: "vos" is used before a plural noun like "amis". Often used to talk politely about someone’s friends: "vos amis" = the friends of the person/people you’re addressing.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me présenter vos amis ?
native_language_example: Can you introduce me to your friends?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (vous) or to more than one person. Common in questions and requests for identification: "Quel est votre nom ?" / "C'est quoi votre nom ?". With "déjà", it means the speaker has forgotten and is asking again ("what’s your name again?").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quel est votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name, please?

additional_notes: Means “your father” when talking to one person politely (vous) or to more than one person. It can also be used when addressing someone directly about their father: « Embrassez votre père. »
target_language_example: Je vais appeler votre père pour le prévenir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call your father to let him know.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask a question with inversion (verb + -tu). It’s the conditional of « vouloir » (to want), often used to soften a request/offer. Common patterns: « Voudrais-tu + infinitive… ? » (Would you like to…?) and « Voudrais-tu + noun… ? » (Would you like a…?). A less formal word order is « Tu voudrais… ? ».
target_language_example: Voudrais-tu venir dîner chez nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come have dinner at our place tonight?

additional_notes: Very polite form of «vouloir» used to make offers, invitations, or requests. It’s the conditional + «vous» (formal/plural “you”), common in restaurants, customer service, and formal situations. Often followed by an infinitive for requests («Voudriez-vous fermer… ?» = “Would you close…?”) or by a noun for offers («Voudriez-vous du café ?» = “Would you like some coffee?”).
target_language_example: Voudriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Would you help me, please?

additional_notes: A polite or formal way to ask what someone wants or to offer something. It uses inversion (verb + subject pronoun), which is common in formal questions. "Vous" can refer to one person formally or to several people.
target_language_example: Voulez-vous venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come with us?

meaning: to be willing to; to kindly agree to (do something)
additional_notes: Used to express willingness or polite agreement. Common in requests: « Voulez-vous bien + infinitif ? » ≈ “Would you kindly + verb?” (polite, but can sound firm depending on tone). Also used to accept a request: « Je veux bien. » = “Sure / I’d be happy to.” Here the infinitive may be expressed or implied.
target_language_example: Merci de vouloir bien m'aider demain.
native_language_example: Thank you for being willing to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used to talk about the meaning of words, signs, actions, or situations. Although the words literally look like 'to want to say,' the common meaning is 'to mean.' Often appears in questions like Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ? ('What could that mean?').
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ?
native_language_example: What could that mean?

additional_notes: "Vous" is the polite/formal singular "you" or the plural "you"; it can refer to one person (formal) or to multiple people. "Vous aider" means "to help you" and is often used after another verb (e.g., "je veux", "je suis venu", "pouvons-nous") or in questions ("Pourquoi dois-je vous aider ?").
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider avec ça ?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

additional_notes: "Vous" is the formal "you" (singular) and also the plural "you" (talking to more than one person). "Vous aimez" can be a statement ("You like...") or a question ("Do you like...?")—in speech, the voice usually rises at the end for a yes/no question; in writing you’ll see a question mark. "Aimer" can mean "to like" or, in some contexts, "to love" (stronger), depending on what follows and the situation.
target_language_example: Vous aimez le café ou le thé ?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee or tea?

additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive to talk about the near future or a strong prediction: vous allez rater, vous allez faire, vous allez rire. Here, vous can mean either plural "you" or singular formal "you." On its own, vous allez can also literally mean "you are going/you go," but in these examples it is the common futur proche structure.
target_language_example: Vous allez comprendre bientôt.
native_language_example: You’re going to understand soon.

additional_notes: Used with vous, which can mean either one person in a formal way or more than one person. It can show possession/state ('you have'), and it is also very commonly used as an auxiliary in the passé composé: vous avez + past participle = 'you did / you have done' (for example, vous avez menti = 'you lied').
target_language_example: Vous avez une question ?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: Polite or plural way to say “you said” (passé composé of dire). Used to refer back to someone’s words: «J’ai réfléchi à ce que vous avez dit.» It can also be used in a question to ask someone to repeat/confirm: «Qu’est-ce que vous avez dit ?»
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez dit que le train partait à quelle heure ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time did you say the train was leaving?

additional_notes: Passé composé of « faire » with the subject « vous » (formal ‘you’ or plural ‘you’). Often followed by a direct object: « vous avez fait + nom » (you did/made + noun). In « Vous avez fait une bonne affaire », it means ‘you got a good deal’ (literally: ‘you made a good deal’).
target_language_example: Vous avez fait du bon travail.
native_language_example: You did good work.

additional_notes: Polite or plural way to ask if someone has seen/noticed something. Literally “you have seen” (passé composé of voir), but in everyday speech it often corresponds to English “did you see…?” or “have you seen…?” Used to draw attention to news, the weather, information, names on a list, etc.
target_language_example: Vous avez vu le nouveau message ?
native_language_example: Did you see the new message?

additional_notes: Present-tense form of avoir used with vous. It can mean either 'you have' when speaking to several people, or 'you have' in a formal/polite way to one person. It is also common in expressions like vous avez l'air de... ('you seem to...').
target_language_example: Vous avez une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it starts the past infinitive, with the object pronoun vous placed before avoir, as in vous avoir vu = "to have seen you." It is used for an action completed earlier, often after expressions like content de, regretter, penser, or se souvenir. vous means "you" (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je suis content de vous avoir vu.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have seen you.

additional_notes: From connaître (“to know / be familiar with”). Used with vous (formal singular “you” or plural “you”). Often followed by a person, place, or thing you’re familiar with: « Vous connaissez cet endroit ? » = “Do you know this place?” Also used reflexively as « vous vous connaissez » (“you know each other”). For information/facts, French often uses « vous savez » instead.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous connaissez le chemin pour aller à la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. "Vous" can mean either plural "you" or formal singular "you". It is usually followed by an infinitive verb: "vous devez partir" = "you must leave."
target_language_example: Vous devez attendre ici.
native_language_example: you must wait here.

additional_notes: Uses the verb devoir + infinitive (être). It can mean obligation (“you have to be…”) or a logical guess/deduction (“you must be…”). With vous, this can address one person formally or multiple people; the adjective that follows often agrees accordingly (fatigué/fatiguée/fatigués/fatiguées).
target_language_example: Vous devez être très occupé aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You must be very busy today.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, recommendations, or mild criticism. "Vous" can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you." It is usually followed by an infinitive verb: "vous devriez attendre" = "you should wait."
target_language_example: Vous devriez essayer ce restaurant.
native_language_example: You should try this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with vous meaning either 'you' (formal singular) or 'you' (plural). Often appears after another verb, as in je peux vous dire or je veux vous dire, with the object pronoun vous placed before dire.
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Most often appears in the full phrase "je vous en prie". It’s used (1) to politely insist or beg someone to do something: "Écoutez-moi, je vous en prie" = "Listen to me, please"; and (2) as a formal/polite reply to "merci" meaning "you’re welcome" / "not at all". Uses "vous" (formal or plural).
target_language_example: Entrez, je vous en prie.
native_language_example: Come in, please.

additional_notes: "Vous" is formal singular or plural "you." "l'" is the shortened form of "le" or "la" ("him/it" or "her/it") used before a vowel sound. Very often, "vous l'avez" is the start of the passé composé (past tense): "vous l'avez + past participle" → "you (did) ..." (e.g., "vous l'avez su" = "you found out/you knew"). Sometimes it can also mean "you have it" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous l'avez oublié ?
native_language_example: Did you forget it?

additional_notes: `vous` means either plural `you` or formal singular `you`, and `le` is a direct object pronoun meaning `it` or `him`. In French, `le` comes before the verb: `vous le savez` = `you know it`. `Le` can also refer to an idea or situation, and in some expressions it may be left untranslated in natural English, as in `comme vous le souhaitez` = `as you wish`.
target_language_example: Vous le voyez maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you see it now?

additional_notes: A pronoun pattern with vous as the subject ('you' formal singular or plural) and me as the object ('me' or 'to me'). In French, object pronouns usually come before the verb: vous me comprenez = 'you understand me', vous me dites = 'you tell me'.
target_language_example: Vous me connaissez ?
native_language_example: Do you know me?

additional_notes: Usually means talking to someone addressed as vous, which can be one person formally or several people. After verbs like pouvoir, vouloir, or devoir, the pronoun comes before the infinitive: je peux vous parler. In some plural/reflexive contexts, it can also mean 'talk to each other.'
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous parler après la réunion.
native_language_example: I'd like to talk to you after the meeting.

additional_notes: "Vous" is the polite singular or plural "you". "Vous parlez… ?" is used both for talking in general and for languages: "Vous parlez français/anglais ?" (= Do you speak French/English?). To say what someone is talking about, use "parler de" + noun/pronoun: "Vous parlez de moi ?" (= Are you talking about me?). You can also say "parler en" + language to emphasize the language being used: "Vous parlez en anglais ?" (= Are you speaking in English?).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous parlez français ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used with the verb plaire. French structures this as something pleasing someone: Cela vous plaît ? literally means “Does that please you?” but usually translates as “Do you like that?” Here vous is the formal singular or plural “you.”
target_language_example: Prenez ce qui vous plaît.
native_language_example: Take whatever you like.

additional_notes: Present tense of pouvoir with vous. It is used for plural 'you' or polite singular 'you', and can express ability, permission, or possibility depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez entrer maintenant.
native_language_example: You can come in now.

additional_notes: Formal or plural form of savoir. It can state that someone knows something, ask a question depending on intonation, or be used as a conversation opener like "you know, ...".
target_language_example: Vous savez où il habite ?
native_language_example: Do you know where he lives?

additional_notes: Future tense of être (“to be”). Used with vous = either formal singular “you” (to one person politely) or plural “you” (to several people). Often followed by an adjective or noun: Vous serez bien ici. / Vous serez payé.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, vous serez prêt à temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll be ready on time.

additional_notes: The object pronoun vous comes before voir. vous can mean one person formally or several people, so this can also mean 'to see you all.' Depending on context, it may imply visiting or meeting with someone.
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous voir demain.
native_language_example: I'd like to see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of vouloir with vous. It can mean plural "you want" or polite singular "you want." In questions, it often translates naturally as "do you want...?" and in offers or invitations it can sound like "would you like...?"
target_language_example: Vous voulez venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Used to start the passé composé with reflexive verbs for "vous" (plural "you" or formal "you"). Structure: "vous" + reflexive pronoun "vous" + "êtes" (être) + past participle: "Vous vous êtes levés" (You got up). With reflexive verbs, the past participle often agrees with "vous" (e.g., "Vous vous êtes rencontrés" for a mixed/masculine group; "rencontrées" for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Vous vous êtes trompés d'adresse ?
native_language_example: Did you get the address wrong?

additional_notes: Literally means “you see” (from voir). Often used to point something out or check understanding, like “You see (this)?” / “You know?” In speech it can also work as a short filler to explain something: « Vous voyez, c’est compliqué. »
target_language_example: Vous voyez ce panneau ? Il faut tourner à droite.
native_language_example: Do you see that sign? You have to turn right.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of être with vous (“you” formal singular or plural). Used for ongoing states, background descriptions, or habitual situations in the past (often with time phrases like hier, la semaine dernière, quand…).
target_language_example: Vous étiez très fatigué hier soir.
native_language_example: You were very tired last night.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être with vous. Vous can mean plural "you" or formal singular "you," so this can refer to more than one person or to one person politely.
target_language_example: Vous êtes en retard.
native_language_example: You are late.

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun «vous» + verb «être» to say what someone is (identity/role). «Vous» can be formal singular (polite “you”) or plural (“you all”). «Un» is masculine singular; for feminine use «vous êtes une…», and for plural use «vous êtes des…».
target_language_example: Vous êtes un excellent professeur.
native_language_example: You are an excellent teacher.

additional_notes: Spoken (and often written informally) version of « il y a quelques… » meaning “there are a few/some…”. Commonly followed by a plural noun: « y a quelques minutes », « y a quelques personnes ». In more formal writing, use « il y a quelques… ».
target_language_example: Y a quelques problèmes, mais ça va.
native_language_example: There are a few problems, but it’s okay.

additional_notes: y replaces a place or destination already mentioned, so y aller usually means "to go there." In some common expressions like il faut y aller or allez-y, it can mean "we have to go / get going" or "go ahead."
target_language_example: On va y aller demain matin.
native_language_example: We're going there tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Means being able to do something successfully (often after effort): «Tu peux y arriver» = “You can do it / You can make it.” The pronoun «y» refers back to a goal/task already mentioned (roughly “at it/there”), so it often translates as “do it” rather than “arrive there.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’re going to manage it / you’re going to make it.

additional_notes: Used in existential expressions, usually with impersonal il: il y a = 'there is/there are'. With other verbs, it gives meanings like 'there can be', 'there must be', or 'there will be' (for example, il peut y avoir, il doit y avoir, il va y avoir). It does not mean 'to have' in the normal possession sense. In informal speech, il is sometimes dropped: va y avoir....
target_language_example: Il va y avoir un problème si on part trop tard.
native_language_example: There will be a problem if we leave too late.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like donner, servir, or demander to mean “(something) to drink”: « Donne-moi à boire » = “Give me something to drink.” In « se laisser aller à boire », it means “to let oneself go and start drinking (often alcohol)”, i.e. drinking when you shouldn’t or drinking too much.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

additional_notes: Used for being on a vehicle (plane, train, boat, bus, etc.) or sometimes figuratively as “on the team/involved” (“Je suis heureux de vous avoir à bord.”). Common with verbs like “être/se trouver à bord” (to be on board), “monter à bord” (to board), and “prendre à bord” (to take on board/pick up).
target_language_example: Il n’y a personne à bord du bus.
native_language_example: There’s nobody on board the bus.

additional_notes: Used to give a cause/reason, usually with a noun/pronoun (e.g., à cause de la pluie, à cause de toi). Often implies a negative cause/blame (“because of you”), but it can also be neutral depending on context. Also used with a clause via “à cause du fait que …” (“because of the fact that …”).
target_language_example: Le train est en retard à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: The train is late because of the snow.

additional_notes: Most often used as « à côté de + noun/pronoun » = “next to/beside”: « Je suis assis à côté de Marie. » It can also be used alone to mean “nearby/next door” depending on context: « Il habite à côté. » As an exclamation (« À côté ! »), it means “Wrong!” / “Not even close!” Finally, « à côté de… » can mean “compared to…”: « À côté de toi, je suis débutant. »
target_language_example: Assieds-toi à côté de moi.
native_language_example: Sit next to me.

additional_notes: Used after another verb to express something that is to be said. Very common in the pattern "avoir + [something] + à dire" = "to have + [something] + to say" (often implying obligation or that you have something to say): "C'est tout ce que tu as à dire ?" / "J'ai un truc à dire." Also appears in set phrases like "avoir son mot à dire" = "to have a say" (to have the right to give your opinion).
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose à dire, mais je ne sais pas comment le dire.
native_language_example: I have something to say, but I don't know how to say it.

additional_notes: Used for directions and location. With movement/turning, it often means “to the right” (Tourne(z) à droite). With position, it can mean “on the right” (à droite de… = to the right of…). In the fixed expression « à droite et à gauche », it means “here and there / left and right,” not literally about direction.
target_language_example: Le café est juste à droite de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The café is right to the right of the bakery.

additional_notes: Usually comes after a noun: quelque chose à faire = "something to do," des choses à faire = "things to do." It can also imply something that still needs to be done or that someone has to do, as in ce qu'il avait à faire = "what he had to do."
target_language_example: J'ai encore quelques courses à faire.
native_language_example: I still have a few errands to do.

additional_notes: Used for location and directions: à gauche = on/to the left (often with verbs like être, se trouver, tourner). In the expression « à droite et à gauche », it means “here and there / left and right,” i.e., in various places or in an unsystematic way.
target_language_example: La banque est juste à gauche de la poste.
native_language_example: The bank is just to the left of the post office.

additional_notes: Usually just the preposition à + the feminine singular article la. Its exact meaning depends on the verb and context: often "to the," "at the," or sometimes "about the." Unlike à + le, it does not contract further (à + le = au, but à + la stays à la). In other contexts, à la can also mean "in the style of."
target_language_example: Nous allons à la gare maintenant.
native_language_example: We're going to the station now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être, aller, rester, venir, passer du temps to say someone is/was/goes/stays/comes at a party (fête = party/celebration). Often contrasts with "en fête" (= in a festive mood/celebrating).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la fête ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we meeting up at the party tonight?

additional_notes: "à" can mean either "at" (location) or "to" (destination), depending on the verb and context. Common with travel verbs like "aller / se rendre à la gare" (to go to the station), "arriver à la gare" (to arrive at the station), and with requests like "me déposer / me conduire à la gare" (drop me off / drive me to the station).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la gare à 8 heures.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the train station at 8 o'clock.

additional_notes: Often refers to food in a general way: apporter à manger = “bring something to eat.” Very common in the expression donner à manger à [quelqu’un/animal] = “to feed [someone/animal]” (literally “to give to eat”).
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose à manger ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

additional_notes: Literally means "to me." It's used after verbs and expressions like penser à moi = "think about me" or venir à moi = "come to me." With être, it often means possession: c'est à moi = "it's mine." After a noun, it can mean "of mine": un ami à moi = "a friend of mine."
target_language_example: Ce sac est à moi.
native_language_example: This bag is mine.

additional_notes: A very common, compositional combination of the preposition à + mon ('my' before a masculine singular noun). The exact English translation depends on context: direction ('to my apartment'), location or setting ('at my place'), speaking to someone ('to my lawyer'), and fixed expressions like à mon tour ('my turn') or à mon rythme ('at my pace').
target_language_example: Je vais à mon bureau maintenant.
native_language_example: I'm going to my office now.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun that belongs to “us” (our): à notre fête (to our party), à notre hôtel (to our hotel). It’s made of the preposition à (“to/at”) + notre (“our”). For feminine singular nouns, use à notre as well (à notre maison). For plural nouns, use à nos (à nos amis). In expressions like « à notre grand + noun » it means “to our great + noun” (often expressing a reaction): « À notre grand mécontentement… » = “To our great displeasure…”.
target_language_example: La route jusqu'à notre maison est fermée aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The road to our house is closed today.

additional_notes: Means something happens one more time, returns, or is restored to a previous state: "Tom est à nouveau ici" (Tom is here again), "être à nouveau amis" (to be friends again). Often interchangeable with "encore" for "again," but "à nouveau" can sound a bit more like "again / anew" (starting over, returning to a previous situation).
target_language_example: Peux-tu répéter à nouveau, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat again, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with great difficulty or in a very small amount: "Il sait à peine parler anglais" (he can barely speak English). It can also mean something happened very recently: "Je rentre à peine" (I’ve only just gotten back). Often placed right before the verb/infinitive it modifies ("à peine + verb/infinitive"), or after the auxiliary with a past participle ("a à peine mangé").
target_language_example: J’ai à peine eu le temps de répondre.
native_language_example: I barely had time to answer.

additional_notes: Usually used with the negation ne…personne to mean “to no one / to anybody” in a negative sentence: Elle ne parle à personne. With imperatives, the ne often drops in everyday speech (but is kept in formal writing): (Ne) dis ça à personne = “Don’t tell anyone.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien dit à personne.
native_language_example: I didn’t say anything to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say you go somewhere by walking (not by car/bus/bike, etc.). Often used with verbs like aller/venir/rentrer: «Je vais à pied», «On rentre à pied». You can contrast it with other transport: «à pied ou en voiture ?».
target_language_example: Le centre-ville est proche, on peut y aller à pied.
native_language_example: Downtown is close; we can go there on foot.

additional_notes: Most often used with "de": "à propos de" = "about / regarding" (a topic). Without "de", "À propos," is used like "By the way," to introduce a new (often related) point or question.
target_language_example: À propos, je voulais te demander quelque chose.
native_language_example: By the way, I wanted to ask you something.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about or asking about: "à propos de X" = "about/regarding X". It can also be used at the start of a sentence to shift topics (similar to "speaking of..."): "À propos de musique classique...". Often followed by a noun or by "ce que..." (what...).
target_language_example: À propos de ton voyage, tu pars quand ?
native_language_example: About your trip, when are you leaving?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the exact time something happens. It can be used in direct questions (À quelle heure pars-tu ?) and indirect questions after verbs like savoir, demander, or décider.
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence le film ?
native_language_example: What time does the movie start?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which person something is directed to, given to, belongs to, or involves. It commonly appears with verbs that take à, such as parler à, donner à, écrire à. In everyday English, it is often translated as 'who ... to?' rather than the more formal 'to whom'.
target_language_example: À qui as-tu envoyé le message ?
native_language_example: Who did you send the message to?

additional_notes: Used in direct and indirect questions after the preposition à, especially with verbs that require à, such as penser à, rêver à, ressembler à, and servir à. In English, it is often translated simply as "what." For people, use à qui instead.
target_language_example: À quoi sert ce bouton ?
native_language_example: What's this button for?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like « servir à rien » (to be useless / to be good for nothing): « Ça ne sert à rien. » You also see it in the insult « un bon à rien » (a good-for-nothing). « à rien du tout » makes it stronger: “absolutely nothing / nothing at all.”
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de crier.
native_language_example: There's no point in shouting.

additional_notes: Usually means 'to' or 'at' + his/her/its before a singular noun. The exact English preposition can change with the verb or expression. son agrees with the following noun, not with the owner, and it is also used before some feminine nouns starting with a vowel or mute h (for example, son explication). In fixed expressions, the whole phrase can be idiomatic, as in être à son compte = 'to be self-employed.'
target_language_example: Elle est retournée à son bureau après la réunion.
native_language_example: She went back to her desk after the meeting.

additional_notes: Means arriving or doing something by the expected/required time. With transportation, meetings, deadlines, etc.: « arriver à temps », « être à temps », « venir à temps ». Often contrasts with « en retard » (late).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à temps pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I arrived on time for the appointment.

additional_notes: Usually means "to you" and uses the stressed pronoun toi after à. It often appears after verbs and expressions like penser à toi (think about you), parler à toi (speak to you, often for emphasis), and à toi seul (to you alone). By itself, à toi can also mean "your turn" or "over to you." It also appears in set phrases like libre à toi (it's up to you) and gare à toi (watch out).
target_language_example: Maintenant, à toi de choisir.
native_language_example: Now it's your turn to choose.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: this is à + ton. ton means 'your' when talking to one person informally, usually before a singular masculine noun. The exact English preposition depends on context: parler à ton oncle = 'talk to your uncle', aller à ton cours = 'go to your class', à ton retour = 'when you return / at your return'. French also uses ton before some feminine nouns starting with a vowel sound, e.g. à ton amie.
target_language_example: J'ai parlé à ton frère hier soir.
native_language_example: I spoke to your brother last night.

additional_notes: A very informal goodbye, short for à tout à l’heure / à toute à l’heure. Use it when you expect to see the person again later the same day or very soon.
target_language_example: Bon, je file — à toute !
native_language_example: Alright, I'm heading out — see you in a bit!

additional_notes: A fragment made of à + votre, used before a noun. Votre means "your" for one person addressed formally or for more than one person. The exact translation depends on the noun and expression: for example à votre disposition = "at your disposal," à votre sujet / à votre propos = "about you," and à votre tour = "when it’s your turn."
target_language_example: Je reste à votre disposition si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: I remain at your disposal if you have any questions.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something occurring. Often used generally ("ça arrive" = "it happens") or with frequency words like "souvent" (often) or "tout le temps" (all the time). Note: although "arriver" can mean "to arrive," with an event/situation as the subject it usually means "to happen"—so don’t translate it as "it arrives" here.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça arrive.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it happens.

additional_notes: Used to make a logical guess or deduction (based on clues): “it must be… / it’s probably…”. Literally “that/it must be,” from the verb "devoir" (to have to / must). Often followed by a noun or an adjective: "Ça doit être elle" (It must be her), "Ça doit être bon" (It must be good).
target_language_example: Il n’y a personne à la maison : ça doit être fermé.
native_language_example: There’s nobody at home: it must be closed.

additional_notes: Very common in time expressions: ça fait + duration means 'it's been ...' (Ça fait deux ans = It's been two years), and ça fait + duration + que + verb means 'have/has been ...-ing' (Ça fait une heure que j'attends = I've been waiting for an hour). Outside of that, it can literally mean 'it/that makes or does,' especially when talking about an effect or a total. In X et Y, ça fait deux, it can mean the two don't go together.
target_language_example: Ça fait trois semaines que j'apprends le français.
native_language_example: I've been learning French for three weeks.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. Literally means “that works,” but it’s used both for something functioning (e.g., a phone, a plan) and to agree to a suggestion (“Ok, sounds good”). In negatives you’ll often hear informal "ça marche pas" (more formal: "ça ne marche pas").
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h ? — Ça marche !
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 6? — Sounds good!

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. It is the common pattern ça + me + verb: ça means “it/that,” and me means “me” or “to me” before the verb. English usually does not translate it word for word: ça me va = “that works for me,” and ça me rend heureux = “that makes me happy.” Ça is the everyday form of cela; before a vowel, me becomes m’.
target_language_example: Ça me fait rire.
native_language_example: That makes me laugh.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself: ça means 'it/that', and se usually belongs to the verb that follows. This pattern is common with pronominal verbs and passive-like meanings, as in ça se produit ('that happens'), ça se mange ? ('is that eaten?/can you eat that?'), and ça se tient ('that makes sense/holds up'). ça is the everyday form of cela.
target_language_example: Ça se fait souvent comme ça.
native_language_example: It's often done like that.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is enough or to tell someone to stop (often with an impatient or firm tone). It can also be a question ("Ça suffit ?") meaning "Is that enough?" or "Is that sufficient?"
target_language_example: Ça suffit, arrête de crier.
native_language_example: That's enough, stop shouting.

additional_notes: A very common everyday expression. As a question, it can mean "are you okay?" or simply "how are things?" depending on context and tone. It is also used as an answer: "Ça va." = "I'm fine / it's going okay."
target_language_example: Salut, ça va aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Hi, how's it going today?

additional_notes: Question form of être with inversion: êtes-vous ... ? It is a fairly formal or written way to ask a direct question. Vous can mean one person formally or more than one person. The hyphen is required. In everyday speech, learners will also often hear est-ce que vous êtes... or just vous êtes... ?
target_language_example: Êtes-vous libre demain ?
native_language_example: Are you free tomorrow?

meaning: not a standard standalone expression in French; it is usually encountered as part of the larger pattern ne ... être que, meaning 'to be only' or 'to be nothing but'
additional_notes: Taken by itself, être que is not a common fixed expression in standard French. If you are looking for the usual French construction meaning 'only', the relevant phrase is ne ... que; with être, this often appears as n'être que.
target_language_example: L'expression « être que » n'est pas idiomatique toute seule en français standard.
native_language_example: The expression 'être que' is not idiomatic on its own in standard French.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives after the expected/expected start time (work, school, an appointment, a train, etc.). Common with "pour ne pas" (in order not to) and with the near future using "aller" (e.g., "tu vas être en retard" = you’re going to be late).
target_language_example: Je suis parti tôt pour ne pas être en retard.
native_language_example: I left early so as not to be late.

meaning: be doing; be in the process of doing
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to emphasize that an action is happening right now or is in progress: être en train de + infinitive. It often corresponds to English 'to be ...-ing', though in many cases French simply uses the present tense without this expression.
target_language_example: Ce que je déteste, c’est être en train de manger quand le téléphone sonne.
native_language_example: What I hate is being in the middle of eating when the phone rings.
